item.title: The President's Report: Broken Promises Have Lasting Consequences
item.dc:creator: Greg Woodfill
item.content:encoded:
By Greg Woodfill

For True North Values to be taken seriously as anything other than a slogan or lip service, they must include honoring your written and verbal agreements, keeping your promises, and following the law. Examples of the opposite of True North Values would include wage theft or false advertising in job recruitment, both of which would destroy trust and render your words and commitments meaningless going forward.

On October 22, 2026, I issued a Union Bulletin explaining that the County had publicly advertised a $3,000 hiring bonus during multiple operator hiring recruitments after this contractual bonus provision expired on November 1, 2025.

On April 6th 2026, the County informed The Union that it had offered the bonuses in error. Management maintains that those who made the offers were not authorized to do so.

The bonus was payable in two installments: $1,000 upon graduation from training and $2,000 upon completion of probation. We understand that, among those hired or placed in training after November 1, 2025, only 53 members received the $1,000 payment. To our knowledge, none received the 2nd installment of $2,000 for completing probation.

Our Union lawyers firmly believe the County has a binding obligation to pay these hiring bonuses and that the law requires it to honor that obligation. Our Lawyers advised us that our Union does not have the authority to bargain an agreement that would result in any of these bonuses not being paid, since the County owes these new hires a binding obligation.

From day one, we have told the County that they must honor these commitments, and the Union could not and would not agree to the County not paying any of these promised bonuses.

The Union strongly disagrees with characterizing these bonuses as a "gift of public funds." These bonuses are part of the pay owed to our new colleagues.

We have waited since April 6th for the County to state unequivocally whether it would pay these promised bonuses. Yesterday we finally got that answer. The County notified the Union that on 10/23 it would send out 53 $1,000 collection letters. Shame on the County! King County should do the right thing and live up to its often-stated County Values, not treat them like disingenuous slogans. The Union is exploring all options going forward; stay tuned for more info.

Benefits Bargaining Update/Review

As of 10/26, benefits bargaining is still ongoing, but we could possibly reach a TA on our health benefits before you read this article. Depending on what's in the TA, our ATU International Constitution and General Laws may require a membership vote, which we haven't done for benefits up to now.

If we reach a benefits TA with the County that requires a membership vote, we will hold in-person and Zoom informational meetings with Q&A sessions, along with worksite tabling sessions. We will announce dates and times for all sessions that give members enough time, information, and opportunities to ask questions to allow an informed decision. As a democratic union, we will respect and carry out the membership's decision by ballot.

Contract Bargaining Update

We continue to meet regularly, making slow, incremental progress on less contentious issues before turning to bargaining, mediation, or arbitration on the major unresolved issues. Bargaining is open, so members can attend to observe and learn about our progress. I will also give verbal updates and answer questions at all Union meetings and whenever I find opportunities to gather a few members for updates. We will not publish contract updates that reveal our strategies or bottom lines to management.

Please don't believe or spread wild rumors that the Union has agreed to, or will agree to, major concessions. That's not true and could divide the Union at a time when unity matters.

If or when the County stalls, attempts to impasse negotiations, or bargains in bad faith, we will respond accordingly. Regardless of how it appears, we are not there yet for either, and we will not risk our union's credibility or integrity by falsely representing how bargaining is going for political expediency.

Happy Thanksgiving! November 26th

From the News Review, November 2026 (Vol. XLIX, No. 11), pages 1, 28. Open in the PDF · Original file on atu587.org

item.title: The 1st Vice President's Report: Pay and Discipline Issues on the Rise!
item.dc:creator: Cory Rigtrup
item.content:encoded:
By Cory Rigtrup

For all those that don't know, I am dyslexic. Prolonged periods of reading and writing exhaust me. That was part of the reason I did not submit a report last month. I really have no valid excuse.

September was a rocking month, followed by October which did not disappoint. The days were long and action packed with intimate member issues. I've watched through the years, the Vice-President duties focus increasingly on being the champion of individual members' issues, then from a leadership position to the masses. Right or wrong, that's where we are today.

Kitsap Transit

Kitsap has consumed large volumes of time. Pay and discipline issues have been off the charts.

Pay: In the beginning of year, Kitsap switched payroll providers to UGK. Goodbye to the days when members were able to view their payroll advice. The new system required an app that didn't work for the vast majority of members. At the same time, some internal processes changed that created issues when pretty much everyone couldn't tell if their pay was correct or not? Recently, we were able to get Kitsap to build a process so members can get a printed copy of their bi-weekly payroll. If you are a Kitsap member and would like a printed copy of your payroll, contact Kitsap payroll and make the request.

Discipline: Wow, Kitsap is burning. Year to date, we've had 11 vested Operators get terminated. This number includes our current Union's Kitsap Executive Board Officer. For perspective, that is 1000% more this year, than the comparable sized Rail Operation has terminated. Kitsap has been exceptionally ruthless to our Access operators. The struggles are real. It's hard not to notice a link from last year's retired Operation manager to the punitive tyranny of today's leadership. I want to give props to all our union reps who are fighting these injustices. We will fight all injustices and we will not rest!

Timbrook Arb

In September we rocked and rolled the Phil Timbrook arbitration. For two days, the full display of how isolated and deplorable the conditions can be for Operators working after midnight, was righteously presented to an independent party. I was watching the arbitrator's face as she viewed the video for the first time. Clearly, the obscene behaviors of the intoxicated rider left a mark.

A Pair of sixes: Timbrook's incident happened in the University district six weeks prior to Shawn Yim's murder. His employment was terminated 6 weeks after the murder.

During the arbitration, we present 19 comparables of other Operators, who at some point in their career, felt the need to touch an unruly passenger. These comparables all happened in the last five years. Only two resulted in termination of employment, that was until Shawn was murdered.

In Addition to Timbrook, the memberships have approved similar terminations for Kassie and Snyder. All three of these don't come close to the behaviors deemed irredeemable just three years ago.

Closing briefs for Timbrook were submitted just before Halloween. We expect a decision/award by year's end.

A friendly reminder to all, please, don't touch the passengers.

Medical

I wrote this article in mid-October. I suspect we've just reached an agreement on medical benefits for the next two years. If we haven't, I'm lost. I spend a lot of time asking questions and running angels through my head before speaking. Even then, sometimes the words don't come out right.

The medical benefit world has changed and so has the game of benefits bargaining. Next year's Washington state open medical market premiums are increasing by 22%. Our plans forecast are not that dyer, but the projected increase are far more than we have ever gotten, and our reserves won't cover the gap.

In 2013, medical benefits we also on the rise, not quite as bad as today, but it still sucked. At the time, we were part of bigger country-wide group, and the union's leadership decided to chart our own course. We choose arbitration. Long story short, we lost.

The arbitrator ruled that members had to pick up some of the rising medical costs. For those that recall a time when we did "Gold, Silver, Bronze" tiered benefits, that was part of the outcome. A lesser-known part decision was to establish a minimum dollar reserve. That minimum was set at 4- Million dollars, and if the number drops below that, we are required to negotiate concessions to keep reserve stable. Fast forward today. We started this year with over 16 million, updated in July to 10-million, and shrinking fast like a keg of beer at a frat party.

If an agreement is reached, it will require a vote. Be educated and draw your own conclusions. The federal government is projecting 15 million Americans will be losing their medical coverage next year due rising cost. Keep developing your critical thinking skills.

From the News Review, November 2026 (Vol. XLIX, No. 11), page 4. Open in the PDF · Original file on atu587.org

item.title: The Maintenance Vice President's Report
item.dc:creator: Jeff Stambaugh
item.content:encoded:
By Jeff Stambaugh

VP Maintenance Representations/Grievances/Arbitrations/Other News

I am happy to report that it appears someone with some authority in Metro read my article last month. I have seen several updated requests for change of hours that Metro has approved for exactly what the new language was designed for, Thank You.

We continue to be very busy with investigations, loudermills, grievances, and arbitrations. There are currently over 120 open grievances, with over 60 of them in maintenance.

We are currently working through a settlement on the wrecker outsourcing, more to come on that.

We held two days of arbitration on October 19-20 for the Meagher seniority grievance. We have scheduled a third day in late November to finish testimony, so far this has been very interesting, more to come on that as well.

We have had several questions regarding how contract negotiations are going. Rumor is that we have given the farm away. We have not. We will have a TA to vote on when we have a contract offer that The Union feels is worthy of bringing to the membership for a vote.

Toys for Tots

The Union will again be coordinating the Annual Toy drive. Keep an eye out at your location for boxes to fill. Pick up at the bases will be roughly December 2nd, late donations will accepted at The Union office through December 4th.

Membership Census

In the month of September, we received 60 new active members, 35 active members were deducted, for a net gain of 25 active members over last month's total is 5,024. Our total active membership is now 5,049, an all-time high for Local 587! A year ago, our active membership was 4,736 for a net gain of 313 in the last 12 months. Three years ago, our active membership was 4,157 for a net gain of 892 members in the last 3 years. Our Retiree Membership is now 851, up 28 from last month.

item.title: The Recording Secretary's Report: Rec Sec World
item.dc:creator: Latrelle Gibson
item.content:encoded:
By Latrelle Gibson

Picks

Pick Season has ended! I can report most picks went without an issue, except for Bus and Rail operator picks. The bus operator pick was the busiest I've ever seen in almost 6-yrs of me working at the Union table during operator picks. What made it busy was……we had 12, yes, TWELVE pages of no-shows during the Full-time operator pick. I cannot stress enough how important it is to be at your own pick, and if this is not possible, or if life is acting a fool, utilize the absentee option we have in place so you CAN be contacted to pick over the phone.

Another issue is during the last week of pick; there's a lot of folks who think their classmate(s) can pick for them without the person indicating this on an absentee. I continually had to explain that it's not that I don't believe the individual, I just cannot go off the word of the person who is saying they're a proxy, and that the person they intend on picking for needed to verify this on an absentee. Another issue was with folks in the same class picking for their absent classmates. The problem with this as I explained to all of them is, someone will now have to forfeit their 20-mins of preview, and that's not fair to either party. In circumstances such as this, I will instruct the person to use their 20-min of preview to pick for themselves, and I also remind them that if they want to help their classmate, tell them the Union will assist them with their pick. And if they're helping someone that's not their classmate, to allow at least 1-hour of pick time between them. To ensure everyone receives their 20-min of preview, I will start looking for their absent classmate, then once they have picked, they are free to help their classmate.

Then there was the Rail Operator issue. What a mess this was. So, apparently, Rail had less work than their workforce. This wasn't realized until the last day, then they added day and night board spots to the bottom of their respective boards. This affected about 4 operators, all who picked the end of the 2nd to last day. They were given board spots in their proper seniority order since the board spots management created during the pick were illegal positions as these positions being added at the 2nd to last day of pick circumvented the seniority of those picking the bottom of their respective boards.

The Streetcar Operator and VM/Track and Row pick went very well. This time, I requested to move the VM/Track and Row 1-hour prior to the Streetcar operator pick, that way I'd have time to conduct the VM/Trac and Row pick and be able to fully conduct the Streetcar Operator pick. This worked great! Rail Service Quality, and LCC picks went well, there was a little confusion with a non-certified seniority list that was sent to them vs the actual certified list, this was cleared up. Streetcar O&M Supervisor pick went well, as did the 1st Line pick.

Chief Shop Steward/Shop Steward Stuff

The Chief Shop Steward Nominations have concluded. Those who didn't run unopposed, the results are posted on the Union Website, posted on the Union Bulletin Boards at the worksites, and placed in this News Review. Nominations to be placed on the revised Shop Steward have also concluded. If you didn't get a chance to nominate for Shop Steward, you will have a chance during the Spring pick to nominate again.

Shop Steward Nominations for Solid Ground have concluded. At some point, we will want to table to try to get more folks at Solid Ground to nominate for Shop Steward, as Shop Stewards are definitely needed there! Clallam Transit Shop Steward Nominations will be open in December. A bulletin will be sent this month with this announcement. If there is to be a vote, this will be announced in December. And Jefferson Transits Shop Steward Nominations will open in January. I want to thank all of you for your willingness to serve as a Shop Steward! Your hard work, dedication, and willingness to help your coworkers are invaluable! Thank you all!

Lastly, take a look at changes to the voluntary benefits that I've placed in this News Review. BBS will be here to sign everyone up for the new voluntary benefits towards the end of the month into December. Be sure to mark your calendars!

In solidarity!

From the News Review, November 2026 (Vol. XLIX, No. 11), page 7. Open in the PDF · Original file on atu587.org

item.title: Metro's New Zonar Inspection System Raises Safety and Accountability Questions
item.dc:creator: Tzur Wilfand, #20149 East Base
item.content:encoded:
By Tzur Wilfand, #20149 East Base

On Sunday, September 20, 2026, I attended King County Metro's Zonar training. The electronic inspection system may improve documentation, but the training left me with serious questions about employee safety, inspection time, road relief and operator responsibility.

Under the new procedure, operators use a tablet to perform inspections, scan inspection points, report defects and photograph damage. Metro's own Zonar training material warns operators to "BE AWARE OF MOVEMENT IN THE YARD."

That warning deserves attention because operators may have to walk around a coach while using the tablet. To photograph damage high on a bus, an operator could need to move 30 to 50 feet away to obtain a clear picture potentially placing the employee in or near an active traffic lane while buses are moving through the yard.

Does Zonar Conflict with Metro's Existing Safety Message?

Metro has long recognized the danger of electronic-device distraction in a bus yard. Metro's The Manual, Section 10.06, identifies PED use while walking in the base yard as a hazard and prohibits employees from walking while using a personal electronic device.

Zonar is an agency-issued device, not necessarily a "personal" device covered by that prohibition. But the safety hazard is similar: an employee looking at a screen may have less attention available for a moving 40- or 60-foot bus.

That raises a basic question: If looking at an electronic device while walking through the yard is considered dangerous, how will Metro safely require operators to walk around buses while using Zonar?

Metro should consider a designated inspection area separated from normal bus traffic, where operators can safely inspect and photograph their coaches without standing in an active traffic lane.

Where Is the Additional Inspection Time?

Zonar also adds steps. Operators must access the tablet, log in, complete the electronic inspection, document defects, take photographs when necessary and submit the report.

Will Metro provide sufficient paid time to complete the entire process safely? What happens when Wi-Fi is unavailable, the tablet freezes or an operator cannot log in? Metro's Zonar instructions tell operators to contact the Transit Control Center if the tablet fails. But the policy should also explain whether operators receive additional time and whether a technology-related late departure can result in discipline.

What About Road-Relief Operators?

An even bigger question involves operators who take over buses already in service. Under current practice, road-relief operators are not required to complete the same full Zonar inspection.

Federal regulations make the underlying safety responsibility important. 49 CFR §396.13 says that before driving, a driver must be satisfied that the vehicle is in safe operating condition and, when applicable, review the previous vehicle inspection report. The regulation expressly allows required reports to be maintained electronically.

49 CFR §392.7 also says a commercial motor vehicle cannot be driven unless the driver is satisfied that specified safety equipment, including brakes, steering, lights, tires, mirrors, wheels and emergency equipment is in good working order. FMCSA guidance likewise describes a pre-trip inspection as occurring before operation so the driver can be satisfied the vehicle is safe.

These regulations do not automatically mean that every road-relief operator must perform a complete new Zonar inspection. But they raise an important question:

If Metro expects every driver to meet the federal pre-driving safety requirements, what inspection procedure and scheduled time are provided when a new operator takes over a bus during road relief?

Operators Need Clear Answers Before Implementation

There is also an accountability issue. If an operator completes Zonar and later damage is discovered, will that operator be held responsible for a defect or damage that was not reasonably visible during the inspection?

Before full implementation, Metro should issue a clear written policy answering these questions: Where can Zonar inspections be performed safely? How much paid time is provided? What happens when technology fails? What is required during road relief? And exactly where does an operator's responsibility begin and end?

Technology should make transit safer. It should not require operators to choose between watching a tablet, watching a moving bus, and watching the clock.

From the News Review, November 2026 (Vol. XLIX, No. 11), page 8. Open in the PDF · Original file on atu587.org

item.title: ATU Latino Caucus Brings Solidarity to the Big Easy
item.dc:creator: Michael Mackay, Executive Board Officer #1
item.content:encoded:
By Michael Mackay, Executive Board Officer #1

Transit workers from across the Amalgamated Transit Union came to New Orleans in September 2026 for the 35th Annual ATU International Latino Caucus Conference. Over several days at the Loews New Orleans Hotel, caucus members learned from one another, built power, and took on the challenges their families and coworkers face today.

International President John Costa opened the conference with a clear message: "We won't stand by while our members live in fear." He spoke about immigration raids near transit hubs and about members who are afraid to go to work because of where they were born, the color of their skin, or the language they speak at home. He tied that fear to money pressures many members already know too well: rising rent, grocery bills, health care costs, and automation advancing faster than paychecks.

"For our members, immigration fear and economic pressure are not two separate fights," Costa said. "They show up in the same household, sometimes on the same day."

Costa also highlighted the caucus's history of organizing and honored Executive Vice President Yvette Trujillo, the first woman and first Latina elected to that position. "Our answer to fear is organizing," he said. "Our answer to fear is each other."

Attendees heard from New Orleans Mayor Helena Moreno, the city's first Latina mayor, and ATU International staff led trainings on grievances and arbitrations that gave members practical skills to bring home to their locals.

Photo caption: From Left to Right, Luis Alzate, President, ATU Latino Caucus; Michael Mackay, President, ATU PRIDE Caucus; and Karima Howard, President, ATU Black Caucus

Latino Caucus President Luis Alzate provided a strong panel on non-domiciled CDLs and what the new restrictions mean for immigrant transit workers. He told me the idea for the session came from the ATU PRIDE Caucus conference earlier this year.

President Costa asked me to speak about Seattle's transit levy, which is on the ballot. I thanked ATU Local 587 President Greg Woodfill for securing the $75,000 our local contributed to the campaign. President Costa and the International Executive Board then doubled that amount. If voters pass the levy, it could add 100,000 service hours to Metro and create many more union jobs.

I thanked President Woodfill for making it possible for me to attend, along with the many people who have supported the ATU PRIDE Caucus. I also walked the room through what we've built together over the past four years.

For me, some of the most valuable moments came in conversations between sessions. I spoke with Raymond Jackson, President and Business Agent of ATU Local 689 in Washington, D.C., and the first-ever recipient of the Yvette Trujillo Award. Local 689 represents 16,888 members under 15 contracts. Raymond told me the local has spent millions of dollars fighting for its members' right to strike, and that it was a fight worth having.

I had a great conversation with Jim Bradley, Financial Secretary-Treasurer of the Boston Carmen's Union, ATU Local 589. He told me Boston wants us to beat $48.55 an hour, because if we go above it, they can use our contract as a comparable in their next round of bargaining. That's solidarity across locals: every raise we win helps lift transit workers across the country.

I also valued building a relationship with Karima Howard, President of the ATU International Black Caucus. She is a powerful voice for our members and a mentor to me.

The city carried its own union history. Members visited Parkway Bakery and Tavern, a New Orleans po'boy institution. The po'boy dates back to the 1929 streetcar strike, when local restaurants fed striking transit workers, members of the union that became today's ATU, and called them "poor boys."

The conference closed with a message for every Latino and Latina transit worker: you are not alone, and the ATU stands with you. ¡Sí se puede!

From the News Review, November 2026 (Vol. XLIX, No. 11), page 9. Open in the PDF · Original file on atu587.org

item.title: 35th Annual ATU International Latino Caucus Conference
item.dc:creator: Stephanie Binschus, ATU 587 Kitsap Transit Executive Board Representative and ATU International Latino Caucus Northwest Regional Representative
item.content:encoded:
By Stephanie Binschus, ATU 587 Kitsap Transit Executive Board Representative and ATU International Latino Caucus Northwest Regional Representative

My interactions with the ATU International Latino Caucus (ILC) began in 2025, when I was asked to help with their registration system for the 34th annual ATU ILC conference, held the weekend before the ATU tri-annual Convention. This task involved creating a website for the ATU ILC and managing their online system; they also allowed paper registrations, which I did not handle. As the conference concluded and the NW rep position was vacant, the current board asked me to step into it; I agreed, and they appointed me about a month after the convention. This has meant more work for me this past year, working with some of our fellow members of 587 to resurrect the SCLC (Seattle Chapter Latino Caucus) (as of writing this [October 14], we still have not received the written response to hold officer elections for the SCLC).

Enough background. Let's talk about the 35th Annual ATU ILC Conference.

This year's Conference was held in New Orleans, Louisiana, from September 16 to September 20, 2026. Each year brings its own challenges, and this year the biggest challenge for the Latino Caucus Officers was the enormous amount of support we had, which forced us to shut down registration early because we hit the capacity of the meeting space where we were holding the conference. We had over 300 participants, including attendees, guests, and vendors/sponsors. The ATU ILC executive board met most of the morning and afternoon of Thursday, September 16, to prepare for the mass check-in expected that evening.

We opened the conference with a local group of Black Masking-Indians (also known as Mardi Gras Indians) in traditional dress and many playing instruments.

During the conference, the NOLA Mayor joined us and gave a nice talk about the need for unions to hold our politicians accountable for keeping their promises by encouraging members to vote.

We had a panel discussion about immigration law and the effects of recent political changes, such as the revocation of non-domicile CDLs. The Q&A session was informative; several attendees shared additional important information beyond what the panel presented.

My favorite presentation at the conference was the one ATU International Staff gave on Grievances and Arbitrations. John Lyons and Rich Otzel, along with attendee participation, made the presentation entertaining when John or Rich took on the personas of the different types of people a Shop Steward (or Union Representative) might interact with and interview to help write a grievance.

The board renamed an award previously named after someone once thought to be a good union leader in the Latino community, but whose reputation was tarnished by actions that recently came to light, to the "Yvette Truillo Labor Leader Award," which was awarded to Raymond Jackson from Local 689.

After the awards, each of the other Caucuses (Black, Pride, and Women's) were recognized, and the solidarity pledge from each of the caucus representatives was inspiring.

The conference concluded Saturday evening with a Masquerade Party, featuring a live band, DJ, and dancing.

Here are the links to the ATU BLOG and more photos by Sarah Saez:

  • https://atu.org/media/blog/2026/the-2026-atu-latino-caucus-wrapped-today-in-new-orleans

item.title: Kitsap Transit LMRC
item.dc:creator: Stephanie Binschus (ATU 587 Kitsap Executive Board Representative), Justin Bollinger (Routed [Fixed Route] Chief Shop Steward), and Fenya Joy (Access [Paratransit] Chief Shop Steward)
item.content:encoded:
By Stephanie Binschus (ATU 587 Kitsap Executive Board Representative), Justin Bollinger (Routed [Fixed Route] Chief Shop Steward), and Fenya Joy (Access [Paratransit] Chief Shop Steward)

Those present on the Zoom session were:

  • ATU: President Greg Woodfill, Vice-President Cory Rigtrup, Executive Board Representative Stephanie Binschus, Access Chief Shop Steward Fenya Joy, and Routed Chief Shop Steward Justin Bollinger.
  • KT: Operations Director Michael Bozarth, Access Operations Manager Jeff Vinecort, and Routed Operations Manager Thomas Gilbert.

ATU presented the following agenda:

10/8/2026 – LMRC Agenda Items

New LMRC items

  • What happened to KT CISM?
  • South base interoffice mail pickup is not happening consistently
  • Dwell time (Access)
  • Excessive Discipline

Follow-up

  • Supervisor Availability/Visibility on the road
  • Unsafe Stops
    • Across from WinCo (Ostrich Bay Ave.)
    • Bremerton Fred Meyer
    • Warren and 14th
  • Emergency Codes for when the head sign says to call 911

These items were added during the meeting:

  • New Radio install update: Dispatchers are required to have both channels in their ears and are missing calls.
  • Safety of operators from heavy passengers with heavy mobility devices

Meeting discussion results

  • CISM (Critical Incident Stress Management) is currently inactive, and Michael said that he will coordinate with HR to reactivate.
  • South Base Mail Pickup: Mailboxes are not being emptied daily, causing missed meeting requests and scheduling errors. Michael said he will communicate with those responsible to ensure they collect the mail.
  • Dwell time for ADA paratransit is managed on a case-by-case basis; if operators feel that there is not enough dwell time, they need to submit a code 10 form so a reevaluation can be completed.
  • Discipline volume is a major point of contention, with the union reporting a perceived surge in punitive actions. The union highlighted eight disciplinary actions in two days and argued for a shift from punitive to corrective/rehabilitative procedures.
  • Reporting Fear: Operators are hesitant to fill out reports for fear that camera reviews will lead to disciplinary action.
  • Emergency Code: Michael says that it has been difficult to come to an agreement on a code word for dispatch to use over the radio.
  • Unsafe Stops: Stop improvements at Wheaton Way and Fred Meyer are blocked by property owners refusing to cooperate in allowing changes. Operators are encouraged to submit run committee suggestions or close call safety submissions every time they experience problems with stops (e.g., almost mirror clips, not being able to merge to make left turns, or passengers crossing in front of their bus).
  • Over 1000lb including wheelchair issue: A specific case involving a heavy wheelchair is causing vehicle damage and operator stress; a supervisor has been deployed to evaluate the passenger's weight against the 1,000-pound lift limit.
  • Supervisor Visibility: There are reports of insufficient "road sups" (supervisors) available, though management attributes this to the onboarding of new hires.
  • Dispatch Radio update: Updates are delayed due to vendor firewall issues, with completion expected in Q1 2027. Dispatchers are currently hearing both channels simultaneously, leading to missed communications and potentially unfair disciplinary actions.
  • Payroll Access: Some employees have not received memos or instructions on how to access digital pay stubs or how to receive hard copies.
  • ARC review: Michael: It was communicated that Fenya's Access to the ARC review files has been denied. Michael will follow up with the team regarding Fenya's lack of access to ARC review files.

item.title: Letter to the Editor: A "Break-Language Win" — But What Did We Give Up?
item.dc:creator: Andy Price, Bellevue Base Shop Steward
item.content:encoded:
By Andy Price, Bellevue Base Shop Steward

Dear Editor,

In the October News Review, President Greg Woodfill announced what he described as "A break-language win for ASM service on the G-Line."

He reported that operators would receive guaranteed breaks after every revenue trip, with a minimum of 12 minutes or 18% of scheduled trip time, whichever is greater.

That sounds encouraging. But after examining the actual Memorandum of Agreement (MOA), I have some serious questions about what we've gained, what we've given up, and why Metro wanted these changes.

And there's another question: Why couldn't I ask about this agreement during questions on the President's Report when the agreement was expressly discussed in his published report?

What the Agreement Actually Says

Our existing collective bargaining agreement, Section 15.3(I), requires guaranteed breaks and layovers to be printed on operators' run cards.

That's an important protection. It gives operators a written record against which their guaranteed rest periods can be checked.

The new G-Line MOA changes that arrangement for ASM operations. Instead of documenting guaranteed breaks on run cards in the existing manner, the agreement provides that they will be referenced in the Operations Manual.

Why remove an existing contractual documentation requirement without clearly explaining what equally enforceable protection replaces it?

At the October 3 membership meeting, Woodfill acknowledged that Metro approached the Union seeking changes to accommodate ASM operations. He explained that departure and break times under ASM are not fixed.

That explains Metro's desire for flexibility. It doesn't fully answer what operators receive in exchange for giving up an established documentation requirement.

And the agreement contains provisions deserving even closer scrutiny.

Operators arriving at an ASM terminal are required to immediately notify the on-duty supervisor when beginning a guaranteed 15-minute break.

Does that mean locating the supervisor? What happens if the supervisor is unavailable? Does the break begin upon arrival or only after notification?

The language doesn't clearly answer those questions.

But perhaps the most concerning provision states:

"In an extreme emergency, Metro may use discretion to ensure functional service for customers while maintaining at least one hour of break time per eight hours."

Read that carefully.

The agreement establishes guaranteed breaks after every revenue trip, yet also provides management with discretion during an undefined "extreme emergency."

Who determines what constitutes such an emergency? Can ordinary service disruptions qualify? Can individual guaranteed breaks be postponed or shortened?

And what exactly counts toward that one hour of break time? Does it include recovery time or only actual guaranteed rest periods during which operators are relieved of duty?

An aggregate hour of break time over eight hours is not necessarily equivalent to guaranteed rest following each revenue trip.

The agreement doesn't expressly grant unlimited management discretion. But it does establish an exception whose limits and application deserve explanation.

A guaranteed break should not become discretionary simply because management encounters operational difficulties.

Negotiating Changes During an Expired Contract

Our principal collective bargaining agreement expired October 31, 2025.

Yet this MOA expressly states that the parties intend to incorporate the new Section 15.3(W) into the successor agreement.

We're therefore negotiating changes to established rest-break provisions while our principal contract remains unresolved.

If this agreement represents a significant improvement, it should withstand careful questioning.

Why Couldn't I Ask During the President's Report?

At the October 3 membership meeting, Woodfill completed his oral report and opened the floor for questions.

I attempted to ask about the G-Line MOA, which he had expressly discussed in his officially published President's Report.

Recording Secretary Latrel Gibson intervened, asserting that the written President's Report and Woodfill's oral presentation were separate. Because Woodfill hadn't mentioned the MOA orally, I was told to wait until New Business.

I had the News Review in my hand and pointed to the heading "The President's Report."

I asked where our bylaws established that restriction.

No governing provision was identified.

My initial motion to proceed to New Business died for lack of a second. Eventually, I was permitted to ask both questions.

Woodfill offered explanations, but important questions concerning documentation and the relationship between existing and new contractual protections remained unanswered.

This Concerns Every Member

The President's Report has appeared prominently in the News Review for as long as I can remember. Frequently, the written report contains considerably more information than the President repeats orally.

Our membership also conducts business through several meetings during each monthly cycle. Oral presentations can vary, and another officer may preside when the President is absent.

Should members' opportunities to question the President's published report depend on what happens to be repeated aloud at the particular meeting they attend?

Article XI, Section 1 of Local 587's bylaws establishes Reports of Officers as part of the regular order of business and directs members to raise questions under the proper heading. Section 17 adopts Robert's Rules of Order for matters not otherwise covered.

I've found no provision stating that matters officially published in the President's Report are excluded from questions merely because the President didn't repeat them orally.

After the meeting, I asked Woodfill to identify the governing rule. I received no response identifying it.

I subsequently sought clarification through a formal appeal to the International. President Costa declined to consider the appeal on procedural grounds, noting that I eventually asked my questions under New Business.

But that doesn't resolve the central question.

May members question the President about matters expressly contained in his published President's Report when his report is opened for questions, even if those matters weren't repeated orally?

And returning to the G-Line agreement:

If this is a win for operators, why are existing documentation requirements being changed, why is supervisor notification being introduced, and why does the agreement give Metro emergency discretion over guaranteed breaks?

An agreement described as a victory should withstand questions about its actual language.

If Metro requested changes to established contractual protections, members deserve to know what changed, why it changed, and how their rights will be enforced.

And when the President publishes a report announcing those changes, members deserve a clear, consistent opportunity to ask questions about them.

ATU 587 reserves the right to edit or refuse all letters to the editor. All letters to the editor are the views of the authors and do not necessarily reflect the views of ATU 587. Letters are expected to be the sincere personal views of the authors as opposed to canned reproduced statements.

item.title: Bad Schedules Are the Greatest Safety Hazard. Help Us Prove It.
item.dc:creator: Chuck Lare #12497, ATU 587 Shop Steward
item.content:encoded:
By Chuck Lare #12497, ATU 587 Shop Steward

Every operator knows the feeling. Traffic backs up, the bus loads slowly, a wheelchair boards, and by the time you reach the outer terminal your recovery time is gone. Your break exists on paper, but the clock says go, "turn-and-burn." So you pull out and keep driving.

That is not a personal failing. It is a hazard built into the schedule.

The Hazard Chain

  1. Schedule design: recovery time is too short.
  2. Late running: congestion, passenger loads, incidents, and construction eat the buffer.
  3. Missed breaks: you arrive at the terminal with no time left, under pressure to leave.
  4. Fatigue builds: sustained attention and workload without recovery wear you down.
  5. Impaired judgment: reaction time, attention and decision-making suffer.
  6. Crash risk: collisions, pedestrian strikes and passenger injuries become more likely.

Metro Knows

Metro cannot claim surprise.

  • CBA Article 15.3.L requires Metro to review routes showing "a pattern of insufficient break time" after operators file OSFRs (Green Sheets).
  • The Transit Operator Manual tells operators to send DDU messages when taking guaranteed breaks, which acknowledges that breaks get missed.
  • The labor agreement created a joint Committee to Address Employee Fatigue. Fatigue is a system-level safety issue, not an individual comfort complaint.
  • FTA Safety Bulletin 26-01 put every transit agency on notice. It counted 133 fatigue-related safety events since 2014, 73 of them from 2022 to 2025.

The science is just as clear. NIOSH says fatigue slows reaction time, reduces concentration, and impairs judgment, and recommends brief rest breaks at least every two hours. FTA research describes transit driving as "active fatigue": dense traffic, a timed schedule, fares, and dispatch communication all at once. L&I policy recognizes that hurried restroom or food stops are not genuine rest, especially when the work demands constant vigilance.

The toll is also personal. A NIOSH-supported study of medical claims found depression in 16.2% of local passenger transit workers, the highest of 55 industries studied and about 55% above the 10.5% overall rate. Chronic time pressure, little recovery, and restricted restroom access wear on people. The fix is changing the work environment, not telling operators to cope better.

Why Your Evidence is Needed

Metro may say this is only a contract issue. It isn't. Washington's safety law (WISHA, RCW 49.17.060) requires every employer, Metro included, to provide a workplace free from recognized hazards likely to cause serious injury or death. That duty exists regardless of the CBA. L&I/DOSH has authority to investigate whether Metro's scheduling and dispatch practices create a recognized fatigue hazard, and to require correction.

But investigators and Metro's own schedulers respond to documentation, not stories. We need a record showing where, when, and how often the schedule fails.

What You Can Do Starting Your Next Shift

  • File an OSFR (Green Sheet) every time a run does not give you the guaranteed break. The CBA says Metro will review them. Make them.
  • Record the facts every time you arrive late at a terminal: date, route, block/run, terminal, scheduled and actual arrival, scheduled and actual departure, and minutes of break or layover lost.
  • Note the cause: congestion, event traffic, construction, passenger incident, dispatch instruction.
  • Note any pressure to leave early, and DDU messages tied to breaks.
  • Know your entitlement: under Article 15.3.J, less than 7 minutes of layover in the previous two hours entitles you to a 13-minute break. Take it, and document what happens.
  • Send copies to Chuck@lareassoc.com / text 206-465-1435 so patterns by route, run dates and time of day patterns of insufficient break time can be identified.

Please don't exaggerate or guess. Accurate, consistent records are the most powerful tool we have.

Where This Goes

With the evidence by route, run, date, and time(s): Metro per CBA Article 15.3.L is required to address routes that have a pattern of insufficient break time. If routes are not fixed, and there is sufficient material evidence that an L&I Worker Rights Complaint and a WISHA safety hazard complaint may be in order. These would request an onsite inspection of Metro's scheduling, dispatch and break-management practices, including run cards, AVI data, OSFRs and dispatch logs. If investigators confirm a recognized hazard, L&I can require abatement/corrective action.

Operators are asked to drive safely, on time, through the worst traffic in the region, without the recovery the schedule promises. A bad schedule is a safety hazard for you, your passengers and everyone on the road.

Document it. Report it. Send it: chuck@lareassoc.com / 206-465-1435.

item.title: October Operators' LMRC Meeting (October 1, 2026)
item.dc:creator: Lisa Nault #3647, Rachael Buchanan #21341, and Latonya Abernathy #22793; ATU 587 Bus Reps
item.content:encoded:
By Lisa Nault #3647, Rachael Buchanan #21341, and Latonya Abernathy #22793; ATU 587 Bus Reps

Labor Management Relations Committee — to discuss, approve and/or propose resolutions to issues or problems of Metro policies which affect the Union and which either party requests to be placed on the agenda, and issues or problems of contract administration other than formal grievances.

Attendees: Rachael Buchanan, Lisa Nault, Travis Silva, Michael Thornton, Amanda Thames, Collin Dunphy, Brian Eggen

Follow Up

Continuing Education Orca: It looks like the absent person from Metro, who was going to follow up is out sick. It is still being worked on and feedback is really appreciated. Metro understands that it should not replace the knowledge of knowing how to look up the turn-by-turn instructions in the Route Book. Its primary purpose will be for unplanned blockages, and the coordinators will be able to send a reroute to the DDU. Most of the major transit systems use this or a similar technology. Metro is still getting the bumps out and any feedback is appreciated. Operators can do reports in SSaM to report issues.

Accident Report SSaM Training: The Union notes that there is some continuing education being carried out, but we do not know what the curriculum is. A lot of time is being used by Shop Stewards assisting people completing SSaM Reports. We have a lot of people who don't want to use a computer, so changes don't really apply to them, but they need a lot of assistance on how to answer questions and how to navigate. Continuing education wouldn't help and at East Base, Stewards help quite a bit. Once in a while, a person from SSQA has been at the base to assist. Metro seeks answers on specific trip ups, and the Union notes that there is weird stuff that happens, and it isn't always consistent. Metro recently did a tabling committee to do with reports. Continuing education is always important. Hopefully we'll have an update next month.

Shakeup Hiccups: Immediately after pick ended, the training offices at South Base closed. This created hardships for Operators to turn in route qualifications. On the first day of shakeup with a large number of new Operators at Tukwila Base, training was closed and Operators had a lot of questions. The Window Dispatcher didn't know any answers because it was their first day at the base as well. To date, this Executive Board Officer has yet to see anyone in the Training Office at Tukwila Base. Metro will reach out to training to find out what the staffing levels are. Follow up next month.

Uniform jackets: The Union has finally seen one of the new safety jackets available at the Uniform Store and they do not have enough pockets and have no liner, or zipper to attach a liner. Winter is coming. Metro has an obligation to provide appropriate uniform items for Operators who are outside in inclement and cold weather. The Metro representative doesn't have any additional information. Metro would like to remove it from the LMRC and move it to the Uniform Committee. There was discussion on how to expand choices. If there is a pressing issue, you can reach out to the Uniform Committee lead.

ADA Zones: There is a new sticker on the bus zone flags. It says, "Limited Lift Space". What does it mean and what are we required to do? Metro representatives don't know, but will reach out to Training. Follow up next month.

Meeting adjourned at 9:24 a.m.

Have a topic you want brought up in the LMRC Meetings? Contact Lisa, Rachael, or LaTonya to submit your topics.

I will keep myself in good standing by paying all dues, fines and assessments required. I will work to promote the best interests of this Union and encourage my fellow workers to become members of the same. I will not take the place of any member of this organization, or any other union worker who may be on strike or locked out. I will not reveal any of the private business to anyone not entitled to know the same.

I will not engage in activity evidencing gross disloyalty nor in conduct otherwise unbecoming a member, and will not knowingly wrong a member or see one wronged if in my power to prevent it. I will not appeal to any legal authority in matters pertaining to this Union until I have exhausted all means of redress provided by its laws. I will be considerate of others in word and action and will never discriminate against a fellow worker on account of race, religion, color, creed, sex, sexual orientation, gender identity or expression, age, disability, citizenship, or national origin. I also promise to promote the cause of trade union principles and defend freedom of thought, whether expressed by tongue or pen, with all the power at my command.

I understand there is nothing in this obligation that will in any way interfere with my political and religious rights or that will be in any way inconsistent with my duties arising from any of the relations of life.

item.title: The President's Report: No Just Cause—No Peace!
item.dc:creator: Greg Woodfill
item.content:encoded:
By Greg Woodfill

Another month has brought more discipline and discharges without just cause at King County Metro and Kitsap Transit—and another unprecedented wave of cases heading to or piling up in arbitration.

About a year ago at King County Metro, and more recently at Kitsap Transit, something changed. Both agencies moved away from corrective discipline and returned to punitive measures. They now seem more focused on limiting liability than on supporting, rehabilitating, and strengthening the frontline workforce in which they have invested so heavily—and which is so costly to recruit, train, retain, and replace.

Ten to 30 years of public service delivering transit with a clean work record now seem to carry little weight when discipline is imposed for one bad day or a split-second questionable decision later dissected frame by frame, in slow motion, from a desk and with the full benefit of hindsight.

Grievance responses routinely say that years of service and a clean record were considered, but those statements read like boilerplate designed to create the appearance that just cause was applied.

Chiefs, superintendents, TLR, and OLR routinely pass responsibility to others and say their hands are tied. Management representatives who meet with us to discuss more progressive, corrective, and appropriate discipline now claim they lack authority to reach agreements—even though the Union and management have made such agreements for decades. The Union has made clear that it will fully litigate any discipline it believes was imposed without just cause.

The good news is that, in recent weeks, management has made several last-minute arbitration settlement offers and told the Union that upper management is reviewing the issue and process in hopes of improving it and breaking the arbitration logjam. Without meaningful change, that backlog will only worsen.

We hope to return soon to progressive, corrective discipline based on all seven tests of just cause: Fair Notice, Reasonable Rule, Proper Investigation, Fair Investigation, Substantial Proof, Equal Treatment, and Proportional Discipline. Until then, we will continue filing grievances and pursuing arbitrations to protect decades-long careers that Metro has discarded as casually as a used tissue. People's livelihoods and lives are at stake. This is not a game, a debate, or a challenge to win for its own sake.

Operator Shield/Partition Update

As of 9/20/26, 80% of Metro's Excelsior coaches have the new operator partition. Installation on the remaining fleets will begin soon, and Metro still expects the entire fleet to be completed by the end of next March, if not sooner.

Metro is working with bus manufacturers to create a glass panel that fills the gap between the new barrier and the windshield. A few prototypes have been installed for initial testing. Next, Metro will install them on several coaches at each base so operators can test them and provide feedback. VM is also addressing lock issues and testing solutions for doors that close too hard because of their weight.

For all safety and design concerns, it is critical to submit an SSaM—not a BO report. A BO report is more appropriate when a partition has a mechanical problem that needs repair, rather than a design concern.

A break-language win for ASM service on the G-Line

Beginning with the spring 2027 service change, Metro will implement ASM/Fallback operation. G-Line operators assigned to this ASM service will not have fixed break times on their run cards. Instead, they will receive guaranteed breaks or layovers after each revenue trip; these are breaks, not recovery time.

ASM G-Line operators will be guaranteed at least 12 minutes or 18% of their scheduled trip time—whichever is greater—after every trip. Shifts longer than eight hours will include either two 15-minute breaks or one 30-minute break, while shifts under eight hours will include one 15-minute break. Look for the newly negotiated MOA on G-Line ASM breaks on the website or the Union's Facebook page.

We've been here before.

No one wants to reach agreement on an expired contract more than the bargaining team negotiating it. The entire bargaining unit is counting on its elected officers to deliver a contract worthy of its members' sweat and sacrifice. None of that is lost on the bargaining team.

While each contract negotiation is different, historically the average KCM contract negotiations take around a year and a half over 60 bargaining sessions. If the current rate of movement in negotiations hold, we may well not get an agreement until around the end of the year. Regardless of what you've heard, no substantial loss or gain has yet been agreed to in contract or benefits bargaining. We're holding the line while fighting for the gains that the membership expects and has instructed us to do.

Lately there has been calls for the "Special Meetings at Contract Expiration" that our bylaws call for upon the expiration of our contract. I don't believe we've held one of those since the contract expired in November1990, 36 years ago. After that special meeting we still didn't reach an agreement until January 1992, fourteen months after the contract expired, with the help of arbitration.

Your contract bargaining team knows fully what the membership expects and demands. We will have some informational membership meetings when we either have meaningful progress or an impasse to report.

Informational meetings and "Still no contract buttons" don't settle contracts. Contracts this large and complex are settled by tedious and numerous bargaining sessions. If and when negotiations grind to a halt, reach impasse, or are being bargained for in bad faith, this Union will act. For now, we plow on with the tedious grind. Remaining unified and patient throughout our long and difficult KCM contract negotiations empowers your contract negotiators to hold the line and fight for what's rightfully yours. When we fight, we win!

With the new SSaM Access Anywhere QR code, you can now report safety and security incidents on mobile devices

(Notice printed with the President's Report on page 24.)

Dear colleagues,

The Safety, Security, and Quality Assurance (SSQA) team is excited to share an alternative way for employees to report security incidents through the Safety and Security Management (SSaM) system without having to use a computer.

The SSaM Access Anywhere QR code allows employees to access SSaM directly on their mobile device (e.g., cellphone) to report an incident, submit a near miss/close call, or share safety suggestions. This functionality was created based on feedback my team received to help improve accessibility and use of SSaM.

SSaM – Security Incident Mobile Update w/ QR Code. Use the QR Code to Report a Security Incident/Drug Use/Other Safety Reports:

  • Using your cell phone, open your Camera app
  • Point your phone's camera at the QR code
  • Follow your phone's prompt to open the link in a browser
  • Click that link and it should open your browser and take you to the SSaM login page

The QR code is on page 24 of the PDF.

item.title: The Maintenance Vice President's Report: Flexible Schedules for Family Care Needs, Carpool or Use of Transit?
item.dc:creator: Jeff Stambaugh
item.content:encoded:
By Jeff Stambaugh

Last month I reported on the Holiday ULP settlement. In that settlement we agreed to a language change in Art 17.3.E around request for change of hours. This change gives the Base Management Team (Superintendent/Chief) the ability to allow flexible schedules for family care needs, carpool or use of public transit.

I also reported on how Bus VM management was working on updating the form for a request of change of hours. Management presented The Union with a draft; a few edits were worked out and there is a new form now being used. That is where the good news ends. It seems that VM bus Senior leadership has decided that family care needs, carpool or use of public transit to not qualify as a hardship therefore, they are not willing to accommodate requests for change of hours. Two problems with that! First, the new language does not require a hardship for a request to be granted. Second, I thought King County encouraged its employees to use public transportation including carpools. I have seen several denials for a 15-minute change to either participate in carpool or use public transportation. Two of these denials were asking for 15 earlier start and quit time to be able to commute on the Sounder train.

Metros response, "Not a serious hardship, does not qualify" when I spoke to a superintendent about this specific request the response I received, they can wait an hour and ride the next train.

Does management flex their schedules to ride the train?

Does management flex their schedules for family care needs?

While I do understand that management is salary and we are hourly it still seems very hypocritical that management flexes their schedule to fit their needs outside of work to achieve a better work life balance but will not allow its employees the same benefit.

Bus Facilities as well as rail have been relatively quiet this last month.

The Fall picks were held system wide, we are seeing more "missed" picks and frustrated members when they are placed per the CBA. Please do not miss your pick, you can submit an absentee and still call in or show up in person.

item.title: Solidarity Isn't a Slogan: What It Is and How We All Benefit From It
item.dc:creator: Michael Mackay, Executive Board Officer #1
item.content:encoded:
By Michael Mackay, Executive Board Officer #1

Solidarity is a simple word for a simple idea: we are stronger together than we are alone. It means standing with a coworker even when the fight isn't yours, showing up on the picket line for members of another union, and understanding that an injury to one is an injury to all. It is not a slogan. It is a daily practice, and this month I got to watch it work.

What I Saw This Month

In Seattle, UNITE HERE Local 8 just settled the longest hotel workers' strike in Washington state history. After 85 days on the picket line, hotel workers at the Embassy Suites in Pioneer Square reached a tentative agreement that delivers real, lasting gains. Eighty-five days is not a headline number to me; it's eighty-five mornings of workers choosing each other over a paycheck, eighty-five days of coworkers, community members, and fellow unions showing up to hold the line. ATU 587 was one of the unions that Paul Neil, Bill Clifford, and I walked with in solidarity. I showed up, I stood on the line, and I watched a group of workers prove that solidarity, sustained long enough, wins.

That is what solidarity looks like from the outside. Here is what it looks like from the inside, in my own local.

Who I Stand With

ATU 587, to me, is not one workplace or one job title. I know it as Clallam Transit, Jefferson Transit, Kitsap Transit, Solid Ground Transportation, and King County Metro. I know it as the local chapter officially organized and chartered on April 8, 1912, to represent streetcar operators working for the privately owned Seattle Electric Company. I think of the mechanics and facilities workers who keep the fleet running. I'm proud to have been a bus operator for 22 years, keeping the system moving alongside them. I think of our Customer Information Specialist, Pass Sales Office Employees, Supervisors in Service Quality, Dispatch, Control Center, and Training. Every one of those roles is different, every one of them is essential, and every one of them is represented under the same union. Today, ATU 587 has more than 5,000 active members — a historic high for us.

That size and that diversity is exactly the point. A local this broad, spanning this many agencies and job classifications, only holds together if its members choose to stand with one another.

Two Questions Worth Asking Yourself

Last year, Mike Haggard, a senior organizer with the ATU International, trained and mentored me, and he put a choice in front of all of us plainly. His first question: what will you ever get from management, on your own, without a union behind you? The answer is nothing but a hard time. His second question: what will you get? The answer is whatever you're willing to take.

That second answer is the harder one to sit with, because it isn't about management at all — it's about you. Contracts, protections, and respect on the job are not handed to you out of goodwill. They are built, negotiated, and defended by workers who are organized enough to demand them and united enough to hold the line when it matters. What you're willing to accept is what you'll get. That's true whether you're negotiating a contract or deciding whether to show up for a picket line three counties away.

What You're Owed

A union rests on three pillars: wages, benefits, and seniority. Seniority binds you to every other member instead of leaving you to compete for the same job. It rewards your commitment over favoritism and gives you, whether you're a new hire or a thirty-year veteran, a clear, fair, and predictable path. Because of that structure, you don't deal with pay partiality. Your job group is paid equally across the board, not based on who you know or how long you've kept your head down. That's not an accident. It's the product of a union insisting, contract after contract, that fairness isn't negotiable.

Why Unity Matters

People at the top benefit from division. A workforce split by job title, agency, classification, or grievance is easier to manage and easier to shortchange. A workforce that sees itself as one union- mechanics standing with operators, dispatchers standing with facilities staff, one agency standing with another is a workforce that's much harder to push around. We are stronger the more we support each other, and weaker every time we let ourselves be divided.

This is the same commitment every ATU 587 member makes formally, in the Oath of Obligation taken upon joining: to promote the best interests of the union, never to cross a picket line, to keep confidences, to never knowingly let a fellow member be wronged, and to be considerate of others without discrimination of any kind. It's a promise to look out for people we may never have met, in job classifications we may never have worked, because they'd do the same for us.

The Takeaway

Solidarity isn't a slogan. It's the reason eighty-five days on a picket line in Pioneer Square ended in a contract instead of a concession. It's the reason 5,000 members across five agencies and a dozen job classifications can call themselves one union instead of a dozen separate workplaces. And it's the reason the answer to "what will you get?" is always up to us, never up to them.

item.title: Get To Know CISM
item.dc:creator: Peter Gladhart, Metro Transit Operator, #22405
item.content:encoded:
By Peter Gladhart, Metro Transit Operator, #22405

Most everyone reading this has had that experience at work - that sudden, jarring, heart stopping incident, that after it has passed, left you shaking and breathless. Maybe it was an E bike that darted in front of you at the last second, or the car that came up fast on your left so it could make an abrupt right turn in front of you into a shopping center. Or maybe it was a passenger who you picked up along the way that started cursing you out. Or worse. Any of these types of incidents has the potential to overwhelm your nervous system which can trigger immediate physical reactions. High stress events can cause a fight or flight response which is your body's automatic, physical reaction to a perceived danger, stressor, or threat. When your brain senses danger it floods your body with hormones, including adrenaline, that prepares you to stay and fight or run to safety.

Once the triggering incident has passed deep breaths, sips of water and body movements are great tools to use to help calm your body down.

Good tools for de-stressing are important for a strong mental health. Critical incidents that you experience at work can build and cause stress or anxiety away from the job. Having positive routines including - exercise, good eating habits, good hydration, fun adventures with friends and family, a spiritual connection - can be positive de-stressors. Miguel Messina, the Program Manager and a counselor with King County's Employee Assistance for Supervisors program, stresses the importance of a wellness practice called Grounding. Physical grounding – standing, walking or lying on natural surfaces allows your body to connect directly to the Earths natural electric charge which provides a calming effect. Mental/emotional grounding - a strategy used to manage overwhelming stress and anxiety by using simple exercises to refocus attention on the present moment. One common method, called the 5-4-3-2-1 method is where you identify 5 things you see, 4 things you can feel, 3 things you hear, 2 things you smell and 1 thing you taste.

Great routines and positive de-stressing strategies are important, however, in rare instances these tools are not enough and additional help is needed. The CISM (Critical Incident Stress Management) team at King County Metro can help by providing confidential, peer to peer support to help you process and recover. The CISM support line is available, you can leave a message 24 hours a day and a CISM team member will call you back.

206 718-9734

Help! I need to talk to someone!!

To talk to someone in the strictest confidence in a safe place about a work related incident, leave a message on the CISM Team Hotline: 206-718-9734

item.title: Don't Trade Away What We May Never Get Back
item.dc:creator: Andy Price, Shop Steward, ATU Local 587
item.content:encoded:
By Andy Price, Shop Steward, ATU Local 587

President Greg Woodfill's September President's Report contains a statement about medical-benefits bargaining that I believe deserves close attention from every member.

Greg wrote:

"And that, for the first time, the Union presented management last week with a proposal for what we believe the membership might accept in trade for agreeing to the slippery slope of a premium share."

He then explained that if the Union reaches an agreement with King County on a package involving monthly premium sharing, it would most likely require a separate membership vote.

Before going further, there is an important distinction members may not always have reason to think about.

We have two separate agreements involved here. Our King County Metro Collective Bargaining Agreement covers wages and most working conditions. It expired October 31, 2025, and negotiations continue.

Our medical benefits are bargained separately under a separate benefits agreement. Local 587 has historically bargained those benefits off-cycle from the main contract, and our own Union publications once described having a separate health-benefit agreement and the ability to bargain our own benefits as an advantage.

That distinction matters because we are now discussing two major protections at two different bargaining tables: premium-free medical coverage and COLA.

I appreciate the commitment to a membership vote if a premium-share agreement is reached. But there is a question that comes before the vote:

What exactly has Local 587 already proposed to King County in exchange for agreeing to premium sharing?

As of September 15, the membership has not been told.

That is particularly difficult to understand when transparency has been such an important part of the current contract negotiations. Members have been given access to bargaining proposals and have been permitted to observe CBA negotiations. That is a positive development.

But transparency should apply to medical-benefits bargaining too.

If our Union has already presented management with a proposal for what leadership believes members might accept in exchange for premium sharing, members should know what that proposal is before bargaining goes further. A vote on a completed package is not the same thing as knowing what is being proposed in our name while bargaining is still underway.

Our own history provides important guidance.

In 2013, King County was also attempting to shift more future health-care costs onto employees. Then-President Paul Bachtel wrote:

"What KC now wants is for its employees to agree to pay for all future cost increases above a negotiated level."

Local 587 rejected that approach and chose interest arbitration.

Vice President Clint DeVoss put it even more plainly:

"Basically, King County wants us to start paying more of the cost of health insurance out of our own pockets. ATU said: NO!"

Local 587 ultimately lost that arbitration. That should be stated honestly. But the Local nevertheless took the dispute through mediation and all the way through an interest-arbitration hearing rather than voluntarily accepting the County's proposed cost shift.

Greg himself calls premium sharing a "slippery slope."

I agree.

Once monthly premium sharing becomes part of our benefits structure, future bargaining starts from a different place. Instead of arguing over whether members should pay premiums, we may find ourselves bargaining over how much members will pay.

Our position should remain simple:

THE EMPLOYER SHOULD PAY 100% OF THE PREMIUM.

We should bargain to improve medical benefits and reduce member costs where possible — not create another permanent employee obligation.

The same principle applies to COLA.

At the August membership meeting, while discussing the parties' wage proposals, President Woodfill indicated that the Union was seeking a guaranteed 6% increase in each year of a three-year contract, rather than accepting Metro's COLA proposal, which was capped at 3% per year.

I strongly support demanding 6% per year.

But I do not believe that should mean giving up COLA language.

A fixed wage demand is the amount we are seeking in this bargaining round. COLA is an ongoing contractual protection against inflation.

And bargaining positions can change before a final agreement is reached. If the eventual wage settlement is less than 6% in any year, COLA becomes even more important. Even if we win 6%, COLA should remain in the contract so members continue to have protection if inflation rises beyond the guaranteed increase.

Our own Local 587 history shows that these protections are not mutually exclusive.

In August 2014, Metro proposed a three-year wage freeze. Local 587 proposed a 3% wage increase in the first year plus its existing 95% COLA language for the remaining two years. Former President Kenny McCormick also made a membership motion demanding current contract language and "a COLA with a 2% floor."

The official history of the Amalgamated Transit Union contains an entire section titled "COLA Protections Challenged." It describes "ATU-developed and promoted COLA protection" and recounts management efforts to eliminate or cap COLA during the inflationary 1970s.

The same page shows Local 788 members voting on a 1976 contract providing both a $1.28-per-hour wage increase and an improved cost-of-living formula.

That history is worth remembering.

Previous generations of ATU members did not view a guaranteed wage increase and COLA as opposites. They fought to preserve both.

In September 2014, President Bachtel reported that Local 587 members had made clear they were "not going to willingly give up their Cost of Living Allowance (COLA) language."

The message to both our Union and management should be clear:

6% AND COLA – NOT 6% OR COLA.

Premium-free medical and COLA have something important in common.

They are long-term protections.

They may be extremely difficult to recover once surrendered.

And members deserve meaningful discussion before either one is bargained away — not simply a yes-or-no vote after the bargaining is finished.

Our Union's history should not merely be something we read after negotiations are over. It should help guide us while bargaining is still underway.

NO MONTHLY PREMIUM SHARE.

6% + COLA.

DEFEND WHAT WE HAVE. BARGAIN FOR MORE.

DO NOT TRADE AWAY PERMANENT PROTECTIONS FOR SHORT-TERM GAINS.

item.title: Police Can't Arrest Their Way Out of a Housing and Mental Health Crisis
item.dc:creator: Chuck Lare, Shop Steward and a Base Safety Committee Chair
item.content:encoded:
By Chuck Lare, Shop Steward and a Base Safety Committee Chair

Route #7, 8:40 a.m. A man is down in the doorway. Forty riders are watching while you radio TCC and handle it alone — again. Bus drivers see people in psychosis, overdosing, sleeping rough, breaking windows, scared out of their minds. It's not fine. Nobody who's actually stood in that doorway thinks it's fine.

So I understand why "just arrest them" sounds like the obvious answer. It feels fast. It feels like something is finally being done. But here's the problem: it doesn't work, and it costs more than the alternative.

Jail removes a person from a bus stop for a few hours or days. Then they come back — to the same street, the same route, the same untreated crisis. We've all watched the tents move down the block and thought: here we go again. That's not a public safety strategy. That's a very expensive game of whack-a-mole, and taxpayers are footing the bill for every round.

The number that should change your mind: Washington's Department of Corrections puts institutional incarceration at roughly $81,000 per person, per year — and that's before police response, court costs, jail health care, and the ER visits that follow. A Central Florida study found cycling a homeless person through jails and emergency rooms costs about $31,000 a year, versus roughly $10,000 for supportive housing. Denver's own randomized housing study found $6,876 in lower public costs per person, per year, after housing was factored in — fewer arrests, fewer jail stays, fewer ER runs. This isn't a mercy argument. It's a math argument.

And it's been tested at scale, not just in theory. Denver's STAR program sends trained health responders — not police — to mental health and low-level crisis calls. Stanford researchers checked for the exact "whack-a-mole" effect skeptics worry about: did crime just move somewhere else? It didn't. Targeted low-level offenses dropped 34%, with no offsetting rise elsewhere — crime even dropped during hours STAR wasn't on duty, because people who got real help stopped cycling back into crisis.

Houston ran the experiment for over a decade, regionwide. Starting in 2011, the city paired aggressive Housing First placement with continued enforcement against holdout encampments — not just kindness, but kindness plus consequences where needed. The result: homelessness down 63% since 2011, over 25,000 people housed, 90% still housed two years later. Houston is now America's fourth-largest city and has cut homelessness harder than any other major city in the country.

None of this means abandoning enforcement. If someone is violent, armed, or making credible threats, call police — full stop. That's not up for debate. But for the rider who's sick, high, confused, or sleeping at the end of the line and posing no threat, sending an armed response over and over is neither cheap nor effective. It's the response that "feels tough" while quietly failing everyone, including the taxpayer.

Seattle has a real opening right now. The mayor and county executive have announced steps to reset the regional homelessness response, with a workgroup meeting November 30. That's the moment to lock in what actually worked elsewhere: mandatory-track treatment options (not just optional ones), funding parity for behavioral-health responders instead of default police dispatch, and a direct crisis-responder line operators can call separately from 911.

ATU 587 needs to require Metro provide a simple reporting system that works for operators and inserts accountability through a simple real time live dashboard — tracking response times, repeat incidents, and operator emergency calls, so results are visible, not just promised. And we need ATU 587 to maintain a constant dialog at all Bases that facilitates two-way communications feedback to the working groups, so if the city's numbers look better but our incident reports don't, we have the evidence to prove problems are just moving, not shrinking.

Operators see this crisis up close every single shift. That's expertise the workgroups need at the table — not silence, while the details get decided without us.

Text your union representative this week: tell them you want ATU 587 to have a seat at the Breaking the Cycle and other such workgroups.

Sources

  • WA Dept. of Corrections FY2025 institutional cost data
  • Central Florida homelessness cost study (Homeless Voice)
  • Denver Housing First randomized study (NLIHC)
  • Denver STAR program evaluation (Stanford SIEPR; NBC News)
  • Houston Housing First results, 2011–present (West Houston Homelessness Partnership)
  • Mayor Wilson & Executive Zahilay, Regional Homelessness Authority announcement, July 2026.
