item.title: The Maintenance Vice President's Report: Busy Times
item.dc:creator: Jeff Stambaugh
item.content:encoded:
By Jeff Stambaugh

I have been in office for two years now and it has never been busier. Currently The Union has 117 open grievances, with over 15 headed towards arbitration. Unfortunately, we have spent too much time and too much money defending The Union from Unfair labor practices filed with Public Employees Relations Commission (PERC) over The Duty of Fair Representation and lawsuits. What does this mean? We have a small number of members upset over the way their issues were handled by The Union and have either filed complaint(s) with PERC or have filed a lawsuit against The Union. I am happy to report that in the last two years there has not been a successful case brought against The Union. The unfortunate piece of this is The Union spends its resources defending its actions instead of being able to invest those resources in making things better for all.

We have resolved the Unfair Labor Practice that was filed by The Union over the issuance of Unexcused Absences issued on Holiday work assignments in bus VM. We now have clear established rules around call in times for Holiday work assignments. We are still working on the request for change of hours; Metro is working on updating the request form and the process for management to follow when a request is made. When making a request in the future, please remember, the original intent of a request for change of hours was for a legitimate need (such as childcare, use of public transit) not a want.

I attended the Northwest Conference in Winnipeg in late June along with Paul Neil, Latrelle Gibson, Hassannoor Aden, Tonya Abernathy, Stan Straker, Abdiwahab Adan and Mary Prather. Winnipeg Local 1505 gave a great presentation on their CISM team and the benefits it provides their members. Along with that, there was a great question and answer session with two renowned labor lawyers that covered a variety of topics, including fiduciary responsibility of Union funds. This turned into a much larger discussion with International President Costa, International Vice President Trujillo and International Secretary-Treasurer Kirk. It was very disappointing to hear how some locals were not following the ATU International bylaws and spending money on shall we say, less that appropriate expenditures and attempting to hide it from the membership and the International.

I also learned that the city of Winnipeg has great labor history, including the General strike of 1919 where a streetcar was turned over and lit on fire.

The Union continues to battle with Metro over open, transparent communication.

Metro continues to change and implement new things with absolutely no communication with The Union. Metro claims to want to be our Labor Partner but their actions say different. If you hear of something headed your way, please drop us an email or attend a meeting to make sure The Union is aware, it is easier to work together and implement change than to undue the harm when it is shoved upon us.

item.title: The Recording Secretary's Report: Rail/Streetcar Pick and Fall Shop Steward Nominations
item.dc:creator: Latrelle Gibson
item.content:encoded:
By Latrelle Gibson

Getting Ready for Pick

All Members are encouraged to utilize the Union Website to preview all the driver timecards, run cuts, and seniority lists. This is also where you can find both LLR Operator and Streetcar Operator absentee forms. If you're experiencing issues with logging on, please give the Union office a call at (206) 448-8588.

Pick Preview Information

Link Rail Operator will be able to preview the work outside of the pick room. For Streetcar, there is no pick preview outside of the 20min each person gets to preview the work prior to their pick time.

Not going to be at Pick?

Please fill out an absentee form. You can locate these forms in the following places: The Union Website, the Rail/Streetcar Dispatch Window(s). You can return your completed absentee pick form to; The window at your work location or emailed to me @recsec@atu587.org. Please remember to leave a good contact number where you can be reached, and if you're going to be out of the country, we can contact you via WhatsApp, just be sure to indicate on the absentee pick form that you will need a call via WhatsApp. If you choose to have a friend pick for you, please make sure they pick no more than 2hrs before or after you pick. For those volunteering to help your classmate, family, or friend pick, please remember that if they pick right ahead or right after you that you will not have your 20min to preview the work, so again, to ensure that you or the person you're picking for will have the 20min pick preview, don't agree to pick for someone that picks within a hour or less of your pick. If I see that you don't have enough time after knowing you're picking for someone else, I will instruct you to go preview the work for yourself, and I can look up the work they want. Remember, this is why the Union is in the pick room, to ensure everyone who is supposed to be picking, can and will pick. Lastly, please remember, Union picks are not subject to the grievance process, so please be sure if you submit an absentee and are not available by phone that you clearly indicate your work choices.

Vacation Pick

This pick is for Jan-March vacation periods. If you're not going to be at pick, please indicate your preferred vacation periods on the absentee form. Please note that the Union does not pick vacations, this is done via the vacation pick room. At the conclusion of picking your work, the vacation pick room will call you to pick your vacation. Please be sure to be available when the vacation room calls.

Not Listed on the Pick List?

If you're not on the pick list, this is likely due to being out on medical or other continuous leave during the shake up(s) and you have not returned to work prior to July 2026. You will want to contact Transit Disability Services and/or your Chief to let them know you're cleared to return to work. For medical, you will want to send your updated medical that clears you to return to work, full duty, no restrictions, to Transit Disability Services prior to your pick date.

Pick Room Phone FOR EMERGENCIES ONLY

Once pick has started, please note that we're in a live pick on the pick room floor and will not always be able to answer the phone, therefore, please only call the pick room during live pick hours for emergencies only, e.g., running late for your pick, not going to make it to pick in time. All other callers' names and phone numbers will be taken for a call back once the live pick ends for the day.

Shop Steward Nominations

The Spring/Summer Shop Steward List is out, and you will be able to find the list in the July edition of the News Review. The list is also available on the Union Bulletin boards at the worksites, and on the Union Website. If you missed the deadline to put in for Shop Steward, no worries, you'll get a chance to nominate for Shop Steward in August. Please remember, every member will have to submit a nomination every shakeup, so for the Fall/Winter 2026 Nomination, all will need to nominate themselves during the open nomination period that has started and will close in August. The reason for this is due to the shakeup being where some may change bases, decide they want a break from being a Shop Steward, want to nominate for Chief Shop Steward, or nominate for Shop Steward for the first time. This is not a live list, so please be sure to read the bulletins and/or the News Review for the Nomination dates. Once the Nomination closes, and the list comes out, please let me know ASAP if you don't see your name on the first SS Nomination list that is posted so I can get you added. Once the second revised SS nomination list comes out, there will be no revisions to this list, and you will have to remember to nominate yourself when nominations open again or send me an email stating you missed the nomination window and I will add you to the list for the 2027 Spring/Summer nomination window. And with that, thank you to all who are willing to step up and sever the membership, you're all very much appreciated by this local and those who you represent.

Hope to see you all at the pick!

item.title: 40th Annual ATU International Women's Caucus
item.dc:creator: Stephanie Binschus, Kitsap Transit Executive Board Representative
item.content:encoded:
By Stephanie Binschus, Kitsap Transit Executive Board Representative

The ATU IWC 40th Annual Conference was held in Niagara Falls, NY, June 17–21, 2026. Registration was open for 5 hours on Wednesday, and most people checked in that evening. Thursday started with registration and additional check-ins before breakout classes began. During the class time, the committees were instructed to meet and develop a plan for how they were going to continue and create their reports for the business session on Saturday. After my committee met, I was one of the six instructors for the How to Start a Caucus & 10 Ways to Break It Up.

Friday began the typical conference days with Speakers on topics including The Power of the Grievance, ATU Workforce Development, and Let's Talk About Parliamentary Procedures. I would encourage everyone to learn about Parliamentary Procedures by investing in a copy of Robert's Rules of Order, Robert's Rules of Order in Brief, or any of the many other helper books available.

Saturday was the business day and the day that everyone was instructed to wear red for the 40th Anniversary. We had one more speaker, Janet Gehard, the Director of Public and Community for FHE Health, who spoke on The Buddhist Principle of the Two Arrows. Several members were recognized for their role in creating the Women's Caucus 40 years ago, and some special members were recognized for stepping up to help advance the caucus. I would like to express my gratitude to the membership for allowing me to be one of those individuals who have been able to step up and be recognized for assisting the ATU IWC.

Officer elections were held, and the current Officers will be serving another three-year term. The Conference wrapped up with a farewell reception before everyone returned home on Sunday.

item.title: Unity on the Grill: A Thank You to Our Summer Cookout 2026 Team
item.dc:creator: Michael Mackay, Executive Board Officer #1
item.content:encoded:
By Michael Mackay, Executive Board Officer #1

This summer, I came together with our union family for a cookout that reminded me why we stand strong as one. Tasty food, good company, and the kind of camaraderie that only comes from a group that truly looks out for each other; that's what the Summer Union Cookout 2026 was all about.

As you know, none of it happens without the people who give their time behind the scenes, so we want to take a moment to say thank you.

Thank you, Paul Neil and Lisa Nault for orchestrating the entire event from start to finish. Your planning and coordination turned an idea into a day the membership will remember. Thank you to Greg Woodfill and Rachael Buchanan for taking the great photos for the News Review.

Thank you, Michelle Penny, Anita James, Mary Prather, Rachael Buchanan, Greg Woodfill, Cory Rigtrup, and others, for volunteering to help serve our hungry members, and thank you, Rachael Buchanan, Tonya Abernathy, Greg Woodfill, Cory Rigtrup, Latrelle Gibson, Brian St. Pierre, Robert Rothwell, Stan Straker, and Karl Niedermann, for volunteering to help with the task of set up, clean up, and everything in between.

Thank you, Felicia Hurt and Tonya Abernathy for volunteering to oversee the membership roster and hand out food and prize tickets to attendees, to Zematra Bacon for volunteering to run the bingo table, and to Abdiwahab Adan for bringing the sambusa's.

Thank you, Jeff Stambaugh and Jerry McKenna for volunteering to work the grill all day and making sure everyone left with a full plate and a smile.

Thank you, Bill Clifford for keeping spirits and cones high, handing out ice cream to members all afternoon.

And to Dorene Kelly, Jeff Cushnyr, Stephanie Binschus, Fenya Joy, and many, many more who lent a hand in ways big and small, thank you.

And to every member who came out, ate, laughed, and spent the afternoon with fellow union sisters, brothers, and siblings, thank you for showing up. A cookout is only as good as the people who fill it, and your presence is what made this day special.

We know that this is the spirit that makes our union strong: showing up for each other, whether it's at the bargaining table or around the grill.

Thank you to everyone named above, and to all who helped make Summer Union Cookout 2026 a day worth remembering. And thank you to all of those who may not be mentioned above for pitching in wherever needed and keeping everything running smoothly, from set up to cleanup.

Here's to more moments like this, together.

item.title: Disability Pride: The Work Continues
item.dc:creator: Chuck Lare, a Shop Steward & Atlantic Base Safety Committee Chair
item.content:encoded:
By Chuck Lare, a Shop Steward & Atlantic Base Safety Committee Chair

July is Disability Pride Month. On July 7th, King County raised the Disability Pride flag outside the County Administration Building, marking the 36th anniversary of the Americans with Disabilities Act. Executive Girmay Zahilay, Council Chair Sarah Perry, Councilmember Steffanie Fain, Councilmember Rhonda Lewis, ADA Specialist Cecilia Black, and KCDEN Chair Karla Lynch stood together to declare: "Nothing About Us Without Us." This year's theme: "The World Works Better with Us."

Google it if you want the official statements. I want to tell you what that flag actually means — and why every bus operator reading this should care.

Look at the flag. Five diagonal stripes (colors top to bottom: green, blue, white, yellow and red), each stripe represents an array of disabilities, including:

  • Red for physical disabilities
  • Gold for neurodiversity
  • White for invisible disabilities and disabilities that haven't yet been diagnosed
  • Blue for emotional and psychiatric disabilities, including mental illness, anxiety, and depression
  • Green for sensory disabilities, including deafness, blindness, lack of smell, lack of taste, audio processing disorder, and all other sensory disabilities.

The five diagonal stripes: physical, neurodiverse, invisible, psychiatric, sensory — cutting across a black background. The black honors the victims of ableist violence, the harm done by the lie that "able-bodied" is normal and everyone else falls short. But those stripes don't sit quietly in their lanes. They cut across the black — across the walls, the barriers, the assumptions. That's light breaking through darkness. That's not decoration. That's the whole story of this movement, and it's a story about buses.

In 1983, a group called ADAPT — Americans Disabled for Accessible Public Transit — organized around one infuriating fact: buses had no lifts. Wheelchair users weren't late to work by choice. They were stranded, by design. So ADAPT didn't write polite letters. They rolled their wheelchairs in front of buses. They chained themselves to the wheels. They made the system physically unable to move until it changed.

Then came the Capitol Crawl. On March 12, 1990, about 60 activists arrived at the U.S. Capitol, left their wheelchairs and mobility aids behind, and started climbing — all 83 marble steps, on hands and knees.

Among them: 8-year-old Jennifer Keelan, who has cerebral palsy. Climbing, she said, "I'll take all night if I have to." Michael Winter, president of the National Council on Independent Living, climbed through real pain — not to prove anything about his own body, but to prove something about ours as a society: the barrier was never the person. The barrier was the building. Paulette Patterson dragged herself up on her hands and told reporters those stairs were the invisible wall that had kept disabled people out of work, out of government, out of full citizenship — suddenly, undeniably visible.

Months later, Congress passed the ADA.

It took people crawling up their own Capitol steps, in pain, on camera, to make lawmakers see what had been invisible to them for years.

That's the legacy in this flag. Not a quiet request for sympathy — an active, defiant demand for justice. And here's the part that should hit close to home: the first fight was about buses. Our buses. The lifts we take for granted, the ramps, the announcements, the kneeling function — none of that existed until people put their bodies on the line to force it into existence.

We're the ones who operate that legacy every single day. Every time we lower a ramp without a sigh, wait the extra minute(s), treat an accommodation as normal instead of a hassle — we're either carrying that work forward or we're not. And we need Metro Management to step-up to create reasonable schedules to prevent accommodating to be only the operators responsibility. There's no neutral option. Indifference is a choice too, and it's the wrong one.

The work isn't finished. How will we chose to hold management accountable to support operators providing the accommodations?

Join King County Disability Equity Network's (KCDEN) monthly gathering — second Friday of every month at noon — and keep building on this legacy with us.

Disability Pride isn't just about looking back at how far we've come. It's about continuing to climb.

item.title: July Operators' LMRC Meeting (July 2, 2026)
item.dc:creator: Lisa Nault, Rachael Buchanan, and LaTonya Abernathy, ATU 587 Bus Reps
item.content:encoded:
By Lisa Nault, Rachael Buchanan, and LaTonya Abernathy, ATU 587 Bus Reps

Labor Management Relations Committee: To discuss, approve and/or propose resolutions to: issues or problems of Metro policies which affects the Union and which either party requests to be placed on the agenda; issues or problems of contract administration other than formal grievances.

Attendees: Rachael Buchanan, Latrelle Gibson, Collin Dunphy, Jabari Hampton, Michael Lam, Cory Rigtrup, William McCoy, Travis Silva, Brian Eggen

Follow Up

Continuing Education Orca

Maps appear to be gone, but the Union Representative has only driven 3700 buses this month. There was supposed to be an operations bulletin, but the turn-by-turn had some issues and 80% of our fleet is Co-Pilot 1, and 20% is Co-Pilot 2. Co-Pilot 1 was not working properly and was off route and showing incorrect times, so they were removed due to compatibility issues. but there is no ETA on getting it rolled out for the Co-Pilot 1 coaches. It was announced in the June 12th Operations Bulletin, but not everyone receives emails.

Accident Report SSaM

Follow up on internet issues and software updates for more efficient use of operator's time. It is on the agenda to include on the next continuing education training, and it will be about 4 hours, and the curriculum should be finalized around the 22nd of July. Metro is highly encouraging the instruction design team to include it. Officially the union has not seen any policy changes come our way, have you been changing policies at all? Are these bulletins changes of policy? It could be just a notification, but the things we're talking about are not demanding to bargain situation. Metro's communication team is aware of what is required before sending Operations Bulletins out.

Uniform Committee/Jackets

Is the travelling vendor truck coming to other bases? The notification goes out on the TV screens at the bases when they will arrive, so be on the lookout. It was the Red Wing truck. The last time they did this was April and then went to Atlantic, Bellevue, Atlantic, Bellevue. Not sure why the other bases weren't visited. Metro will ask them to consider asking them to include other locations.

Re-read Calendar

We've had some discussions and the piece we're missing is can you pre-authorize the person to be there. How do we streamline the operation? Is there a way to make this easier? The Union gave Metro a list of names for the year, and how do we go about detailing that person and the Union would like to make it streamlined, so it's easy on everyone. Metro will follow up on SSQA so they can send details in a timely manner. SSQA said they had challenges, so the Union decided to send it to Operations. It seems to be a circular argument with no one taking responsibility. When Upper Management gets involved, it's mostly about getting Chief's and Superintendents to attend, but we do want to make sure they have a process to make it easier. Follow up next month.

New Business

Eastside Road Reliefs, Spring Station

The Union heard that Metro is going to require Operators to take the train to road reliefs in the fall shakeup and will no longer be given cars. Is this actually a thing that is going to start happening? The Planners make that call and they're ATU, so ask them. The Union has sent a demand to bargain over this, and nobody has said anything. Are the Base Planners responsible for making the decision to decide who gets a car and who takes the train? The Run Cards do not indicate whether you take the train or a car. People are concerned that the practice will change. Currently, they take a base care to those locations. Is the concern a pay issue? That is part of the concern, because the job description doesn't say you have to walk and all the Union is trying to do is verify that it's happening or not. Follow up next month. Is there a point in time where we can expect some communication from Metro on this. Metro will double check with the East Side bases. Follow up.

FIFA

The Union would like to see Metro celebrate the Operators who are doing the hard work of driving the FIFA Shuttles on Match Days. Metro does appreciate the Operators and seeks input on how to do that? Would the Union like a message on the TV Screen.

Meeting adjourned at 9:51am.

Have a topic you want brought up in the LMRC Meetings? Contact Lisa, Rachael, or LaTonya to submit your topics.

item.title: Bulletin: Resolution of Holiday Unexcused Absences and ULP
item.dc:creator: Jeff Stambaugh, Vice President Maintenance
item.content:encoded:
Read from a scanned image on pages 18–19 of the PDF, so it may contain errors. View pages 18–19 in the PDF.

By Jeff Stambaugh, Vice President Maintenance

Bulletin dated July 17, 2026. To: Bus Vehicle Maintenance Members.

The Union and Metro have reached resolution on the issuance of Unexcused Absences for Holiday work assignments. We have agreed to the following language changes for holiday work assignments and overtime assignments.

For Holiday Assignments, please see the new highlighted sections below:

17.3.F. For holiday work assignments, METRO will determine the staffing needs for each shift. When METRO has determined which classifications will be required to work, Employees in those classifications will be offered the holiday assignment in seniority order, first to Employees that are scheduled to work that day as part of their regular work assignment. If after offering the holiday assignment, by seniority, to Employees who are regularly scheduled to work that day and there are more assignments available, it will then be offered to Employees on their RDO until assignments are filled. Should no Employee accept the holiday assignment, Employees from other shifts within the base will be offered the work before assignments are made by inverse seniority to Employees that are scheduled to work that day as part of their regular work assignment. Except in the classification of Transit Parts Specialist (TPS), holiday assignments shall be offered by seniority within the base. With at least 2 hours' notice to Metro, an employee may cancel a holiday assignment.

X. An employee who has volunteered for a holiday shift may cancel without penalty by providing notice to their supervisor at least 72 hours before the scheduled shift start time. If an employee provides notice of cancellation less than 72 hours but two hours before the scheduled shift start time, the absence shall be recorded as excused. If the employee provides less than two hours' notice, the absence shall be recorded as unexcused and will be subject to the attendance procedures defined in this AGREEMENT.

What does all this mean?

If you report your unavailability to work a planned holiday assignment at least 72 hours prior to the start of the assignment no penalty, if you report your unavailability 2 hours to 72 hours prior, your chief may inquire what happened. If you report your unavailability, other than sick with less than two hours' notice, you will receive an unexcused absence and you are able to request the removal through the standard process.

For Overtime assignments please see the highlighted changes below:

17.8.D. With at least 48 hours' notice to an Employee, METRO may cancel preplanned overtime assignment in its entirety. An Employee who has volunteered for a preplanned overtime assignment may cancel without penalty by providing notice to their supervisor at least 48 hours before the scheduled shift start time. When an employee provides fewer than 48 hours notice of their intent to cancel, METRO, if possible, will attempt to find someone to cover the work; otherwise, the employee will be required to work. An Employee requesting and assigned to work on their RDO, who fails to report for work or who reports for work late, will be subject to the attendance procedures defined in this AGREEMENT. For the purpose of Section 17.8.D, preplanned overtime is defined as overtime that is both offered and accepted at least 48 hours before the scheduled shift start time.

What does all this mean?

If you report your unavailability to work a planned overtime assignment 48 hours prior to the start of the assignment no penalty. If you report your unavailability, other than sick with less than 48 hours' notice, management will make a good faith effort to replace you, if they are not able to replace you and you do not work, you will receive an unexcused absence and you are able to request the removal through the standard process

We have also agreed to changes in the request for accommodation of start or quit time language, pick language, vacation language and move up timeline language.

Please see the Union web page for the full MOA.

Signed by Greg Woodfill, President; Cory Rigtrup, Vice President; Jeff Stambaugh, Vice President Maintenance; Paul Neil, Financial Secretary/Treasurer; and Latrelle Gibson, Recording Secretary.

I, .................................., in the presence of God and the members of this Union, do solemnly promise and pledge (without any reservation or evasion) to support the Constitution and General Laws of this Amalgamated Transit Union. I will keep myself in good standing by paying all dues, fines and assessments required. I will work to promote the best interests of this Union and encourage my fellow workers to become members of the same. I will not take the place of any member of this organization, or any other union worker who may be on strike or locked out. I will not reveal any of the private business to anyone not entitled to know the same.

I will not engage in activity evidencing gross disloyalty nor in conduct otherwise unbecoming a member, and will not knowingly wrong a member or see one wronged if in my power to prevent it. I will not appeal to any legal authority in matters pertaining to this Union until I have exhausted all means of redress provided by its laws. I will be considerate of others in word and action and will never discriminate against a fellow worker on account of race, religion, color, creed, sex, sexual orientation, gender identity or expression, age, disability, citizenship, or national origin. I also promise to promote the cause of trade union principles and defend freedom of thought, whether expressed by tongue or pen, with all the power at my command.

I understand there is nothing in this obligation that will in any way interfere with my political and religious rights or that will be in any way inconsistent with my duties arising from any of the relations of life.

item.title: The President's Report: Still No Contract?
item.dc:creator: Greg Woodfill
item.content:encoded:
By Greg Woodfill

This is the question Union officers get daily. Members are frustrated and can't understand why it always takes 12–18 months to negotiate a new contract.

The answer is we'll have a contract when Metro offers one that is worth the membership voting on.

We could have a tentative agreement tomorrow if we just agreed to a paltry raise, restrictions on overtime, and watering down of just cause. We will keep fighting for what the members have asked for.

We'll present a contract to vote on when it's right, and not one day sooner.

Benefits Bargaining Update

Every two years, we renegotiate our medical benefits, separate from contract bargaining.

The County's projections on medical cost increases for the next two years, on top of the last two years' cost increases, paint a picture of the sky falling, as they always do.

These County projections show that our current $16 million surplus in the medical benefits reserve fund would turn into a $13 million deficit if the County's monthly contribution were to remain at its current level.

Contractually, if at any point the reserve fund falls below $4 million, we are required to meet with the County and negotiate replenishing the fund.

I'll leave it to your imagination who the County proposes to cover the vast majority of this projected $17 million shortfall, and what unacceptable funding mechanism they propose to use to cover it. The union's position is that the employer should fully cover the cost of our medical benefits, PERIOD! Buckle up and stay tuned; this could get ugly.

Hiring Bonus Update

On 8/14/2023 the Union and King County agreed to a recruitment/retention bonus which was added to the last contract on Page 245.

The MOA stated that these bonuses were for those hired before October 31st, 2025. Recently King County OLR contacted the Union, stating that they had mistakenly continued paying these bonuses past 10/31 to around 50 members and would need to recollect those payments due to not having the budgeting authority to give those bonuses. Additionally, they stated that they would not be paying others who weren't paid these bonuses.

The Union objected, and King County won't recollect while they are talking with the Union on this. Not paying a recruitment/retention bonus that was listed on a job recruitment feels like false advertising, breach of contract, and wage theft all rolled into one. These members should be paid these bonuses.

Ultimately, it's The County that will decide whether to pay these bonuses or not. Once they make their decision, we'll take it from there. Do the right thing King County, your word is your bond, keep your promises! True North Values shouldn't just be a slogan.

Non-domicile CDL Update

As most of you know some of our members you reside and work here legally are losing their CDL's. Imagine waking up one day and being told for no fault of your own that the Federal Government has made a rule to revoke your right to your job.

We battle daily with King County Metro Bus and Rail on contract violations, discipline & terminations without just cause. Or not holding managers to the same accountability standards as their front-line workforce.

But we still do find common ground and work together on mutual interests. We won't hesitate to call things out but should and will give credit where credit is due.

The County has gone above and beyond in dealing with the non-domicile CDL issue by offering temporary employment to those who are affected by this issue. But these aren't long term solutions, and they don't make our members whole or wipe away the indignity and injustice.

A Washington State Supreme Court Justice during their COPE endorsement interview with our Union suggested that Washington State could create their own CDL and gave the following similar examples.

Washington State Created L&I because OSHA was not doing enough to protect our citizens in terms of safety standards, wage protections, adequate breaks, etc.

Washington State created WAFSA because FAFSA was not offering aid to non-domicile students and children of non-domicile parents (Dreamers).

Washington State could, in theory, create a division of WDOL that oversees and regulates WA State Intrastate CDL License requirements.

Essentially saying that the Federal Law is not doing enough to provide for the needs of our state residents and we need to write laws that govern our state that are more specific than the Federal Laws.

Our COPE committee has engaged with State House and Senate members who are committed to try and write and pass legislation that could solve this injustice. The Governors office reached out to me and is very interested in this possibility. All of this is happening solely because of the political clout this Union has cultivated over decades of actively endorsing candidates. Please contribute to COPE, your contributions make a real and tangible difference. Our Voice Our Power!

Union Business Travel Report

I spent the first 12 days of June first in Washington, DC, and then in Minneapolis. First up was the ATU International Legislative Conference for ATU Presidents in DC. We spent 3 full days being brought up to speed on the International's legislative agenda in preparation for lobbying visits with our US Senators & House Members that ATU set up. I participated in seven meetings with members of Congress, including one with Senator Patty Murray, who had broken her ankle a week earlier but still attended.

We lobbied hard on issues like not removing or watering down job protections such as 13C and PTASP. We lobbied on AI and Autonomous vehicle protections. I highlighted how non-domicile CDL loss is affecting our members and advocated strongly for transit funding.

From DC I flew directly to Minneapolis for the 30th AFL-CIO Convention. I had the honor of being nominated and elected as an ATU International alternate delegate and served as a delegate on the floor for the last two days. I stood with ATU International President John Costa on the floor as he advocated for a resolution on operator assaults where he recognized Brother Shawn Yim.

There were good updates on current labor battles and priorities, and some good training sessions. I gained knowledge and got good advice from Union Presidents, and International officers, all paid for by the International.

item.title: In Loving Memory…
item.content:encoded:
"It is not length of life but depth of life" ~ Ralph Waldo Emerson

We were saddened to learn of the passing of:

We are saddened to announce the sudden passing of Bellevue Base operator, Dean Alan Jenne. Dean was hired as a part-time operator in 2007. He loved being a part-time operator as this gave him time to live his best life. Dean had a personality that would light up a room, although slightly quiet, he would always be upbeat and speak to his fellow coworkers in passing. Dean also received many awards and accolades for his dedication and service. Outside of work, Dean enjoyed his lifelong passion of running, and especially loved running in marathons. Dean is survived by his wife and beloved family. Dean will be greatly missed. Services have not been announced at this time.

It is with great sadness that we announce the passing of retired sheet metal worker, Michael Larson. Michael was hired in 1985 in the VM department. He worked in the VM department until his retirement in March 2009. Dean will be greatly missed by his family, friends, and coworkers. No services have been announced at this time.

Please place these members and their families in your thoughts and hearts

Please notify the union office of any member's passing so that this information may be shared with the rest of our union family.

item.title: The 1st Vice President's Report: Benefits
item.dc:creator: Cory Rigtrup
item.content:encoded:
By Cory Rigtrup

If you think back to what originally drew you to apply for this job, maybe things haven't changed that much? Unless you expected the transit world to be full of glamour and glitz, the core attractions remain mostly intact. I suspect most of us came here for reliable work, good benefits and the steady incomes that go hand in hand with a strong unionized job. This article is about our benefits and the fight to keep them attractive.

We have five different bargaining units in our Local. Four properties are in the public sector, while the other is private. All five offer different variations of benefit packages. Four out of the five properties offer a variation of a Kaizer plan, along with a PPO plan. Three out of the five buy benefits from Washington state's exchange. The remaining two, contract benefit independently through a competitive bid process. Yes, it's a bit confusing, so bear with me as I try and explain how this all works.

When our Local negotiates the next contract, our future benefits are part of that. Often, benefits don't get the attention that wages and working conditions get when members are deciding to accept, or reject an offer, but we should. We are in a time where medical benefits cost are increasing nationwide at levels not seen in 15 years.

During open enrollment, members are allowed to select the next year's benefits for their families. I suspect these decisions are made on what works best for them and what they can afford. For my family, I chose the PPO plan. My wife is a Swedish SEIU hospital worker and my daughter is an out of state student. In my case only the PPO offers coverage for both, and I pay additional money for my choice. By choosing the PPO, it not only comes at a cost to me, but also to everyone in the bargaining unit.

Unless you're working at SGT, the taxpayers of Washington state are paying the vast majority of your benefits. If you've paid attention to what's been happening with tax monies in the last year, less federal dollars are going to states for medical costs the before the Affordable Care Act was passed into law. Washington state, like most states, are trying to find ways to compensate for the loss, while medical providers are increasing their cost, trying to remain solvent. For folks like us with medical insurance, the cost has increased.

Currently, we are bargaining the benefit packages with King County for years 2027 and 2028. The benefit packages are not purchased through the state's exchange, but rather independently offered through a provider. This allows for custom modification to plans, and the group rate charges are based on the expenses of our bargaining unit, not the larger group like the state. Simply put, whatever the cost of benefits we use, is what is charged to King County.

Last year for 2025, we had 4,511 members enrolled in benefits for all of Metro, Rail and Streetcar. The total benefits King County paid for 2025, was $93,516,849. If you look at our agreement, or a paycheck advice from last year, you will see the funding rate was $1,694 per month. If you're good at basic math, take monthly investment, $1,694, multiply it by 12 months, multiply it by 4,511 members, we get $91,699,608. If we take the $91,699,608 and subtract it by the $93,516,849 we used in benefits, we come up deficit of $1,817,241.

For 2026, our funding rate increased by 4% to $1,762. Keep in mind our local bargained for this increase in the summer of 2024. Well before knowing what would happen with the federal funding changes in 2025. It is likely that our 2026 benefit cost will increase more than 4% causing an even bigger deficit.

So here we are today, bargaining for the next couple of years of benefits. Medical costs are up, we either need more funding or to lower our average cost per member to stabilize our benefits. King County's proposals are for us to pay for the increases, ours is for them to pay the increase. Every fiber in my body revolts against us paying, but we need benefits and have to come to a deal before open enrollment. So, we need to get cheaper and drive the average cost per member down.

In 2018, when I first started attending medical bargaining, our Local was the most expensive group in King County for medical. We had the highest average cost per member and incurred the highest deductible for using our benefits. Fast forward to today, we are the cheapest cost per member and don't pay any premium share like our bosses. This did not happen by accident, rather a partnership between members getting healthier and a successful bargaining strategy. Folks who do not use medical don't pay, and incentives members to choose the lower cost medical plan, Kaizer. Year after year, Kaizer is between $6,000 and $3,000 a year cheaper per member, than the PPO. Over the years, we have seen enrollment increase in the Kaizer plan, and a slow reduction in members in the PPO plan. As a result, our medical costs grew slower than all the other groups in King County.

Getting a deal without us paying is one hell of a challenge, the struggle is what makes us strong! This is where I stop, bargaining continues and I won't put in writing the union's strategy.

In Solidarity, Cory Rigtrup

item.title: The Maintenance Vice President's Report: Change of Hours Request, Heavy Handed Discipline, and Holiday ULP
item.dc:creator: Jeff Stambaugh
item.content:encoded:
By Jeff Stambaugh

Change of hours request

As I reported last month Metro Bus VM has made the decision to honor very few change of hour's request, while most of the denials seemed unjustified without any clear reason, we did have an in-depth discussion at LMRC about the issue. We spoke of a few specific denials, management had a different perspective on what prompted the request, and why it was denied vs my conversation with the requesting employees. In short management claims it's too difficult to manage a crew that comes in at different times.

As a Lead Mechanic myself I recognize those challenges, however, I was always able to get the crew to work despite the varying start times. It seems Metro management wants to continue to drive down morale and continue to exert authority rather than uphold the True North Values they claim to have. I was promised a more in-depth review of the denials, but I have yet to get it.

Heavy handed discipline

Both Bus VM and Bus Facilities continue to issue heavy handed discipline and fail to follow provision in the contract that says, "discipline is subject to just cause and that the intent of discipline is corrective, rather than punitive, in nature."

Part of that discipline is based off of the use of AVL data that The Union believes Metro is using in violation of the MOA, more to come.

Holiday ULP

Metro requested summary judgment to dismiss the ULP filed with PERC. PERC has denied the motion, we now move closer to PERC hearing, and the membership has approved an arbitration request over the issuance of an unexcused absence where the member called in and reported his unavailability 63 minutes prior to his shift. The Union has had discussions at the bargaining table with Metro in an attempt to resolve this, at this point Metro and The Union have been unable to come up with an agreeable solution, we make look to PERC and an arbitrator to help out if we can't get there.

On a positive note, The Union was able to work a deal with Rail and was successful in returning a Rail Maintenance employee back to work after being terminated. The employee and The Union would like to thank Rail management for being able to work this out.

Lastly if you do not already have plans on July 12th come to the annual Union cookout at the Tukwila Committee Center from 12pm to 4pm

item.title: The Recording Secretary's Report: Fall Pick and Fall Shop Steward Nominations
item.dc:creator: Latrelle Gibson
item.content:encoded:
By Latrelle Gibson

Getting Prepared for the BIG DAY, Pick:

It's time to start thinking about your Fall plans and what you will pick for the Fall/Winter Shakeup.

This will be the LONG shakeup, so this pick will be the pick to really make sure you're picking the right schedule, route, or base that you really want.

Come prepared with the work you desire on paper so you can easily scratch off what's been picked and move down your list. If you plan on picking O.T trippers, PLEASE, make sure the work you want to pick will not create an illegal pick due to not having the required 8 hours off or time in between assignments. Prior to your pick date, it's recommended to research all the work you're interested in picking and lining this up with the O.T trippers you would want to ensure it will be a legal pick, this would include making sure you have at least a 5 minute buffer time between the off at the base time and sign in time of the O.T tripper of vice versa. Be sure to write these combinations down so you can have an easy reference in the pick room that way, you won't burn up your 20min of preview time trying to piece this all together.

If you pick via Absentee, please follow the same process to help us ensure that you're getting what you want and that it won't create an illegal block.

Pick Preview Information:

  • Dates: July 13 – 17
  • Times: 0800 – 1600
  • Location: 2nd Floor at the Atlantic/Central Base Pick Room

Shop Steward Nominations

The Spring/Summer Shop Steward List is out, and you will be able to find the list in the July edition of the News Review. The list is also available on the Union Bulletin boards at the bases, and on the Union Website. If you missed the deadline to put in for Shop Steward, no worries, you'll get a chance to nominate for Shop Steward in July. Please remember, every member will have to submit a nomination every shakeup, so for the Fall/Winter 2026 Nomination, all will need to nominate themselves during the open nomination period that will start during the July pick preview. The reason for this is due to the shakeup being where some may change bases, decide they want a break from being a Shop Steward, want to nominate for Chief Shop Steward, or nominate for Shop Steward for the first time. This is not a live list, so please be sure to read the bulletins and/or the News Review for the Nomination dates. Once the Nomination closes, and the list comes out, please let me know ASAP if you don't see your name on the first SS Nomination list that is posted so I can get you added. Once the second revised SS nomination list comes out, there will be no revisions to this list, and you will have to remember to nominate yourself when nominations open again or send me an email stating you missed the nomination window and I will add you to the list for Spring/Summer nomination window. And with that, thank you to all who are willing to step up and sever the membership, you're all very much appreciated by this local and those who you represent.

Not going to be at Pick?

Please fill out an absentee form. You can locate these forms in the following places: The Union Website, the Window, and in the pick room during pick preview. You can return your completed absentee pick form to; The window at your base, emailed to me at recsec@atu587.org, and during pick preview, to the pick room. When pick starts, please turn in absentees to your base window or email them to me, please don't enter the live pick room to turn in your absentee. Please remember to leave a good contact number where you can be reached, and if you're going to be out of the country, we can contact you via WhatsApp, just be sure to indicate on the absentee pick form that you will need a call via WhatsApp. If you choose to have a friend pick for you, please make sure they pick no more than 2hrs before or after you pick. For those volunteering to help your classmate, family, or friend pick, please remember that if they pick right ahead or right after you that you will not have your 20min to preview the work, so again, to ensure that you or the person you're picking for will have the 20min pick preview, don't agree to pick for someone that picks within a hour or less of your pick. If I see that you don't have enough time after knowing you're picking for someone else, I will instruct you to go preview the work for yourself, and I can look up the work they want. Remember, this is why the Union is in the pick room, to ensure everyone who is supposed to be picking, can and will pick. Lastly, please remember, Union picks are not subject to the grievance process, so please be sure if you submit an absentee and are not available by phone that you clearly indicate your work choices.

Vacation Pick

This pick is for Jan-March vacation periods. If you're not going to be at pick, please indicate your preferred vacation periods on the absentee form. Please note that the Union does not pick vacations, this is done via the vacation pick room. At the conclusion of picking your work, the vacation pick room will call you to pick your vacation. Please be sure to be available when the vacation room calls.

Not Listed on the Pick List?

If you're not on the pick list, this is likely due to being out on medical or other continuous leave during the shake up(s) and you have not returned to work prior to June 2026. You will want to contact Transit Disability Services and/or your Chief to let them know you're cleared to return to work. For medical, you will want to send your updated medical that clears you to return to work, full duty, no restrictions, to Transit Disability Services prior to your pick date.

Pick Room Phone (206) 477-0208 FOR EMERGENCIES ONLY

Once pick has started, please note that we're in a live pick on the pick room floor and will not always be able to answer the phone, therefore, please only call the pick room during live pick hours for emergencies only, e.g., running late for your pick, not going to make it to pick in time. All other callers' names and phone numbers will be taken for a call back once the live pick ends for the day.

Thank you all for taking the time to read all of this information. I'm here to help and make your pick easier, so please feel free to reach out to me if you need any assistance. Happy Fall Pick!

item.title: Good Investigations Identify Causes—Shortcuts Identify Culprits
item.dc:creator: Andy Price, Union Member
item.content:encoded:
By Andy Price, Union Member

Missed stops are not new. What appears to be new is the growing tendency to treat every missed-stop complaint as though the only question that matters is whether somebody can later be identified on a video.

That should concern every operator.

Many operators have noticed an increasing reliance on surveillance footage and a growing tendency to reduce investigations to a single question:

"Was someone standing there?"

If the answer is yes, the conclusion increasingly seems to be that the operator must have done something wrong.

But transit is not that simple.

A person visible on a paused video image reviewed later in an office is not necessarily visible to an operator approaching in real time while monitoring traffic, pedestrians, cyclists, mirrors, signals, and roadway hazards.

You cannot stop for what you cannot reasonably see.

Many Eastside operators know exactly what we're talking about. Some bus zones are hidden behind hedges. Some stop poles are placed far back on private-property setbacks. Some are poorly illuminated. Some are so rarely used that the only reason operators know they exist is because years of experience have taught them where they are.

If a stop can disappear behind a hedge, then the problem is bigger than the operator.

Operators are increasingly finding themselves disciplined for passing up passengers who made little or no effort to indicate they wanted service. Standing motionless in dark clothing, several feet back from the curb, looking at a phone, and giving no visible indication of intent may be enough for a surveillance camera to identify someone afterward. That does not necessarily mean the person was reasonably visible to an operator approaching in darkness.

Some passengers quite literally stand like statues in the dark and then, after the bus has gone by, become clearly visible on a paused video image viewed later in an office.

Management points to the video and says, "See, they were there."

But that is exactly the problem.

Article 3.8 was negotiated because surveillance footage was never intended to become the basis for routine minor discipline. Policy 15 exists because customer complaints are supposed to be investigated, not reduced to a freeze frame and a predetermined conclusion.

The increasing dependence on video may actually be narrowing management's vision rather than improving it.

Technology should assist investigations, not replace them.

Metro already has a customer complaint policy. Policy 15 exists for a reason. Complaints are supposed to be investigated. Customers are supposed to be contacted. Circumstances are supposed to be considered. The goal should be to understand why something happened and how to prevent it from happening again.

Instead, many operators are concerned that investigations increasingly begin and end with video review.

Ironically, this growing dependence on surveillance can undermine protections intended for both customers and operators. In the process of showing videos to operators, the identities of complaining customers can effectively become known, even though the complaint process was designed to protect those individuals.

Nobody benefits when policies designed to protect everyone are gradually ignored.

Across the transit industry, agencies recognize that visibility is a shared responsibility.

Island Transit instructs riders to stand where they can be seen, signal approaching buses, and even use flashlights during darkness or fog. Kitsap Transit encourages riders to wave, so operators know they intend to board.

Around the world, passengers are expected to make their intentions known. Anyone who has used transit systems in places like London understands this. Simply standing near a bus stop without making your intentions obvious can easily result in being passed by. That isn't poor service. It's common sense.

King County Metro already recognizes this principle in some locations. Passenger-activated flashing lights already exist at certain stops to alert approaching operators that someone is waiting. If these systems improve safety and reliability at some locations, why not expand them?

Why not trim vegetation more aggressively?

Why not relocate hidden stops?

Why not move stop poles to locations visible from the operator's seat?

Why not review locations generating repeated complaints?

Why not focus on prevention instead of discipline?

Assigning blame is easy.

Solving problems is harder.

Operators accept responsibility for doing our jobs professionally. We always have.

Management should accept responsibility for the system it creates.

Missed stops are not simply operator problems.

They are system problems.

And system problems require system solutions.

Operators are not asking for special treatment.

We are asking management to follow the contract, follow its own policies, and recognize that missed stops are rarely caused by one factor alone.

Good investigations identify causes.

Shortcuts identify culprits.

Those are not the same thing.

item.title: Resolution from Executive Board Report: Responsible Investment of Washington State Funds
item.content:encoded:
Resolution to support responsible investment of Washington State funds, to ensure our public pensions, college tuition savings accounts, and taxpayer money are invested responsibly for our collective future.

WHEREAS, workers in ATU 587 overwhelmingly support universal human rights, environmental sustainability and good corporate governance; and

WHEREAS, The Washington State Investment Board (WSIB) manages pension funds, the state's Graduated Education Tuition Fund, Long Term Care Tax, worker's compensation and educational trusts, such that that this body's investment choices impact all Washingtonian workers, including members of ATU 587

WHEREAS, ATU 587 members believe WSIB's fiduciary duty to "maximize profits at a prudent level of risk" can, and should, go hand in hand with applying a framework for responsible investing. Companies that are engaging in major environmental harm, human rights abuses or actions that contradict our state's policy priorities have an inherent risk. Our money is invested toward a thirty year horizon: we know that it is not sustainable to continue these practices and turn consistent profit; and

WHEREAS, under the direction of the WSIB, these funds are invested in hundreds of companies that are contributing to and profiting from severe human rights violations, ecosystem destruction, and reckless business models that harm workers; and

WHEREAS, WSIB's fiduciary duty is to Washington state workers and residents. The WSIB hasn't fully considered or communicated the risks of investing in companies profiting from gross human rights abuses, accelerating climate disaster, conducting surveillance, detention and deportation of immigrants, or committing serious financial crimes.

THEREFORE, BE IT RESOLVED, that ATU 587 asks the Washington State Labor Council to support the passage of the WA Responsible Investment Act in the State Legislature. This legislation would require the WSIB to publish a clear Responsible Investment Framework, outlining exclusion criteria (e.g., severe human rights violations, ecosystem destruction, reckless business models) and engagement strategies.

BE IT ALSO RESOLVED that ATU 587 will include support for the Fund Our Futures legislation as evaluation criteria when endorsing political candidates.

BE IT ALSO RESOLVED that an ATU 587 representative will testify on behalf of the union supporting the WA Responsible Investment Act when it is being considered in the State Legislature.

BE IT ALSO RESOLVED that ATU 587 support the Fund Our Futures campaign in its effort to encourage the Washington State Investment Board to follow responsible investment practices, and encourage the WSLC to support this campaign for investment that aligns with the values of Washingtonians, the laws of the United States, and international laws.

item.title: Washington's Risky Investments that Affect Our Pensions
item.dc:creator: Ross Kirshenbaum #22409
item.content:encoded:
By Ross Kirshenbaum #22409

Hello union siblings, my name is Ross Kirshenbaum, I've been a proud ATU member since 2016.

I wanted to bring your attention to an issue that impacts all of us. For those of you unaware, our pension money is managed by the Washington State Investment Board (WSIB), which is a panel of both elected and appointed members. They determine where our pension money is invested.

As it turns out, over a billion dollars of our money is invested in companies that are actively committing human rights violations and contributing to the destabilization of the social fabric of our society:

Companies like the private prison company, Geo Group, which is profiting from the kidnapping of our immigrant friends and neighbors. Conditions inside GEO Group facilities are so terrible that hundreds of immigrants have been participating in hunger and labor strikes at their facilities across the country, including here in Tacoma.

And the tech company Palantir, which is providing ICE with data tracking software to surveil undocumented immigrants, as well as the cell phones of US citizens.

Or Chevron, which is contributing to climate change, while spreading misinformation about the impacts of greenhouse gases on our health, as well as committing human rights violations across several continents.

And there's also RealPage, which provides rental management companies with an algorithm that predicts the maximum rent management companies can charge. This has been linked to skyrocketing rental and housing prices here in King County.

These are just a few companies the WSIB has our money invested in, but we can say no! There is a broad coalition of unions and human rights organizations here in Washington state called Fund Our Futures (futures-wa.org), which is putting forward legislation calling for responsible investments for our hard-earned pension money. This legislation will demand the WSIB adopt ethical investment guidelines, ensuring that we're not invested in these risky companies who are often paying out millions and millions of dollars in settlements because they don't respect the law in their business practices.

This legislation will protect the value of our pensions and ensure the money we collect when we retire is not blood money.

Several unions have already passed resolutions to support, including WEA, AFTWA, WFSE, UAW and PROTEC17 to name a few.

Let's join the call and take a stand as a union and sign on to support the Washington Responsible Investment Act. I am planning to put forward a resolution that our union supports this legislation, and I hope you will support this resolution and vote to approve it at our next union meeting!

Personally, I believe we deserve better. We work too hard in conditions that are growing harder by the day because of this ongoing divestment in us…the city, the county, the state and the country…they're all divesting from our basic needs as workers.

Let's lead the way and demand investments in a future that we want to see.

item.title: Stranger Than Fiction: When Safety Policy Starts Writing Its Own Story
item.dc:creator: Michael Mackay, Transit Operator Rep #1
item.content:encoded:
By Michael Mackay, Transit Operator Rep #1

I have spent enough time inside this system to know what it is supposed to be: precise, accountable, and fair. That is the foundation accident preventability was built on, grounded in National Safety Council standards and reinforced through decades of policy meant to correct behavior, not punish it. But what I have been seeing lately does not always match that promise. At times, it feels like the narrative is no longer guided by facts, but by something else entirely, something closer to fiction than reality.

Nearly twenty years ago, when I was operating out of North Base, I was accused of striking a truck while merging onto I 5 in the early morning hours. By midday, the decision had already been made preventable. Case closed.

But it was not closed.

With guidance from a seasoned shop steward, Neal Safron, I returned to the scene with a Polaroid camera and a measuring tape. I was not there to argue. I was there to document. What I found told a different story. The damage on the bus sat nearly three feet higher than where the truck's mirror could have made contact. Even after factoring in tire height variations for that vehicle model, the conclusion became unavoidable: the narrative did not hold up.

That ruling was overturned.

That experience stayed with me because it proved something essential. The system works when facts are allowed to lead. It also showed how quickly a conclusion can be written before the facts are fully understood.

In my current role overseeing accident rereads and arbitrations for the Union, I am seeing a troubling pattern. Since stepping into this position, I was informed that we have experienced an 84 percent turnover rate. That level of turnover does not happen in isolation. It raises a necessary question: are we applying policy in a way that aligns with its intent? Too often, the answer appears to be no.

I see small errors turning into major consequences. Preventable designations are issued without full context. Point totals escalate in ways that feel mechanical rather than deliberate. With the matrix, fifteen points become twenty four, and suddenly a career is on the line.

I have seen tires at the end of their lifecycle unzip at worn seams and be labeled preventable. I have seen coaches, physically unable to move, still deemed preventable when another vehicle struck them. I have seen inconsistencies in accident probation, where lower seniority employees are granted second chances while higher seniority operators with decades of service are not.

And then there is the math.

You are told this system is objective, built on clear thresholds and consistent application. But when a Safety Quality report explicitly states, "no visible injury," and two points for visible injury are still added, the numbers begin to tell a different story. When a 15,000 dollar vehicle damage claim is treated as if it crosses a 28,000 dollar threshold, triggering additional points, the calculation no longer reflects reality.

Somehow, two plus two becomes eight.

At that point, it is no longer just a miscalculation. It is a narrative being imposed on the facts rather than drawn from them.

In Stranger Than Fiction, the main character begins to hear a voice narrating his life, dictating outcomes before they happen. He initially assumes the system around him is fixed and inevitable. As the story unfolds, it becomes clear that the narrative itself can be challenged, and that it is not beyond correction.

That is where you are now.

You are told the system is straightforward: resolve issues at the lowest level, keep safety and discipline separate, keep safety and base chiefs separate, and focus on correction rather than punishment. On paper, that looks simple. In practice, that simplicity often breaks down. Outcomes drift. Decisions lose connection to context. The line between what happened and how it is recorded starts to blur.

There are moments when the system corrects itself. I served as the partisan arbitrator in the Ben DeMonte arbitration last year, where termination was pursued despite the absence of a fatality or external claim. The arbitrator rejected that approach and reinforced a key principle: the most severe discipline must be reserved for the most severe circumstances. The result was reinstatement with back pay.

That decision made something clear. The system is not beyond repair, but it does not correct itself automatically.

We now have to decide what kind of system we are operating in. We can continue to rely on a framework that is sound on paper but inconsistently applied, or we can insist that its principles are followed in practice.

We know what Metro's policy says. It calls for fairness, accuracy, and proportionality. It is designed to correct behavior, not to produce outcomes that feel disconnected from reality.

But when similar cases produce different results, when calculations become flexible, and when context is overlooked, confidence in the system erodes. People stop believing that decisions are anchored in facts. They start feeling like characters in someone else's story, waiting for a conclusion that has already been written.

Like any story, this one is still being written. If we are not paying attention, it can drift into something unrecognizable, structured, documented, and official, yet just a little too strange to be true.

But it can also be corrected.

That requires attention to detail, a willingness to question outcomes, and a commitment to ensuring that decisions reflect facts, not assumptions. It requires us to insist that accident preventability remain what it was meant to be: precise, accountable, and fair.

Because in transit, as in any system built on trust, accuracy is not optional. Fairness is not negotiable. And the line between reality and interpretation must remain clear.

From the News Review, July 2026, pages 12–13. Open in the PDF · Original file on atu587.org

item.title: Thank You
item.dc:creator: James E. Reese
item.content:encoded:
By James E. Reese

I can't speak for every operator at King County Metro; that would be presumptuous, but I can speak for myself. And if others feel the same after reading this, then maybe these words will finally give voice to a gratitude many of us have carried quietly for far too long. Because before any bus rolls out of a base, before a single passenger steps aboard, before an operator even clocks in, there is an entire workforce behind the scenes holding this system together with skill, sweat, and pride. Maintenance, Facilities, every crew who cleans, repairs, inspects, welds, replaces, rebuilds, and responds, you are the backbone of this operation, the reason any of us can do our jobs at all.

People see operators every day. They hear our voices, watch us navigate traffic, and sometimes blame us for everything from late trips to the weather. But they rarely see you — the ones who keep these buses breathing. You're out there in the cold, in the rain, in the middle of the night, crawling under coaches, swapping out parts, cleaning up messes no one wants to talk about, and coming to our aid when we break down miles from base. Some folks wish every bus could be spotless every day, but anyone who's ever stepped foot in a base knows the truth: you're already performing miracles with the time and resources you have.

So let me say this plainly, without ceremony or corporate gloss: thank you. Thank you for the work that goes unseen until the moment something goes wrong. Thank you for keeping us safe, for keeping the public safe, and for carrying a burden most people never even realize exists. Without you, we couldn't do our jobs, and the entire system would collapse before sunrise. It is an honor to work alongside you, even if our paths cross only in passing. You deserve recognition, respect, and genuine gratitude every single day, not just when a crisis hits.

item.title: Take the Wheel: Our Stories Are Our Power
item.dc:creator: Chuck Lare, a Shop Steward & Safety Committee Chair
item.content:encoded:
By Chuck Lare, a Shop Steward & Safety Committee Chair

You already know what it feels like when the road is against you — a brutal schedule, a behavioral health crisis at your stop, and backup that shows up late or not at all. What you might not fully feel yet is just how much power you actually hold.

It starts with a story.

On May 29th, Metro's Refugees & Immigrants Support & Empowerment (RISE) affinity group and Equity, Inclusion and Belonging (EIB) team gathered operators for "The Stories That Shape Us." An operator described her father's Vietnam service and gave us a name that fits: Bus Pilots. A Samoan brother got the whole room clapping with two simple hand motions. A Hawaiian operator couple explained what it truly means to be a chief. Different routes, different backgrounds — one coach.

That is not sentiment. That is strategy.

Cohesion Is a Safety Tool

When operators know each other's stories, they move differently. They cover each other. They communicate. The bus ahead of you is not just your leader, the bus behind you is not just your follower, we are partners. When you work in unison with your leader and your follower, you stop being commanded by a bad schedule and start controlling your own trip.

That is not a small thing. That is your livelihood.

The more cohesion we build through shared stories and mutual trust, the more authority we earn over our own working conditions — not handed down from management but generated organically from the floor up.

What We're Demanding Right Now

Your Base Safety and Security Committee reps are not venting. They have come together to advocate for specific, concrete changes:

  • Visible security at high-incident stops — site-specific deployment, not vague reassurances. Metro Transit Police need to operate as a full-service model. Coverage gaps need to be mapped and closed.
  • Chronic offender accountability — real removal mechanisms and real-time exclusion information shared with you, the operator, not delivered after an incident.
  • Real crisis response — expanded CARE teams and KC Outreach Group behavioral health coverage during evening and overnight hours. You should not be alone at 2 a.m. with zero backup.
  • Regional coordination — unified data infrastructure and cross-agency partnerships so a crisis on your route does not vanish into a gap between three agencies that do not talk to each other.

These are not policy wishes. These are the distance between what you face every shift and the support that should be there.

The KC Transit Safety Regional Task Force and the Contract Action Team are the vehicles we use to push these demands beyond the individual trip level. Get connected. Show up.

The Story We Want to End With

There is an operator operating for the longest time who picked off that route. On his new assignment, he received five rider accommodations almost immediately. He will tell you why: his attitude changed when his environment changed.

When operators are supported, riders feel it. Service improves. The job becomes something worth doing again.

The story we are working toward is the day that operator — and every operator running a hard route — can bring that same renewed spirit back with them, because the environment finally earned it.

That is the finish line. Tell your story. Know your leader. Cover your follower. Show up for each other.

The narrative belongs to us.

item.title: Bulletin: Dues Increase for July 2026
item.dc:creator: Paul Neil, Financial Secretary Treasurer
item.content:encoded:
Read from a scanned image on page 18 of the PDF, so it may contain errors. View page 18 in the PDF.

By Paul Neil, Financial Secretary Treasurer

Bulletin dated June 10, 2026. To: ATU Local 587 Members.

The bylaws of ATU Local 587 provide in Article VIII "Dues and Assessments":

Section 1. Dues, Computation and Deduction

The dues for each member of the Local shall be based upon two times the average hourly wage for represented employees in effect on January 1 of each year at each bargaining unit. (The average hourly wage shall be computed by adding the top hourly wage of the lowest and highest represented job classifications at each bargaining unit and then dividing this figure by two.) Any increase in the dues based on this average hourly wage will be subject to the approval of the membership at the regular January Union meetings.

  • (a) The monthly dues shall not include any special assessments as outlined in Section 2.
  • (b) The first 50% of the monthly dues shall be taken out of the first paycheck of the month. The remaining 50% of the monthly dues shall be taken out of the second paycheck of the month.
  • (c) After the first year of implementation, no increase in union dues shall be considered for any bargaining unit where the average hourly wage increased by less than 1% in the previous calendar year.
  • (d) Members hired for a part time position shall only pay the ATU International per capita tax plus the initiation fee until the initiation fee is fully paid. After the initiation fee is paid, these members shall pay the ATU International minimum dues or the dues for their bargaining unit whichever is lower during their first year of membership.
  • (e) All increases in the ATU International per capita taxes after June 30, 2014, will be passed on directly to members.
  • (f) For properties outside of King County, the job classification used for dues computation will be based on each division.

The chart shows the updated dues amount by each bargaining unit. Per notification from the ATU International Secretary Treasurer the International Per Capita has increased from $20.25 to $20.75 per month, based on a change in the Consumer Price Index (CPI-W) published by the US Dept. of Labor. The net change is $0.50/month. These dues rates will become effective for July dues.
