item.title: The 1st Vice President's Report: Kitsap Transit, Shop Steward Class, Organizing Bases and Arbitration Updates
item.dc:creator: Cory Rigtrup
item.content:encoded:
By Cory Rigtrup

April was a drop-dead busy kind of month. I like to come in early, load up on caffeine and pound out as much work as I can, before the commerce of the day begins. However, I have been failing on many levels. In April we've been able to temporarily set up a new workstation and start staffing it with Board Officers to help with the workload. Optimistically, by mid-May, we'll have the logistics worked out, so we can become more effective. Any help is greatly appreciated.

Kitsap Transit:

In April, we were able to get our fourth operator fired this year, their job back. Anyone who is not from Kitsap, is likely not to know what's going on over there. Kitsap isn't just one of the places where if you can hit something with a bus, you probably will. Kitsap has been changing to enforce all kinds of work rules, both old and new. They also like to relive any moment a member does almost anything, and sharing the video viewing experience with members , lots of videos. Our Local has some incredible and rapidly experienced stewards, that are close to being overwhelmed, but do amazing work holding management accountable.

I took the Saturday night Kitsap meeting off to spend time with my wife. Monday, Greg reported that members are riled up and want to speak with the authority board. As luck would have it, the board was meeting next morning, so I jammed over there. Not my typical Cory kind of speech filled with aggression and absolution innuendoes, rather challenging the board as to what kind of employer do they want to be? The following two days I went to a Kitsap termination and suspension grievance. Stay tuned, we are in the thick of it, one side has to give and we are made of sterner stuff.

Shop Steward Class:

If the plan works out, May is going to be exciting! Our Local should be hosting Shop Steward classes at the Union office, also in Bremerton and Sequim. We are going full tilt on providing various classes that are designed to teach property specific stewards as our annual steward rosters have just changed.

This is a great time to become a shop steward. If you're a self-motivated kind of person who doesn't like to see people struggling, becoming a steward could be rewarding for you. If you're the kind of person who's got fire in the belly and energy to burn, becoming a steward is probably great for you. A steward is a position of service, a person who likes to help others. Often times, the people needing help aren't the most popular and don't look like you, but they really need help. Answer the call.

Organizing the bases:

There is some excitement mounting! The idea that our Local will focus on increasing organization with the bases, is spreading like fire. Now that it's May, you should see the new list of names posted on the Union boards. We are working on getting base meetings set up, where we can get as many stewards as possible on those lists together, so we can strategize best commutation methods and what a base's needs are.

In broad strokes, once we get everyone on the same page and communicating, we can assess a base's strengths and weaknesses. With that we can start to structure an action plan for representations and development of stewards. I am a big proponent of mentoring, getting burned, then learning from those mistakes to get better. Remember scares are cool in the steward world, as we learn more from losing than winning.

Parts of this plan are still conceptual at this point; all the help is well appreciated!

Arbitration updates:

If you look at page three of our News Review, you will see a column labeled "Arbitration Update." Last month, we had ten Arbitrations listed. Only the wrongful termination of Ryerson base operator Timbrook had an arbitration date scheduled. Today we have seven exciting arbitrations scheduled. All seven have hearings ranging from June through October, plus the two new ones were just approved in April.

What happened? Well, four arbitrations got resolved, settlements without holding the arbitration. We also added a one from February, Oda. From 2020–2025, we averaged two arbitrations held a year. Cleary that doesn't work. The system was broken; we just couldn't get enough hearings held to keep up with the workload. About a month ago, there was big meeting with our lawyers and the prosecuting attorney's office. I don't believe they broke bread, but they did get every arbitration on the books scheduled. This is great, some of these grievances are many years old. We need resolution.

item.title: The Maintenance Vice President's Report: Bus Facilities Maintenance and Bus Vehicle Maintenance
item.dc:creator: Jeff Stambaugh
item.content:encoded:
By Jeff Stambaugh

The Saga of Facilities maintenance continues. While the Pick was finally posted and conducted, the final posting was not what we had hoped to see, while the number of "Usually shelter maintenance positions" and "supplementals" were reduced, it appears that games are still being played to erode seniority and limit picked work out of South Facilities. TFD management now has an opportunity to update the route sheets to reflect the work that is being done and post the work for employees to pick in the fall. I would suggest that The Union and management put a joint committee together to work through this process.

The Union has also Filed an Unfair Labor Practice (ULP) against Metro for grievance retaliation. It has appears that TFD management has retaliated against our members for exercising their protected right to file grievance(s). We will let PERC decide.

Speaking of ULP, we are scheduled to meet with PERC in early May over the ULP filed for Bus VM issuing unexcused absences for Holiday work assignments. More to come.

After the VM bus pick, many of our members requested a change of hours to meet the work life balance we all strive to achieve. Most of these 15-to-30-minute requests were for Childcare or Carpool, and VM has been granting many of these types of requests for years. Not anymore apparently. First, I would like to thank the chiefs and superintendents who were able to accommodate their employee's needs, additionally I would like to thank the superintendents who took the time to sit down and listen to their employees needs and provide reasonable feedback on why they felt they could not meet the accommodation, while we may not agree on the ability to accommodate, we have a better understanding of why you denied the request. All that being said, I am a bit confused at the number of denials that were sent to the Union and the various information included (or not), some simply denied by the superintendent "Does Not Meet Business Needs," others with with chief approval, and a denial from the superintendent "Does Not Meet Business Needs".

Many of these denials were from CSC, which only added to my confusion, most of our members at CSC have routine work that they perform daily, and they usually know what that work is, and what is needed from them. While what they do every day greatly contributes to the day to day VM operations, no one in management has been able explain to me how a 15–30 minute schedule change "Does Not Meet the Business Needs," very few employees at CSC receive or provide turnover to the next shift, so I ask of senior leadership, "What business need does this not meet?" I always thought King County was a benevolent employer and could reasonably accommodate these types of requests to help achieve a greater work life balance. Maybe I need to rethink that?

One last thought, FIFA. The Union has been asking leadership for the past few months if OT will be used prior to FIFA to be prepared, in the various responses and through other conversations is appears that management has taken the position that if OT is limited then AC requests will also be limited and more employees will be at work and not requesting time off, I actually had one "manager" tell me "if we limit OT, they wont have AC to take off."

Way to boost morale!

item.title: The Recording Secretary's Report: Pride in Toledo!
item.dc:creator: Latrelle Gibson
item.content:encoded:
By Latrelle Gibson

I had the pleasure of attending the ATU International 2nd Annual Pride Caucus Conference April 26 – 29, in Toledo, Ohio.

On the date of arrival, we checked in, gathered our credentials and were invited to a tour of the TARTA (Toledo Area Rapid Transportation Authority) system. We were all bused to the main garage where TARTA's Local 697 President, Krissy Bofia, worked with management in putting together a welcome social for us. While at the worksite, we toured the yard, maintenance shop, and operator bull pin. After leaving the worksite, we were bused to TARTA's main transportation hub in the city center. I had the pleasure of being the only one on the bus and was able to have a great conversation with the operator and ask about their working conditions, management support with unruly passengers, and how they deal with unruly passengers. Once we arrived at the transit hub, we were given a tour of their facilities there. This is where the IVP and I grilled a manger on issuing discipline and when the operators are invited to provide input for their workspaces and what this looks like. I did make the comment that I wished we were being guided by an actual boots on the ground transit operators, and not management, but was happy that the Union President was able to help get this organized.

IVP Carly Allen welcomed all of us to Toledo and was happy to host and show us what Toledo has to offer. She also thanked the Pride Caucus Board for selecting Toledo to hold the conference, knowing other offers were made by other locals to host the caucus.

We heard from the ATU Local 113 Attorney, Simon Blackstone, who spoke about LGBTQIA+ rights in the workplace, and writing protections in the CBA for these rights.

Conference Day 1

ATU International Pride Caucus President, Michael Mackay opened the conference with a Land Acknowledgment. After the invocation, we learned the history of the labor movement and queer history from the yester queer group. We heard from the honorary speaker, Tammy Parish, who spoke on Women's history month and her being the first woman in the maintenance role at TARTA.

Mayor Wade Kapszukiewicz spoke about the lowering crime rate in Toledo, private companies not recognizing Unions in the 30's, Toledo's history of sit down strikes, Toledo being ahead of the curve when it came to LGBTQIA+ rights, being the first city in Ohio to offer medical benefits to domestic partners of city workers, and about Toledo not making time for the divisions and un-inclusiveness of their population.

Panelist and facilitator, Lillian Brents on how to be an ally:

Ways to take action as an ally:

  • Sit down and listen to the LGBTQIA+ community
  • Speak out against injustices, don't wait until it happens to you or someone you know
  • Try taking these actions back to your local
  • Listen and learn
  • Stop listening to respond
  • Allies showing up to support and learn, and those allies bringing more potential allies to these events to learn
  • Work on listening

How to be an ally:

  • Acknowledge your privilege
  • Listen actively
  • Educate yourself
  • Speak out on Anti-LGBTQIA+ statements and jokes
  • Negotiating for your ENTIRE unit

Why be an ally:

  • Promote equality and justice
  • Create a safer and more inclusive environment
  • Amplifying marginalized voices
  • Personal growth and learning
  • Building stronger Unions
  • Taking actions
  • Challenging bias and stereotypes
  • Creating a workplace that values diversity and inclusion

We also heard from Karima Howard who spoke on the struggles on the fight the LGBTQIA+ community faces. She spoke on her own experience with her granddaughter struggling with her sexuality and her not thinking anything of the behavior change, discounting this as normal teenage issues. Her granddaughter tried to commit suicide by taking pills because of this struggle, and Karima spoke to why it's important to address these issues early and not put them on the back burner, because you never know what someone is struggling with.

Other panelist spoke on how they stood up for their family members struggling with their sexuality, with the President of Local 697 Krissy Bofia, spoke about her mother losing custody of her and her siblings and the threat of being placed in foster care unless a family member would step up and take them in. The only family member who would step up was her aunt, who is gay, and this was a fight with the state due to her aunt being gay, however, luckily, the courts allowed for her aunt to take them in. Experiencing this firsthand and defending her aunt against homophobic comments made by her teacher has made Krissy an ally since she was a child.

Conference Day 2, last day

John Costa opened the conference with an opening speech and spoke about his brother who was closeted and didn't come out until he was 40yrs old.

TARTA CEO, Laura Koprowski, spoke on transit safety and advocating penalties that match the crimes committed against transit workers. Spoke on the funding short falls of reliance on property tax and legislating sales tax instead to fund transit and close these short falls.

We heard from City Council member, Nick Komires, who spoke on being the 2nd openly gay elected Council Member in Toledo. He spoke on laws passed under the first openly gay Council Member to protect gay rights. We heard from Carlos Mayorga, ATU local 758 Pride Caucus President, who shared slides on how to get a local Pride Caucus started, how to form a local Pride Caucus, the obstacles to getting this started, and recruiting and maintaining members.

And lastly, we heard from Brittany Anderson from Pride At work, who spoke on Union values, fighting the billionaire agenda, trans and non-binary 101, common workplace and Union challenges trans workers face, trans rights are labor rights, Trumps Executive order stripping collective bargaining rights from 1 million federal workers, the repeal or weakening of over 60 workplace safety regulations. We also participated in an interactive crowd participation exercise where we wrote our own 5 words of Union solidarity.

In closing, I want to thank the ATU 587 membership for supporting sending us to this Conference, as it was an honor to be able to attend the 2nd Annual Pride Caucus Conference. Moving forward, I plan on trying to attend all the Caucus Conferences, I do not mind paying my own way to immerse myself in the experience. I truly believe the experience is invaluable, and I'm able to learn the experience of others which will help me be a better advocate.

Photo caption: From Left to Right, ATU International Executive Vice President, Yvett Trujilo, Geroge DeCuir, ATU International President, John Costa, ATU International Pride Caucus President, Michael Mackay.

item.title: The Stories We Tell: Clearing the Mush at Metro (Part 1 of 2)
item.dc:creator: Balaramdas Stern, Shop Steward, SLC Rep, Wellness Champion, Mentors Moving Metro – Bellevue Base
item.content:encoded:
By Balaramdas Stern, Shop Steward, SLC Rep, Wellness Champion, Mentors Moving Metro – Bellevue Base

We work in a place where people are always reading…the route, the radio, people's tone of voice, the look on someone's face, and the silence that sometimes follows.

Sometimes this is where problems arise: less in what happened, and more in the stories we create in our minds about "what happened."

When we don't know why someone did something, our brains naturally try to fill in the blanks. This space, between what someone intended and what was received, has been called The Interpersonal Gap.

Usually, when we let our guesses and unverified assumptions run the show, we end up in what organizational psychologist Gervase Bushe calls interpersonal mush: the foggy, sticky, fear-fed mess where trust starts to break down and fester. The interpersonal mush erodes the kind of trust that is vital to an agency grounded in sustained partnership on behalf of all those we serve...including each other.

Here is what struck me when I first learned about this: the mush is not a malfunction, it's the normal default. It forms automatically every time human beings interact, because none of us can see inside another person's mind. The question is never whether mush will form. It always will. The question is whether we have a way to notice when we're doing this, and clear it.

For a long time, this was a blind spot for me. I wonder how many of us are in the same boat.

Here's an example. A new recruit in training finishes a rough pull-out. They see the Instructor lean toward a Supervisor and whisper while looking in their direction. The trainee's heart sinks, and their mind goes immediately to the worst case scenario: "They're talking about me and what I did wrong. I'm sure to get fired."

What the Instructor is actually thinking: "They held it together through a difficult start. We should give them a later report time tomorrow."

Same situation. Two completely different ideas about what's happening. I have been on both sides of this one.

Now picture a vehicle maintenance Lead walking through the bay multiple times in an hour. No greeting. No stop. Just that slow, thinking face we all know so well. The mechanic asks herself: "I'm sure they're watching me because they don't trust my work."

The Lead is actually buried in a parts delay, a schedule problem, and a vendor issue, trying to solve three fires with limited time and resources.

Same walk-by. Different story being fabricated.

Or consider a Superintendent who sends a vague email to a Chief at their base: "See me at 2:00 PM." That is all it takes. The rest of the afternoon becomes a full internal trial. "I'm being called in for bad news. Maybe they've already decided."

The Superintendent wants to talk about a mentoring opportunity. They think you'd be good at it. No one does their best work while imagining the worst case scenario. One added sentence…"It's a positive conversation, wanted to give you the heads up"…and the whole day changes. That is a leader who understands human nature and chooses to get ahead of the story before it starts. What if more of us did that for each other?

Here is the question that can be hard to sit with: how many times this month have you been the person someone else was building a story about, and you never knew it?

What if the worst version of you that lives in someone else's head was created on a day you don't even remember, and the story they made up about you isn't true?

That is what makes the Interpersonal Gap relevant in our work and home lives. It doesn't just happen to us, it happens by us. We are all doing this, every day, without realizing it. Every time we rush past someone without a greeting, make an expression we're unaware of, send a vague message, or sit in silence when interacting with others, someone else's story machine starts spinning.

A skeptic might say: "Sometimes the story IS right. Sometimes they ARE talking about you."

This may very well be true. However, even then, the conversation is how you find out. This possibility of resolution isn't available to anyone when we don't sincerely inquire.

The clearing conversation is simpler than you think. We can name what we saw. Name the story we started telling ourselves. Then, ask a clear question: "I noticed you and the Supervisor talking while looking my way. The story I started telling myself was that I was in trouble. Is this true or is it something else?"

One sentence, and the chaos in our minds lifts.

Our roles in transit are integral to communication with others. We rely on kind, respectful communications that fortify trust and sustain partnership. A missed signal, a rough tone, a vague message…these things spread faster than good news, especially if nobody checks out the stories they're making up about others, and then lives from that story as if it were the truth.

So here is an invitation: try it once this week (or more if you like!). Pick the smallest moment…someone's look, a flippant comment, their tone…and instead of being absolutely sure of your story and keeping it to yourself, or trying to make sense of it with others, ask those involved. See if your assumption is correct. I've found it takes courage to do that. It may even surprise you.

So here is what I find myself wondering:

What would happen if we brought that same character to the stories we tell ourselves about each other? What would it look like if we chose to ask instead of assume? And what might we discover about ourselves and each other that the silence was never going to reveal?

Next month in Part 2: What happens when the story isn't wrong. Why the conversation still matters. And what it takes to build the kind of trust that works for everyone.

Sources and influences: Gervase Bushe's Clear Leadership; John Wallen's work on the Interpersonal Gap.

About the author: Balaramdas is a Transit Operator and Shop Steward at Bellevue Base. He enjoys spending time with family and friends, along with practicing hot yoga and Aikido.

item.title: One Union, One Voice, Unity Is Strength; Division Is Costly
item.dc:creator: Hassannoor Aden, Minority Affairs, ATU 587/King County Labor Delegate
item.content:encoded:
By Hassannoor Aden, Minority Affairs, ATU 587/King County Labor Delegate

Who Are We? Unity Across the black communities. In recent years, as a minority affairs executive Board ATU587 I have seen something troubling: growing division within communities that have long shared common struggles. These divisions are especially visible within Black communities, where questions of identity, history, and belonging are being debated in ways that can either strengthen us or pull us apart.

As a first-generation immigrant, I have personally experienced moments where my place within Black spaces was questioned. I have been told that because my family was not part of the history of slavery in the United States, I could not fully belong in Black caucuses or conversations. That perspective, while rooted in real historical pain, risks overlooking a broader truth.

Our histories may be different, but they are deeply connected. In the United States, the Black experience has been shaped by slavery, Reconstruction, Jim Crow, and the long fight for civil rights. This struggle produced powerful leaders like Martin Luther King Jr., who called for unity through nonviolence and justice, and Malcolm X, who emphasized dignity, self-determination, and global awareness of Black struggles.

At the same time, across Africa and the Caribbean, nations were fighting their own battles against colonial rule. Countries like Ghana, led by Kwame Nkrumah, gained independence in 1957, while others followed throughout the 1960s. Leaders such as Julius Nyerere guided their people through liberation movements that challenged exploitation and demanded self-governance.

These movements were not isolated. They were connected by a shared desire for freedom, dignity, and self-determination. Martin Luther King Jr. himself attended Ghana's independence celebration, recognizing that the fight for justice in America and the fight for independence in Africa were part of the same global struggle.

This idea is rooted in Pan-Africanism, a philosophy advanced by thinkers like W. E. B. Du Bois, who believed that people of African descent, no matter where they are in the world, share a linked destiny.

So why the division today?

Part of it comes from the need to protect history. For many African Americans, identity is tied to a specific and painful legacy that must never be erased or diluted. That concern is valid.

At the same time, immigrants from Africa and the Caribbean bring their own histories of colonization, displacement, and struggle. Being excluded from Black spaces can feel like a continuation of the very marginalization we are all trying to overcome.

When we focus only on what separates us, we weaken our collective voice. When we recognize what connects us, we strengthen it.

The leaders we often look to for guidance understood this clearly: Martin Luther King Jr. spoke of the "Beloved Community," a vision where justice and equality are achieved through unity across differences. Malcolm X, especially later in his life, expanded his view to see the struggle for Black liberation as part of a global human rights movement. Shirley Chisholm built coalitions across race, gender, and background because she understood that real change requires solidarity.

None of them argued for division. They argued for expanding the circle while still honoring the unique histories within it.

Unity does not mean ignoring differences. It means respecting them while recognizing that our futures are tied together.

In the workplace, in our unions, and in our communities, unity has practical power. It strengthens our ability to advocate for fair treatment, equal opportunity, and protection from discrimination. It ensures that no group is isolated or left behind. It builds the kind of collective strength that institutions cannot ignore.

Division, on the other hand, weakens our influence and allows inequality to persist.

So the question "Who are we?" is not meant to divide us. It is meant to remind us.

We are descendants of resilience. We are products of different histories, but shared struggles.

We are stronger together than we are apart.

The path forward is not about choosing one identity over another. It is about building bridges between them. Because in the end, unity is not just an idea. It is a strategy for justice.

Probationary Discharges and the Impact on Minority Workers

Article 4, Section 7 of our agreement states that employees who are discharged during their probationary period are not subject to the grievance and arbitration procedure. However, the language does provide one safeguard: upon request, an employee has the right to a termination review. This review must be requested within 15 days of notification, and Rail is required to schedule the review and respond to the Union in writing within a reasonable timeframe.

On paper, this may appear to strike a balance between management authority and employee rights. In practice, however, this language has had a disproportionate and concerning impact on minority employees, particularly within the training department.

As a representative in Minority Affairs, I have witnessed firsthand how this provision operates. It places probationary employees in a vulnerable position, where decisions about their future often rest on subjective evaluations rather than clear, consistent standards. Many members are released without being given a meaningful opportunity to improve, demonstrate their abilities, or fully learn the job.

There is a growing concern that this process has been inconsistently applied across training classes. Outcomes often vary depending on trainers, instructional approaches, and expectations. This inconsistency raises serious questions about fairness and equity, especially when patterns emerge showing that minority employees are disproportionately affected.

The situation also creates tension within Amalgamated Transit Union Local 587. The union represents both trainers and trainees, which can make accountability difficult and leave Minority Affairs caught in the middle. Despite this, it is our responsibility to speak up when we see patterns that undermine fairness and equal opportunity.

For many in our membership, particularly those of African descent and other underrepresented groups, the current process does not feel neutral. There is a growing perception that bias, whether intentional or not, is influencing outcomes. When individuals are judged as "not capable" without being given a fair chance to develop, it raises serious concerns about the integrity of the system.

The termination review process, while important, is limited in its effectiveness. It does not carry the same weight as a grievance or arbitration process, and in many cases, decisions are upheld without meaningful reconsideration. This leaves employees without a true path to challenge their discharge.

It is clear that this language needs to be revisited. We must ask whether it still serves the purpose of fairness, or whether it has become a tool that allows too much unchecked discretion. A system that gives management full control without strong accountability measures risks undermining trust across the workforce.

Engaging in the Political Process and The Role of ATU-COPE

I had the privilege of serving on the Committee on Political Education (COPE), the political action arm of the Amalgamated Transit Union. This committee plays a critical role in connecting transit workers to the political decisions that shape our daily lives.

COPE is more than just a committee. It is the collective voice of transit workers, ATU-COPE ensures that working people have a seat at the table at every level of government.

By law, union dues cannot be used to fund political campaigns. Instead, ATU-COPE is powered by voluntary contributions from members who believe in advancing pro-labor and pro-transit leadership. These contributions help support candidates who understand and respect the needs of frontline workers. But the work does not stop after Election Day. ATU-COPE continues to engage with elected officials to make sure our members' interests are represented in policy decisions.

Many of our members hold strong and diverse views about politics. Some are skeptical of politicians altogether, while others fall on different sides of the political spectrum. Regardless of where we stand individually, one thing is clear: political decisions directly affect our jobs, our safety, and our communities. Choosing to disengage does not remove the impact, it only removes our voice.

We have seen firsthand how political races, such as the recent King County government executive election, can create division within our union. Endorsements are not always easy, and they can bring strong opinions. However, the purpose of COPE is not to divide, but to ensure that our collective interests are considered when policies are written and implemented.

During my time on the committee, I had the responsibility, as part of Minority Affairs, to ask critical questions of candidates seeking endorsement. These questions focused on issues that matter deeply to our members and our communities.

These conversations are not symbolic. They are essential. They help us understand how those seeking power intend to use it, and whether their values align with fairness, justice, and the well-being of working people.

ATU-COPE makes endorsements as needed each year, always with the goal of protecting and advancing the interests of our members. Participation in this process is one of the strongest tools we have as union members.

Being part of COPE reinforced something important: whether we engage or not, politics will always shape our workplace and our future. Through COPE, we choose to engage, to ask questions, and to make sure our voices are heard.

item.title: Adding a Third Vice President: Questions of Representation and Responsibility
item.dc:creator: Andy Price, ATU Local 587 Member
item.content:encoded:
By Andy Price, ATU Local 587 Member

In the April edition of the ATU 587 News Review, President Greg Woodfill published a President's Report outlining the reasoning behind the proposal to add a third Vice President position to our Local. The membership voted to adopt that proposal during the March cycle of meetings. While that vote should be acknowledged, it is also appropriate to continue discussing the broader issues raised during the debate.

Union democracy does not end with a vote. Ongoing discussion about governance decisions—especially those involving long-term financial commitments—is a normal and healthy part of any democratic organization. Many of the concerns raised during the debate were not simply matters of opinion or preference, but questions about structure, cost, and long-term planning for the Local. Those questions remain relevant regardless of the outcome of any single vote.

Representation and Structure

One of the main arguments in favor of the new position is that two vice presidents were no longer sufficient to represent a membership of roughly 4,800 members. Yet the structure that was ultimately adopted raises its own questions.

The newly created position is largely justified on the basis of light rail operations along with several smaller properties. At present, light rail operations include roughly 200 operators, and even when including related classifications such as streetcar operations, the broader rail grouping still represents a relatively small portion of a membership that is primarily composed of bus operations. Whether creating a full-time executive officer position to represent that segment of the bargaining unit is the most efficient structure is a question many members raised during the discussion.

Another issue raised during the debate involves how representation and voting rights are structured. If implemented as approved, the position would be funded largely through dues paid by the entire membership—particularly the much larger group of Metro Transit bus operators—while those same members would not be eligible to run for or vote for that position.

Questions about representation, eligibility, and accountability are not unusual when unions adjust their governance structures. These are exactly the kinds of questions that thoughtful discussion can help clarify.

It is also worth noting that other large locals within the Amalgamated Transit Union have addressed representation challenges using different structural approaches. Some combine certain executive offices, while others utilize part-time vice presidents rather than expanding the number of full-time officers. These variations demonstrate that there are multiple ways to approach representation issues without necessarily increasing the number of full-time executive positions.

Financial Responsibility

The President's Report states that under any metric the Local can afford another Vice President. That conclusion deserves careful consideration.

The new position is expected to cost approximately $226,000 per year when salary, benefits, and associated expenses are taken into account. While the Local currently enjoys budget surpluses, the concern raised by many members was not whether the Local can afford the position today, but whether it represents a prudent long-term commitment.

Public transit funding and agency budgets are influenced by economic cycles and political decisions beyond our control. Recent discussions about potential federal transit funding reductions illustrate exactly why uncertainty should be part of any long-term planning conversation.

Financial decisions made during periods of surplus can become more difficult if economic conditions change. Once a full-time officer position is created, eliminating it later becomes politically and organizationally challenging. That is why questions about long-term financial commitments deserve thoughtful consideration before new permanent positions are added.

Process and Alternatives

During the debate, some members suggested alternative approaches to strengthening representation without immediately creating another full-time executive position. These included expanded use of detailed positions, rotating assistant roles, and other structural adjustments that could help support the workload of the Vice Presidents.

It is encouraging that the President's Report indicates the Local is exploring additional support structures such as rotating assistant-to-the-vice-president positions. That suggests there may be multiple ways to improve representation and support the work of union officers.

Exploring these kinds of structural improvements may offer opportunities to strengthen representation while maintaining flexibility in how the Local allocates its resources.

Looking Forward

The bylaw change has not yet taken effect. As noted in the President's Report, it must still be reviewed by the International to determine whether it aligns with the International Constitution and General Laws. That review process exists to ensure that local bylaw changes remain consistent with the broader governance structure of our union.

Regardless of the outcome of that review, the broader questions raised during this discussion remain important: how our Local balances representation, financial stewardship, and long-term planning.

Strong unions benefit from open discussion about these issues. Continued thoughtful dialogue helps ensure that our Local remains accountable to its membership and prepared for whatever challenges the future may bring.

Andy Price Shop Steward ATU 587

item.title: Building Representation Through Unity: The Role of the Third Vice President
item.dc:creator: Abdiwahab Adan
item.content:encoded:
By Abdiwahab Adan

The recent passage of the Third Vice President position marks an important and long overdue step forward in strengthening representation within our Union. This change is not just about adding another seat, it is about recognizing voices that have historically felt underrepresented and creating a pathway for meaningful inclusion.

For many years, members at Rail and across our smaller properties have shared similar concerns about representation. These groups play a critical role in the success of our union, yet their perspectives have not always been fully reflected at the leadership level. The creation of this position acknowledges that reality and provides an opportunity to correct it.

What makes this moment especially significant is that whoever is elected to this role, whether from Rail, Kitsap, Clallam, Jefferson and/or Solid Ground, will bring firsthand understanding of these challenges. That ensures that decisions are not made in isolation, but instead are informed by the real conditions, concerns, and priorities of the members they serve. Representation is strongest when it comes from those who have walked in the same shoes.

I want to take a moment to sincerely thank every member who participated in the voting process. Your engagement is what drives progress in our union. Change does not happen without involvement, and this outcome reflects a collective commitment to improving how we move forward together.

At the same time, it is important to recognize that this is not the finish line, it is the foundation. Creating a position is only the first step. The real work lies in how we continue to build trust, strengthen communication, and ensure that every member, regardless of classification or location, feels heard, valued, and represented.

As we move forward, we must remain grounded in a shared principle: our strength comes from unity. In Swahili, the word UMOJA means oneness or unity. It is more than just a word; it is a reminder of what binds us together as union members. When we stand united, we are stronger in our advocacy, more effective in our negotiations, and more resilient in the face of challenges.

The creation of the Third Vice President position is a step in the right direction. Now, it is up to all of us to continue that momentum, working together, staying engaged, and holding ourselves accountable to the values that define our union.

Together, through UMOJA, we move forward.

From the News Review, May 2026, page 15. Open in the PDF · Original file on atu587.org

item.title: In Loving Memory…
item.content:encoded:
"It is not length of life but depth of life" ~ Ralph Waldo Emerson

We were saddened to learn of the passing of:

It is with great sadness that we announce the passing of south Base Operator, Tyrone Freeman. Tyrone was born in Youngstown, Ohio and moved to Seattle in 2002. Tyron began his career as a Part-time Transit Operator in 2018, then promoted to Full-time in 2012. When Tyrone wasn't working, he enjoyed fishing, bingo, going to the casino, and fixing cars. Tyrone was also a known to be a big family man, he deeply loved his wife of 27 years, his 18 children, 62 grandchildren, and 13 great-grandchildren. Tyrone will be deeply missed by his loving family. Services were held on Friday, April 17, at the Jaylex Center in Youngstown, OH.

We are saddened to announce the passing of East Base operator, David Lockridge. David began his Part time transit career with Metro in 2007. David will be missed by his sister and everyone he touched. Services have already passed

It is with deep sorrow that we announce the passing of retired Revenue Processor, Paul Pioli. Paul was a Seattle native, and before coming on at Metro, he served in the United States Army, including time stationed in Korea during the Vietnam War, and later continued to serve through the Washington State National Guard. Paul started his Transit Operator career at Metro in 1973. He later moved into the Revenue Processing Center where he remained until retirement in 2008. Paul had deep roots in Seattle's Italian Community where he held several leadership roles with the Sons of Italy and also ran a catering business, Pioli's Catering, with his wife of 56 years until her passing in 2023. Paul also enjoyed being a mentor, coach, and attending the retiree breakfasts in the South and North Ends as a 50-year member. Paul will be greatly missed by his family and friends. A celebration of life was held April 15. In lieu of flowers, the family requests donations be made to the Tunnel to towers Foundation in Paul's name at www.T2T.org

With heavy hearts, we share that Kitsap Transit Routed Operator, Norkay Sherpa has passed. Norkay started his career with Kitsap Transit in 2021 and was very well known to be a dedicated hard work who always brought a positive spirit with him that he shared with everyone he encountered. Norkay will be greatly missed by his loving family and all who had the pleasure of working with him. Services were held April 16 at Acacia Memorial Park and Funeral Home in Bothell, WA.

Please place these members and their families in your thoughts and hearts

Please notify the union office of any member's passing so that this information may be shared with the rest of our union family.

item.title: Play Ball! Open Bargaining Is the Big League — And You've Got a Front-Row Seat
item.dc:creator: the Atlantic Base Shop Steward and Contract Action Team (CAT) Player
item.content:encoded:
Read from a scanned image on pages 16–17 of the PDF, so it may contain errors. View pages 16–17 in the PDF.

By the Atlantic Base Shop Steward and Contract Action Team (CAT) Player

Alright, members — grab your peanuts, your crackerjacks, and maybe a jumbo hot dog (no beer, sorry — this is a dry ballpark), because the biggest game in town is already underway. That's right: Open Contract Bargaining between ATU 587 and King County Metro is happening twice a week, and your ticket? Absolutely FREE. No scalpers. No nosebleed seats. Just you, your coworkers, and a ringside view of the negotiators swinging for more break time, better pay, a contract that actually works and much, much more for the people behind the wheel, turning a wrench, cleaning, ...

Think of it this way: Metro shows up every bargaining session with its lineup, its stats, and its game plan. Our negotiators step up to the plate with YOUR interests at bat. Now — who do you want in the stands cheering them on? A bunch of empty seats? Or a packed house of fired-up members who are watching every pitch?

Why You Need to Be in the Stands

Here's a little secret they don't put on the scoreboard: when members show up to open bargaining, it changes the game. Management sees a full house and knows this team is united. Our negotiators feel the energy and play harder. And YOU get to see exactly what's happening with your contract — no rumors, no hearsay, no mysterious negotiations leaving you guessing.

Open bargaining means transparency. No back-room deals. No "trust us, we got this." You sit in those seats and you watch the game unfold in real time. That's power, folks. And as we like to say:

"where there are members, there is power."

The C.A.T. Advocates Are Headed Your Way!

The Contract Action Team — your very own CAT squad — is prowling the worksite, talking to members one-on-one, answering your questions, and gathering your concerns to bring directly to the bargaining table. They're your fellow ATU 587 members who volunteer to be the connective tissue between YOU and YOUR negotiators.

Every member who attends an open bargaining session scores runs for our side — because every seat filled is a signal: We are watching. We are organized. We mean business.

So when a CAT member pulls you aside between runs and says "hey, got a minute?" — give them a minute. Your feedback on break times, pay, scheduling, security/safety - working conditions goes straight into the data that shapes this contract. No suggestion box that nobody reads. Direct. To the table. Like a line drive up the middle.

Sing It!

(To the tune of "Take Me Out to the Ballgame")

Take me out to the open bargaining, Take me out to the making of the contract! Bargain me more break time and money, I don't care if I never get back on time! Let me root, root, root for the bargaining team, If they don't win it all, it's a shame — But I won't be to blame! For it's one, two, three strikes, Metro's OUT — At the OPEN BARGAINING!

What to Bring to the Ballpark – Tukwila ATU 587 office

  • ☑ Your curiosity — you'll learn more about your contract in one session than in a year of hallway rumors
  • ☑ A friend — drag a coworker along; the more the merrier (and the more powerful)
  • ☑ Popcorn — because watching Metro get called out on bad proposals deserves a snack
  • ☑ Hot dogs — you've earned them, you drive the whole city around
  • 🚫 Beer — sorry, it's a dry game. Hydrate with solidarity instead.
  • ☑ Your CAT button — wear it proud. Every button is a statement that we're in this together.

GAME ON — DON'T MISS YOUR AT-BAT

Open bargaining sessions are held TWICE A WEEK. Contact your CAT team for dates, times, and location. Show up. Sit down. Watch your team play ball.

Want to Learn More About Open Bargaining?

  • "Open Up Bargaining!" — NewsGuild Workshop: https://youtu.be/BcDht-BRPgQ
  • "Winning a Strong Contract" Parts I & II — April 14 & 21, 2026, 4:30–6 PM: https://labornotes.org/events/2026/workshop-winning-strong-contract-parts-i-ii
  • "Steward's Corner: For Open Bargaining, Start Early and Build": https://labornotes.org/2023/08/open-bargaining-start-early-and-build

item.title: Second Annual ATU International Pride Caucus at Toledo, Ohio
item.dc:creator: Rachael Buchanan 21341, ATU 587 Pride Caucus Chair
item.content:encoded:
By Rachael Buchanan 21341, ATU 587 Pride Caucus Chair

On March 27th, we opened the Second Annual ATU International Pride Caucus Conference in Toledo Ohio. ATU Local 697 hosted the conference and UAW Local 12 generously opened their Hall to us for the first day. ATU International Pride Caucus President, Michael Mackay opened with remarks welcoming us and thanking ATU 697 President, Krissy Bofia for hosting us in Toledo. We had a roll call of officers and local Pride Caucuses, and I was happy to see that we went from 2 local Pride Caucuses last year to 7 this year!

Toledo passed legislation to protect LGBTQIA+ rights and was the first city in Ohio to extend domestic partnership rights to city employees. Toledo has about 12 sister cities and Toledo, Ohio was the first City in the United States to have a sister city, and paired with its namesake, Toledo, Spain in 1931.

International Vice President, Carly Allen said, "when we go home, we should bargain for everyone." Carly felt welcomed into this space even though she is cis/white/traditional family and noted, "we're here for a good time, not a long time." Gary Johnson Sr., International Vice President said, "we are all one. We may be different in many ways, but we all have the same goals. We hope we can turn some of this around in the political climate"

Michael Cornelius, International Vice President thanked UAW Local 12 for allowing us in their space. One of the most important things about our caucuses is our solidarity. We can never ever forget that this is not just a fight of one. We are organized and we are true to each other and when one of us falls, the rest of us pick them up. Michael thanked our allies. He noted that the world doesn't revolve without the allies who stand with us. Without the allies, we are going nowhere.

We had a Moment of silence for our Transgender Siblings who were murdered this past year

Other International Vice Presidents spoke and noted that "As a country, we are going through a tremendous struggle. Especially with this administration, it's very sad. I want to make sure we understand the struggles we are going through as labor. The Pride Caucus has an ally in Ohio State. We need to stay strong in the labor movement."

Local Caucus Presidents and Chairs were invited to speak.

Some key takeaways were that not everyone has to like you, but they will learn to respect you if you stay engaged. The sky is not the limit; you make your own limit. Do what you can to make everyone safe in your local. Come together any way you can. You can't make a change by sitting on your ass. Never be ashamed to use your voice!

After lunch, Simon Blackstone, Ursel Phillips Fellows Hopkinson LLP, Canada spoke on collective bargaining agreements and LGBTQIA+

Collective Bargaining Agreements are fluid events, and he ran through a bunch of different language ideas but didn't try to dictate to us what we need to have in our contracts. One key idea is to change pronouns in the agreement to they/them instead of he/him or she/her to make it more inclusive for everyone. He urged members to add the words "gender identity" and "gender expression." Ensure the language protects the privacy of the individual. In the United States we have the Civil Rights act of 1964, and in Canada they have Provincial and Federal Human Rights legislation that defines deliberate outing, deadnaming and misgendering defined explicitly as constituting harassment.

I was honored to present ATU 587's Article 2 Non-Discrimination proposal and TA. There were some fantastic questions put to me afterwards, and several ATU Locals asked for some tips on writing theirs. There were ally discussions and I felt like everyone, including myself, learned a lot.

International Black Caucus President, Karima Howard gave the invocation for day two, and then ATU International President, John A Costa spoke.

President Costa recognized the work of International Caucus Presidents and Leaders and told us that we have a lot of work to do and it's a dangerous time.

"LGBTQIA+ Members belong in this Union, and for the 2nd meeting means that we have a movement and it is here to stay." Worker power is how we protect each other when governments fail us and think about the member in your local who hasn't been plugged in yet. Organizing is how we grow power. Pride isn't just a celebration but a declaration. Showing up matters!

Carlos Mayorga Local 758 TTPC President spoke on forming a local caucus

We have only grown since the first conference and social justice, and union rights are intertwined and can't be separated.

As a caucus, it's important that we are seen at our Union Meetings and events. A Caucus is independent of your Local and make decisions separate from their leadership. A caucus supports the Union as works to strengthen it. It does not seek itself to bargain with management, rather it seeks to have a mission and work towards something.

Pride At Work Executive Director, Brittany Anderson spoke next about A Communications Guide for Labor Unions. She urged the attendees to learn how to talk about trans workers in a way that upholds are union values, and noted that it's vital for unions and workers to stand up for trans rights

The attendees engaged in discussion about pronouns, and it was wonderful to see people understand why they are important. Always remember to avoid assumptions about which bathroom trans and non-binary people want to use or should use.

At the end of the Conference, two Local Caucuses volunteered to host the 3rd Conference. ATU International Pride Caucus members then voted on the next location.

The 3rd Annual International Pride Caucus Conference will be hosted by ATU 587 Local Pride Caucus in Seattle Washington!!

Photo captions: Rachael Buchanan ATU 587 Pride Caucus Chair addresses the Conference; International President John A Costa addresses the Conference.

item.title: Mentorship Program Update
item.dc:creator: Patrick Brady, ATU Coordinator
item.content:encoded:
By Patrick Brady, ATU Coordinator

On March 2, 2024 we saw the local launch of the new "Mentors Moving Metro" with the first training class of 40 Mentors held at the Union Hall. The MMM program, then in a pilot stage, was birthed from a presentation to KCM and 587 from ATU International. Our program is one of dozens of partnerships between agencies and ATU Local around the US and Canada. Since then we have trained a total of 155 Mentors with another 20-25 registered for our next training on May 2nd. We have a high retention rate for Mentors but have lost several dozen to them pursuing other opportunities, most often with SIT or SDAs.

I am one of two Coordinators. I represent the ATU side and Debbie Fraizer from Employee Services/Apprenticeships and Pathways represents the Metro. Debbie drove for 25 years prior to her 11 years now working in Metro management. We report to a Coordinating Committee with equal numbers from our Union and Metro. In March we reported these numbers: Since June of 2024 Metro has hired 630 new Full Time (off the street) Operators. Only 33 have been terminated or resigned. 10 probation term. 11 terminated, 12 resigned. That is a 95% retention rate-plus 6 have gone to Rail, 1 SDA, 1 LOA, so total not driving since June of 24 of the 630 is 41.

I'm happy to say that we have graduated out of the pilot phase and have funding in the Metro biennial budget again in 202/28. In addition to Debbie's position Metro has hired our Ryerson Base Lead Mentor, Tevvis Tillman as our new Project Manager. There is now a multi-year work plan and a draft program manual. Soon there will be a new "Working Committee" appointed which will be able to have more hands-on involvement.

As most everyone will have already heard Metro has returned to hiring new operators starting as Part Time. The role of Mentors will change again back to our approach from two years ago. Our goal is to have 25 Mentors at each base. Last summer I published in the News Review these findings from our program survey conducted early in 2025. "Being involved with the MMM program has positively impacted my work." 76% strongly agree and 14% somewhat agree. On this question, I would recommend the Mentors Moving Metro program to other Mentees/Mentors'. 88.3% strongly agree.

I want to thank the support of President Greg Woodfill and our Full Time Officers and the Metro Leadership. As we continue to grow and mature we see the value of replicating our program into other operational divisions. Working with the International Staff has been a great part of this partnership along with my day-to-day work with Debbie. BUT—my greatest appreciation goes out to our Mentors and Lead Mentors. These are truly "pay it forward" Operators who live up to the highest standards of professionalism. I wish I could name each one of them in this article, but sometime soon I will publish their names. I thank everyone on our MMM team, Management and Union, for truly making a difference.

item.title: Celebrating Every Woman: Honoring Stories of Strength, Leadership, and Legacy
item.dc:creator: Michael Mackay, Transit Operator Rep #1
item.content:encoded:
By Michael Mackay, Transit Operator Rep #1

On March 21, a spirit of empowerment filled the ATU 587 halls "I'm Every Woman" was sung, setting the tone for an evening dedicated to honoring women across generations and professions. Esther Hankerson, President of the Women's Caucus, opened the event by welcoming all who identify as women and reaffirming the caucus's commitment to inclusion, leadership, and solidarity.

Standing for Mayor Katie Wilson, Labor Liaison Evan Woods shared remarks emphasizing the administration's continued partnership with women in labor and public service.

Voices of Determination and Legacy

Tamieko Cook captivated the audience with her story of growing up inspired by her single mother, a Metro employee and union member who encouraged her daughter to pursue every opportunity. From military service on the flight line to honoring Judy Young, former ATU secretary, Tamieko underscored how her mother's union values shaped her career and resilience.

King County Councilmember Wanda Luis, the first woman and first Black woman to represent District 2, shared how generations of women from her grandmother to her colleagues shaped her own journey. She encouraged everyone to recognize that "people may know your name, but they don't know your worth until you get the chance to show it."

Operator Addie Ortiz, who joined Metro in 2001, spoke about raising her children while building a business and pursuing her dream of becoming a mechanic. After years in various roles, including equipment service work, she proudly declared her determination to join the apprenticeship program, proving that persistence defines possibility.

Women Who Inspire Change

Erica Evans reflected on her family's remarkable legacy from her father, Keith Evans (ATU 1765), to her activist grandfather, a two-time Olympic medalist who stood up to the KKK. Erica described winning her election with over 67% of the vote as a tribute to her grandmother, who never had the chance to finish law school.

Council member Alexis Mercedes Rink, representing Seattle's Position 8 At-Large, urged everyone to remember the women "whose names were forgotten but whose courage opened every door we stand in today." Dionne Foster, also of the Seattle City Council, joined her and spoke passionately about building equity and representation for all women.

Recognizing Leadership and Change

Awards were presented to several inspiring women. Lisa Nault and Rachael Buchanan, ATU 587 Pride Caucus Chair, were both honored for their dedication and advocacy, Rachael underscoring that "trans women are women," with Michael Mackay shouting "once and for all"!

Other speakers included Corliss Barnes, Penny L. Scott, who called for more visible diversity across all units, and Eric James, who gave a heartfelt reflection on his mother's strength. Greg Woodfill, Paul Neil, and Latrelle Gibson shared personal stories of mentorship and gratitude, with Latrelle acknowledging Tamieko as a guiding influence in running for Recording Secretary.

Council members Claudia Balducci and Teresa Mosqueda closed the program with powerful words on why representation matters, reminding everyone that inclusion fuels progress and that every story strengthens the collective voice of women in the workplace.

The evening's message was clear: when women rise, entire communities move forward.

item.title: April Operators' LMRC Meeting (April 2, 2026)
item.dc:creator: Lisa Nault #3647 and Rachael Buchanan #21341, ATU 587 Bus Reps
item.content:encoded:
By Lisa Nault #3647 and Rachael Buchanan #21341, ATU 587 Bus Reps

Labor Management Relations Committee — to discuss, approve and/or propose resolutions to issues or problems of Metro policies which affects the Union and which either party requests to be placed on the agenda, and issues or problems of contract administration other than formal grievances.

Attendees: Lisa Nault, Rachael Buchanan, LaTonya Abernathy, Cory Rigtrup, Richard McKinney, Jabari Hampton, Collin Dunphy, Greg Woodfill

FOLLOW UP:

INTRODUCTION:

LaTonya Abernathy Executive Board Position #3 joins the committee. Welcome!

ADA Placards:

The County has news, and they have been unable to find money in the budget and will not be moving forward with providing ADA placards on the fleet at this time. Metro cited they don't have $500,000.00 to make stickers. The Union would like to know if we can get a commitment from Metro that all new buses will have that, like the 89 new BEB Gillig buses? That's something that can be requested through the procurement committee. Is it required by ADA laws? No, it's not required, but it's basically information for the customers to show what the requirement is, and the intent was to give support to the operators.

Customer Relations Classes:

Training is working on final details for FIFA. Out of 2600 AVADE classes, there are only a few left remaining so over 2000 classes have been finished. There are details going on for front line staff around FIFA. Operators are asking once they finish the AVADE training if they can have a certificate. Are there refreshers planned? Metro doesn't know about attendees, but certifications do expire for trainers.

Tukwila Base:

The Union has completed the Union bulletin boards for Operations but noted that there isn't one for Vehicle Maintenance. Metro is happy that everything is going well, buses are performing well, though there have been a few issues. The Union thanks Metro for getting TOMS up for the Operators at Tukwila Base. Metro notes that there will be things that might slip through the cracks, so Metro would be grateful if the Union will let them know if there is anything else. Metro is learning as we go and they're a little rusty setting up a new base since it has been so long since the last one opened.

Building a Successful Probationary Program for FTO:

Metro has got several things in place and new operators being assigned to mentors and follow up with training and follow ups. Metro needs to practice them consistently. The Union notes that if someone has a hearing next week, and Metro reaches out to the Union so we can extend probation, the Union will respond. Regarding probationary points, the Union has heard rumors of them and when you get to the end of the period, the Chief will just decide if you've successfully completed probation. Can the County clarify? Metro claims there are no contractual requirement to use points, so the use of them in the probationary termination letter is going away. Is the system still being used, or is the whole system being thrown out? Will it be a known process, or the whim of whomever wants to decide. Metro is leaving it to the Chief, and it won't be referenced in the termination letter. They will be evaluating at the staff meeting. The Union notes that we have had a process for we don't know how many decades and there were points and if you crossed that threshold, you knew you were done. Are we hearing that that won't be used at all, and each Chief will decide on whatever criteria they decide to use? What Metro is trying to do is get away from that and let the Chiefs do their reviews and being accountable, so they can talk to the employees if they are on a bad track.

The Union can't express how upsetting this is because nobody is going to know how to finish probation.

This doesn't sound like an open and fair process and is a disaster waiting to happen. The Union is going to push back on Joint Leadership pretty hard on this. Metro can do a lot more to help new operators. You must have a standard if you're going to hold people to it and we're not hearing the Chief's are actually reaching out. Are Metro and The Union in this together? We're not hearing from management. We've been through this process at one base and there seems to be miscommunication and the language for direct full time is not in the contract and it makes this discussion imperfect. The points are a tool for metro to readdress someone coming back in 6 months. Metro insists the points just aren't being referenced in the letter. Do we all know how many times we've had probationary firing? Metro contends that less than 5% have probationary firings from performance issues. The Union pushes back on that statistic. Metro tries to explain numbers. The Union understands the numbers and doesn't appreciate Metro discussing it in a condescending manner in this meeting. Metro claims using points is in the rubric in the decision to terminate, and that is up to the Chief, it just won't be referenced in the letter. Metro is still going to use the form used to address performance issues. Metro wants to be clear that they are still doing those check-ins. The Union believes the sky is falling and we want to see what the criteria are in writing. The way it's been stated, it sounds like the standard is optional for the Chief's to use. Are we just going back to management rights and picking and choosing which employees we want? That's the Union's fear. How can Metro control Base to Base and Chief to Chief? Metro claims they are not going that and, they have a sheet. An Operator with 0 points would never go in to see an update, but if they do something wrong, they will still get the check in. Metro is trying to sell the idea that all firings are being reviewed by base staff. Per the manual page 46, medical verification, are we changing this language? Once the operators come to the base, are they being given clear expectations? Is the only time operators see the Chiefs when they've done something wrong? Why can't the Chiefs welcome them to the base and give expectations? Metro believes they have a process where Chiefs are meeting with new operators. The Union knows that hasn't happened at all Bases. The probationary employees are telling the Union that they are not receiving that. Probationary Employees tell the Union, "We never see the Chief until we're being disciplined." The Union wants Metro to walk us through this; will new hires know what the specific standard is to get through the process? Does every single operator have the same standard?

Do we not see a problem with not having set standards?

Metro contends that no one is coming down to the last day and then being fired. Is every Chief going to use their own standard? Metro says, "No." Metro is trying to make it more standardized. If the Chief recognizes an issue, they're going to bring the operator in. Metro insists that it's now less than 10% for performance issues. It doesn't matter to the Union if it's just 1 person. Is the Process fair? That seems to not be the case anymore. Metro insists that probationary employees are "At Will" and they want to fire them whenever they want to and not reference probationary points in the letter. Metro claims they can't determine what the standards are, its Chief by Chief. Metro tries to walk it back and say that no termination is unilateral by one Chief or another. Did the Union understand that there are no maximum points and that any number can be used? Metro isn't aware of a probationary point threshold, and the Union is astounded at the lack of understanding on Metro's part. The Union believes that the threshold is 11 points and did we hear Metro correctly that there's no threshold? Applying the part-time standards to full-time was never fair. The Union points out that maybe we'll use some points and sometimes more points, but it doesn't matter now because the probationary standard won't be used and that's a problem. The Union President wants to see the set standards in writing at the next LMRC for probationary employees. Metro will get back to us. Follow up next month

Shawn Yim Memorial:

Regarding the bench, Metro believes a plaque is in the works and once that's in place, there will be a ceremony. The problem is that when the bench came in, it didn't have the ATU and Metro logos and the Union has not had any communication from Metro, and we would very much like to remain in the loop.

Preventability Process Before Imposing Discipline:

Metro talked about his and reviewed it, and talked about putting people on PAL, but Metro is going to stay with the same process they've always used. At the end of the process, if the accident preventability is overturned, the Operator will be brought back. The Union is happy to hear this because we want our people to be brought back when the accident is overturned.

Back Door Entry outside of CBD:

This has been elevated to demand to bargain and not discussed

Vacation Verification:

Not discussed due to time constraints

New Business:

Accident Report Ssam Training: Base Computer Improvements:

The Union brings this topic up again, because there are ongoing and persistent issues with computers, network, login, and printer issues at all Bases. Union Shop Stewards and Executive Board Officers work with individuals at the Bases to fill out reports, and they still don't understand a lot of software changes. Metro states that all Bases should have a dedicated terminal. The union describes the process that when the computers aren't working, you have to find a Chief available to talk to, then you have to follow up with them to tell them what the issue is and the Operators don't have the time to do all this run around and the equipment needs to be maintained by the employer without needing to use an exorbitant amount of time and it is incredibly inefficient. Operators shouldn't be responsible for maintaining the equipment and the base personnel need to make periodic checks to ensure it works properly. We still don't understand Origami because of all the updates, and we haven't been trained at all. Other bases have consistent Wi-Fi issues. Metro promises to look into the computers and check with training for availability of classes.

Union Arb & Re-Read Operator Appointee Calendar:

NOT DISCUSSED DUE TO TIME CONSTRAINTS

Meeting adjourned at 10:03.

Have a topic you want brought up in the LMRC Meetings? Contact Lisa or Rachael to submit your topics.

The SSaM Access Anywhere QR code allows employees to access SSaM directly on their mobile device (e.g., cellphone) to report an incident, submit a near miss/close call, or share safety suggestions. This functionality was created based on feedback my team received to help improve accessibility and use of SSaM.

SSaM – Security Incident Mobile Update w/ QR Code

Use the QR Code to Report a Security Incident/Drug Use/Other Safety Reports:

Instructions:

  • Using your cell phone, open your Camera app
  • Point your phone's camera at the QR code
  • Follow your phone's prompt to open the link in a browser

I will work to promote the best interests of this Union and encourage my fellow workers to become members of the same. I will not take the place of any member of this organization, or any other union worker who may be on strike or locked out. I will not reveal any of the private business to anyone not entitled to know the same.

I will not appeal to any legal authority in matters pertaining to this Union until I have exhausted all means of redress provided by its laws. I also promise to promote the cause of trade union principles and defend freedom of thought, whether expressed by tongue or pen, with all the power at my command.

I understand there is nothing in this obligation that will in any way interfere with my political and religious rights or that will be in any way inconsistent with my duties arising from any of the relations of life.

item.title: The President's Report: The 3rd VP
item.dc:creator: Greg Woodfill
item.content:encoded:
By Greg Woodfill

The membership voted 90% in favor of adding another Vice President at our March cycle of meetings. It's a historic day for our Union! The membership had a spirited debate on this proposal and spoke with their vote. Since some consistent concerns were raised during this process, I would like to take one last opportunity to revisit how we got here and the ramifications going forward.

Given that the membership at Rail was eventually going to bring forward a motion to add a VP to better represent Rail, the Union's Full-Time Officers have spent the last 20 months trying to reach a consensus on adding a 3rd VP. Whether we should add one, when to do so, whether we could afford it, and how to structure and distribute duties among the three VPs.

The Officers could all agree that two VPs were not adequately representing our rapidly growing membership of 4,800, and that we could afford another VP if the membership chose to add one. We could not all agree on the structure for adding another VP and on how to distribute duties among 3 VPs.

After spending a year and a half searching for the perfect structure, it became obvious that there was none. That any structure would have drawbacks and be opposed by some members. A majority of the Officers eventually settled on the structure that the membership just approved. While not perfect, a majority of the officers believed this was the best option for the membership as a whole.

Once we have the next elections our Vice President will be able to focus on and represent just one contract: Metro Bus operations. And the new Vice President position will focus on representing Rail operations and the other four properties. For those concerned that whoever is voted into that position will need to understand and represent 5 contracts and properties, including bus and rail, in King County and on the Peninsula.

That is the exact argument in favor of this change, because that's what the current Vice President is responsible for knowing and representing, and, on top of that, for overseeing 3,800 Metro Bus Operations members.

The ATUs International Constitution and General Laws require that at least one Vice President be elected by the membership at large. This is why everyone can run and vote for the Vice President.

Additionally, the ATUs International Constitution and General Laws allow for the creation of additional Vice President positions to represent designated subsections of the membership.

In 2009, when our local created the Vice President for Maintenance, the membership approved the bylaw change establishing the position, which only members from maintenance can run for and vote for.

Fairness is in the eyes of the beholder, and no matter which way you choose on this issue of who can vote and run for these added VP positions, some of the membership will feel that it's unfair.

If everyone can run and vote for the additional VP position, Rail operations, and the other properties members may feel like the odds are that a member from Metro Bus Operations will always be chosen to represent them. And if you limit running and voting for this position to Rail operations and the other properties, Metro Bus Operations members may feel excluded from the process.

There is no right or wrong answer on this. It's a matter of everyone's individual opinion and preference.

A choice needed to be made, though, and it was decided that these subsections of the membership would elect their VP from within their ranks to represent them.

Just like in 2015, when we created an additional VP for maintenance, now that the membership has voted to adopt this new bylaw change, it will be sent to the International to decide whether it is in alignment with its Constitution and General Bylaws, or if not they will send it back to our local to bring it into alignment, which is what happened in 2015. Our Local may find out that answer before or shortly after this article is printed, stay tuned.

If or when this bylaw change is approved, we'll need to start thinking about and planning for next year's officer election cycle, which isn't far off. Our Union leadership is committed to helping train and provide exposure to members who step forward and express interest in running for union office in the future.

The more members who run for full-time and E-board positions, the more choices the membership will have in selecting their next leaders.

Whether you agreed with this change or not, having worked side by side daily with our Vice President, first Ken, and now Cory, I can assure you that Metro Bus operations members will be much better represented as a result of this bylaw change. Both would tell you that and were both highly supportive of this change. The same goes for Rail and the other four properties represented by ATU 587.

Under any metric that you choose, there is no argument that can factually be made that our Local can't afford this additional VP. The questions and concerns expressed concern about what happens if we go from budget surpluses to deficits. The answer to that is we've been there before and made the necessary budget cuts when our reserve was around $100k.

Our Union is currently a $6 million-a-year operation. We'll find the cuts if disaster hits. But worrying about a potential disaster shouldn't keep us from investing in better representation for an expanding membership.

Lastly, on the suggestions that we should spend this money on restructuring to a model that details more members to assist the VPs. We need to, can, and will do both. We currently detail members practically daily to help out. And Vice President Cory Rigtrup is currently working on the structure of a rotating assistant-to-the-vice-president-type detailed position; stay tuned.

Our Voice, Our Power! ATU 587 – We Are One.
