item.title: The 1st Vice President's Report: Wave of Restructuring
item.dc:creator: Cory Rigtrup
item.content:encoded:
By Cory Rigtrup

Since being appointed, I've been in the trenches. Fighting the daily battle, one after another. It's relentless, consuming and at moments suffocating. But there are also times when I get to look up and see daylight. This daylight comes in the form of helping hands, that always seem to be offered. Let's focus on the light.

I was inspired last month to see such strong turnout at the membership meetings. Dozens of first-time union meeting attendees turned out to support increasing our Local's ability to provide representation. Way to see the small groups organize, message received!

March also consisted of getting more of our folks trained on accident re-reads and ARB. There are different groups of workers lacking trained people familiar with their work rules and equipment to step in when needed. Additionally, there is an overall shortage of trained folks available, and the process for selecting the union appointees seems off. Working on building a planned rotational system, hang tight, more to come on that.

Restructuring base representation:

If you've seen me at a worksite, it's usually because I was attending a grievance hearing or a termination and I loitered around trying to engage in positive relations with whoever wants to talk. One theme I've heard a few times, "Can we get a base meeting and get everyone on the same page?" A similar message was brought up during the membership meetings last month. The answer to both is YES!

Currently our Union's bylaw appoints each bus operating base their own executive board representative, plus a spare. The spare may change by the time the next executive board meeting takes place, as new base is about to go live. Think about that, each operating base has its own representative in union leadership to talk about your worksite issues, so let's utilize it!

About the time this article goes to print, a new shake has begun. Along with folks starting new work, a host of old and new shop stewards eager and willing to help will be made available. Shop stewards will elect their base chief steward, and the Union will take those names, plus your base's executive board officer and post for all to see.

Here is where things hopefully change. I believe it's good for all of us to empower your bases union representation team in getting better organized, and our Local provide more support at the base level. Shop stewards are responsible for defending members rights, bear witness, provide assistance and communicate. The base Chief steward is responsible for communicating their base members' needs with other stewards and request/provide assistance as needed. The base executive board officer is responsible for addressing their base needs and providing union leadership on location. Depending on which base you are at, the currently set up may be working, or be coming up short.

Maybe that is how it's supposed to work, maybe not, it makes sense in my head. As this work in progress rolls out, be proactive, be part of the build. The Local can say we empower your base's union leadership with what we think you need, but stewards taking part at the base level pounding the issue, helping you, is how we really grow. More to come, stay tuned.

Kitsap Transit:

My goodness, our Local is spending a lot of time lately dealing with Kitsap issues. Policy changes, memo's, lots and lots of discipline. Just an overall abundance of work, for a non-contract bargaining year. It's clear something has changed.

There is profound rubble in my soul; to see so many good Kitsap members rise to these challenges. Last month I saw at least 20% of all our Kitsap members attend our Saturday meeting. Make their voices heard, tell us what is going on, and break bread together! This participation gives credence to our Local's solidarity for each property within. We are currently working on setting up a steward training class for April, stay tuned.

Mellissa Thomas Arb:

The Thomas arbitration was scheduled for March 2 and 3, a last second reinstatement agreement was reached the day before arbitration. This Agreement reinstates Sister Thomas back as a Metro Operator, under terms that will allow her to succeed! Let us all welcome Sister Thomas back to work!

Brother Searcy:

Searcy was a north base operator terminated for refusing a post-accident drug test by being transported to Harborview by ambulance. Metro did the right thing by admitting their mistakes and making brother Searcy whole. Welcome back Brother Searcy!

item.title: The Maintenance Vice President's Report: Bus Facilities Maintenance and Bus Vehicle Maintenance
item.dc:creator: Jeff Stambaugh
item.content:encoded:
By Jeff Stambaugh

Bus Facilities Maintenance

Will the drama ever end? Apparently not. TFD management continues to erode seniority and destroy employee morale. As of this writing management has not posted or conducted the pick, this is now affecting lives. Our members and their employees have things to plan, like vacations and childcare, only they can't because TFD management has failed to do their job. As I reported last month, they have proposed positions outside the collective bargaining agreement. The more I learn the more upsetting it gets. One of the largest classifications in TFD is called Utility Laborer, their main job is to clean the Bus Zones and make them presentable to our customers. In 2019 there were 43 pick positions for this job classification, 6 of these were marked "Usually shelter maintenance as assigned--see supplemental". Basically, what that meant was you came into work and were assigned that day's work based on need for the day, similar to a report operator. For the most part the other 37 picked positions had known work to pick, basically you knew what you were going to do nearly every day, part of knowing your picked work was a route sheet. The route sheet (like a run card) spelled out the location of bus stops you would clean and how often you would clean them. Now, the proposed pick sheets have 46 pick positions with 27, yes you read that correct, 27 "Usually shelter maintenance as assigned--see supplemental". Why would you need 27 of these you ask? Well, I did and TFD management gave me a song and dance about the ability to get the work done and lack of equipment to do it. The reality? The route sheets haven't been updated in over a decade, and management doesn't seem to be able to figure out how get the work done in a timely, consistent, cost-effective manner. Instead, they want to be able to direct the workforce to run around and service the stops that are not being serviced frequently enough because the route sheets haven't been updated. Would operations expect over 50% of the workforce to come into work and be assigned work daily?

The Union has made management a proposal that in our opinion will both get the work done and restore seniority. Management's response? That doesn't work for us.

Hopefully by the time you read this we have reached an agreement that works for everyone.

Bus Vehicle Maintenance

As most of you are aware we just concluded the Spring VM pick, it was going smooth until the final day when management announced Superintendent promotions and location changes, right behind that announcement the chiefs had a move-up with considerable movement causing frustration that employees could now be working with a chief or superintendent they intentionally avoided during the pick. The Union immediately asked for a repick and was denied. Hopefully in the future we can find a way to get management movement announced prior to the pick or find a workable solution that doesn't leave employees upset.

Rail Maintenance was fairly quiet last month, Hopefully that is good sign.

item.title: The Recording Secretary's Report: Workers Comp, Short Term Disability, and Long-Term Disability
item.dc:creator: Latrelle Gibson
item.content:encoded:
By Latrelle Gibson

An injury that is severe enough that one will need to take time off work to heal can most certainly be an extremely stressful and scary world to navigate. I truly understand the stress related to Workers Comp not approving physical therapies, necessary injections, or surgery. I am here to help you navigate this world and try to take some of the stress off your shoulders. I answer on average 8 member calls a day for this very issue alone. In this article, I will walk you through the basics of both on the job and off the job injury.

For those who have an OJI (on the job injury), FMLA time runs concurrently with your L&I leave to offer leave protection while out on an OJI. What does this mean and how does this work? For FMLA, one has the ability to take protected leave for up to 12 weeks per year, granted that each in preceding 12 months a full-time employee works at least 1,040 hours, and for part-time, this will be 510 hours. KCFMLA will kick in once one is out beyond the 12 weeks, this leave allows a total of 18 weeks of protected leave within a twelve-month period. Now, keep in mind that if you've used FMLA within the same twelve months of you being injured, this will be part of the 12 weeks. For example, in March 2025, I used four weeks of FMLA for family reasons. In July 2025, I was injured on the job. I will now have 8 weeks of FMLA for the rest of 2025.

When you're out on Workers Comp, for the first 260 workdays, we have bargained in our contract for metro to pay a supplemental. This supplemental keeps you on the payroll, therefore not affecting medical benefits for the first 260 days. The supplemental payment reduces every 60 workdays missed, so the first 60 workdays missed, one is paid 100% supplemental, the following 60 workdays missed, 90% supplemental, and the next 140 workdays missed, 80% supplemental. It's important to note that you will still receive time loss payments from Workers Comp at 60% of your wages. 60% will come from Workers Comp and this is not taxed, however, the supplemental payments are taxed. Please make sure your address is up to date as the Workers Comp check will most likely be mailed to your address on file.

Once your supplemental payments are exhausted, if you're still out on OJI for more than 30 days, your benefits may be at risk of turning off. The Benefits department will contact the individual and ask if the individual would like to utilize their accruals, e.g., vacation, AC time, to keep them benefit eligible. This is completely up to the individual. If one elects not to utilize their accruals, you'll be without benefits. Transit Disability Services can steer you to the open market to get benefits through COBRA or Apple health. I don't suggest COBRA as those are the benefits we currently have, and they're very expensive when paying for individually.

Now the stressful part (although all of it can be stressful for some), if you're going through recovery, and Workers Comp denies the number of physical therapies your doctor has asked for, denied the injections needed, or even denied surgery, your doctor will need to appeal this decision. If your doctor is siding with Workers Comp, this will be an uphill battle for you. I would strongly suggest finding another doctor to get a second opinion and if the you're able to find another doctor who agrees with you that your injury was in fact work related, the doctor will need to communicate this with the initial doctor who is siding with the Workers Comp decision, as Workers Comp needs the initial doctor to make this appeal on your behalf. If the doctor is filing appeals, and treatment is still being denied, contact me and I can help with this.

Medical Separation. If you've run out of protected leaves, FMLA/KCFMLA, Transit disability services will ask the base Superintendent/Chief to extend leave as "an accommodation". Bases will extend these leaves so long as you have a projected return to work date in the near future. If your doctor states you're not able to return to the job of injury for an indefinite period, Metro will seek medical separation sooner. The ultimate decision lies with your doctor and what they report to Transit Disability Services. If you've been out on Workers Comp for a year or more, give me a call and I can walk you through the process. There's a lot to explain with this process, so a phone conversation is best.

I hope this helps some understand the Workers Comp world, and if you want to look this information up, all the Workers Comp components are located in the CBA under Article 12.8.A.

item.title: Congested Tracks and Compressed Training: The Struggle for New Rail Operators
item.dc:creator: Hassannoor Aden, Minority Affairs, ATU 587/King County Labor Delegate
item.content:encoded:
By Hassannoor Aden, Minority Affairs, ATU 587/King County Labor Delegate

Rail has been growing quickly, and the demand for manpower continues to increase. As service expands and more trains are added to the system, the need for qualified Light Rail Operators grows with it. In many cases, the shortage has reached a point where supervisors are stepping in to operate trains themselves just to maintain service levels. That alone shows how much pressure the system is under.

To address the shortage, rail has accelerated hiring and is currently running two training classes per day to bring in new operators as quickly as possible. On paper, that sounds like progress. But the reality on the ground is more complicated. The pace of hiring has increased, yet the training environment has become far more difficult for students who are trying to learn the job.

The mainline is already heavily congested. With trains running on roughly a four-minute headway, there is very little room for error and very little opportunity for trainees to practice in a controlled environment. New LRO students are trying to learn a complex job while operating in one of the busiest conditions the system has ever seen. Every movement on the line must stay on schedule, and controllers are focused on keeping service moving. That pressure naturally carries over to the trainers and the students.

For trainees, this can create a stressful learning environment. Instead of having the space and time to develop confidence behind the controls, many students feel rushed. Trainers are balancing two responsibilities at the same time: teaching a new operator while also making sure the train stays on schedule and does not disrupt the flow of service. When the system is running at maximum capacity, training can easily take a back seat to keeping the line moving.

The impact of these conditions can be seen in the graduation numbers. Success rates vary widely from class to class. In some classes of 11 to 15 students, only four or five make it through to graduation. In other classes with similar numbers, 11 or even 12 students complete the program successfully. When outcomes swing that dramatically, it raises legitimate questions about consistency in training, evaluation standards, and the environment students are learning in. It also raises the question of whether students are being given a fair and equal opportunity to succeed.

Another concern is the reduction in on-the-job training hours. In the past, trainees received about 80 hours of hands-on operating experience before completing the program. Today that number has been reduced to 64 hours. That means new operators are getting less real-world practice at a time when the system itself has become more demanding and more congested. Those lost hours matter. Operating a train safely and confidently takes repetition, experience, and time behind the controls.

Learning the system involves much more than just moving a train from one station to another. Students must learn signal systems, station procedures, communication protocols, passenger safety, incident response, and how to operate in unusual or emergency situations. These are skills that develop through practice, not just classroom instruction. When hands-on training time is reduced, students may graduate with less confidence and less experience than operators in the past.

At the same time, trainers are under pressure to move classes through the system quickly in order to fill staffing gaps. That pressure can create uneven expectations and evaluations. Some trainers may allow students more time to develop their skills, while others may apply stricter standards under tighter timelines. The result is inconsistency from class to class.

If rail service continues to grow, training must grow with it. Expanding service without strengthening the training structure will only create more pressure on new operators, trainers, and the system as a whole. Adequate hands-on training time, consistent evaluation standards, and a training environment that allows students to learn without excessive operational pressure are essential.

Rail operators carry enormous responsibility. They move thousands of passengers every day and operate within a system where safety and precision are critical. Preparing them properly is not optional. It is an investment in safety, reliability, and the long-term success of the rail system. When new operators are given the time, support, and environment they need to succeed, the entire system benefits.

Representation Must Keep Pace with a Changing Transit System

Congratulations to Rail and the smaller properties for having the option to elect a Vice President Three dedicated to your needs, while Vice President One focuses fully on Transit Operators. That structure creates balance and gives different parts of our membership the representation they need. In many ways, this is a win for everyone.

Over the last few weeks there has been a lot of discussion about the proposal to establish a Vice President position focused on operations, particularly rail. Members have raised questions about cost, voting eligibility, and whether the position is necessary. These are fair questions, and every member deserves clear information before casting their vote.

But before we get lost in the details, it helps to step back and look at the bigger picture. Our union has grown and changed, and our leadership structure must evolve with it.

ATU Local 587 represents workers across many different properties and systems. Our membership includes King County Metro bus operators, Link Light Rail operators, Streetcar workers, and members from Kitsap Transit, Jefferson Transit, Clallam Transit, and other agencies across the region. Each of these systems operates under different contracts, rules, and workplace conditions.

One area in particular has grown rapidly over the past decade: rail. Link Light Rail continues to expand across the region. Lines from Lynnwood, to Eastside, and Federal Way. With each expansion comes more operators, controllers, maintenance staff, and supervisors. Rail is no longer a small part of our union. It is a major and growing division within our membership.

Rail operations also come with technical challenges that are very different from bus operations. Rail members work under a separate collective bargaining agreement and operate in an environment with its own safety systems and procedures.

These are not abstract concerns. They are real situations that affect real members. As rail continues to grow, so does the number of grievances, investigations, and disciplinary cases involving rail operators and other rail employees. Expecting the same leadership structure that existed years ago to keep up with a rapidly expanding rail system is becoming increasingly difficult.

This is why many members believed the time has come to establish a Vice President position dedicated to rail operations. The goal is not to divide the union or create unnecessary positions. The goal is to ensure that members working in a complex and growing system have representation from leadership that understands their work environment, while allowing other union officers to focus on the needs of the rest of the membership. Strong unions adjust when the industry changes. Our transit system is changing, and our union must be able to keep up.

Some members have raised concerns about the cost of adding another position. Those concerns are understandable. But representation always requires resources, and the cost of inadequate representation can be far greater. When a member faces discipline, contract violations, or unfair treatment, having leadership that understands the job can make the difference between protecting a career and losing it.

Others have pointed out that the change would not take effect until 2027 and therefore does not solve immediate problems. But structural decisions are always made with the future in mind. The rail system will continue expanding for years to come. Preparing now ensures that the union is ready to represent the workforce that is still growing.

At the same time, this conversation should not turn into a conflict between different parts of our membership. Bus operators, rail operators, streetcar employees, and members at other properties all face different challenges. Our strength as a union comes from recognizing those differences while standing together.

item.title: Operators' Empathy for All: Because We Deserve Better Too
item.dc:creator: Chuck Lare, Atlantic Base Shop Steward
item.content:encoded:
By Chuck Lare, Atlantic Base Shop Steward

Let us be honest with each other for a minute.

If you have driven a bus in King County for any length of time, you have been there. End of the line. A passenger who clearly is not okay — maybe they are in crisis, maybe they have not slept in days, maybe they just need help that none of us were trained to give. And what happens? You call it in. A supervisor shows up, or fare security, or a deputy. The passenger gets walked off your bus. And two hours later, they are back on somebody else's.

Nothing gets resolved. Nobody gets helped. And you are left carrying the weight of it for the rest of your shift.

That is not good enough. Not for our riders, and not for us.

That is why I want to talk to you about Operators' Empathy for All — an initiative that could genuinely change how we handle these situations and make our working conditions safer and less stressful in the process.

The idea is straightforward: partner Metro operators with King County Behavioral Health Specialists who are actually trained to de-escalate, treat, and connect people in crisis to real services. Not shuffle them off to the next bus. Programs like CAHOOTS in Oregon and STAR in Denver have already proven this model works — fewer 911 calls, less reliance on emergency rooms, and fewer repeat situations clogging the system.

For us, that means fewer of those tense, unresolved end-of-line moments that eat at you. It means having the right backup — people trained for exactly this — instead of hoping a deputy arrives in time or a supervisor knows what to do. It means focusing on what we actually signed up for: moving people safely through this county.

There could also be an opportunity here for operators to take on additional hours outside of driving — engaging directly in expanding Behavioral Health Specialists' reach into our communities. This initiative is not just about making our shifts more manageable. It is about recognizing that we are on the front lines every single day, and we deserve the tools and support that match the reality of this job.

King County's own executive priorities "Breaking the Cycle," "Boots on the Ground," putting the right people in the right places — line up directly with what this initiative is pushing for. We have a real opening to press leadership to turn that rhetoric into something we actually feel on the bus.

We have always shown up for our community. It is time the system showed up for us.

If Operators' Empathy for All sounds like something you want to be part of, reach out: chuck@lareasssoc.com

item.title: Membership Meetings, Transparency, and Representation
item.dc:creator: Andy Price, Shop Steward, Local 587
item.content:encoded:
By Andy Price, Shop Steward, Local 587

Membership meetings are where the democratic life of our union is supposed to take place. They are where members raise concerns about working conditions, discuss contract issues, debate proposals, and vote on the direction of the Local. When members take the time to attend a meeting, they should be able to expect that the meeting allows meaningful participation and that the procedures being followed are clear and transparent.

Recently, a number of members have raised concerns about how some meetings are being conducted and how certain votes are handled. These concerns are not about personalities or about taking sides on any particular proposal. They are about making sure the process works the way members expect it to.

One concern raised by members who attended the most recent meeting was how little of the meeting was devoted to regular union business. From what was described by those present, the meeting moved very quickly to the bylaw proposal under consideration, the vote was taken, and shortly afterward the meeting was adjourned. Members who attempted to raise other issues reported that they were not given the opportunity to do so.

Membership meetings exist so that members can bring forward concerns affecting their jobs, their contracts, safety issues, and other union matters. When a meeting becomes focused almost entirely on a single item of business and then ends immediately after that vote, members understandably question whether the meeting served its broader purpose.

Parliamentary procedure exists to help ensure fairness in situations like this. Our bylaws recognize Robert's Rules of Order as the authority for questions of procedure when they are not otherwise addressed. One of the basic principles in Robert's Rules is transparency in voting. Once ballots are counted, the chair normally announces the result of the vote to the assembly, including the number of votes for and against the motion and whether the motion is adopted or lost.

That practice exists for a simple reason. When members attend a meeting and participate in a vote, they reasonably expect to hear the outcome once the tally has been completed.

Another question that has come up concerns voting eligibility during meetings. At one meeting I personally observed individuals arriving and handing in paperwork at the door before participating in the vote. I did not examine the documents, but they appeared to be membership-related forms. I also observed a full-time officer coming over to collect those forms.

To be clear, I am not suggesting any improper motive. However, situations like this can raise understandable questions among members about how eligibility is determined. Normally members sign in when attending a meeting and verify their eligibility before voting. When someone submits paperwork during the meeting and then participates in the vote in the same voting cycle, members may reasonably wonder how those procedures are being applied.

Clarifying these procedures would help ensure that members have confidence in the fairness and transparency of the process.

Representation within the union is another subject that often comes up in discussions about governance. Many members may not realize that while our Executive Board includes a number of representatives, many of those positions are not full-time. At the same time, the traditional full-time officer positions recognized in the ATU Constitution and General Laws—such as President and Vice President—are typically elected at large by the membership and represent the entire Local.

There is a reason for that structure. Officers elected at large are accountable to the entire membership rather than to a single department or classification. That approach encourages broader representation and helps ensure that decisions are made with the interests of the entire Local in mind.

Different locals structure their leadership positions in different ways depending on their size and needs. Some locals have additional vice presidents elected at large, while others create positions tied to specific departments or groups of members. These are reasonable topics for members to discuss, and thoughtful discussion about representation can help determine what structure best serves the membership as a whole.

Open discussion about procedure, transparency, and representation should not be viewed as criticism. It is simply part of a healthy union. When members understand how meetings are conducted, how votes are counted, and how decisions are made, confidence in the union's democratic process grows.

Our membership meetings should always reflect those principles.

Looking ahead, I would also encourage the Local to consider modernizing how bylaw proposals are voted on. Rather than relying only on a small number of meeting votes during a cycle, bylaws could be submitted to the membership for ratification by vote, still requiring the same two-thirds threshold to adopt a change. Allowing members to vote at or near the bases where they work would likely increase participation and awareness of union governance. In addition, we should seriously consider providing informational meetings online where members can hear explanations, participate in discussion, and debate proposals before voting. In 2026, secure online voting technology exists and is used by many organizations. It is probably inevitable that unions will move in that direction eventually. If the goal is to strengthen participation and engagement among our members, exploring those options sooner rather than later may be worth considering.

item.title: Bylaw Proposal Ruled Out of Order
item.content:encoded:
To: All Members of Local 587

I, .................................., in the presence of God and the members of this Union, do solemnly promise and pledge (without any reservation or evasion) to support the Constitution and General Laws of this Amalgamated Transit Union. I will keep myself in good standing by paying all dues, fines and assessments required. I will work to promote the best interests of this Union and encourage my fellow workers to become members of the same. I will not take the place of any member of this organization, or any other union worker who may be on strike or locked out. I will not reveal any of the private business to anyone not entitled to know the same.

I will not engage in activity evidencing gross disloyalty nor in conduct otherwise unbecoming a member, and will not knowingly wrong a member or see one wronged if in my power to prevent it. I will not appeal to any legal authority in matters pertaining to this Union until I have exhausted all means of redress provided by its laws. I will be considerate of others in word and action and will never discriminate against a fellow worker on account of race, religion, color, creed, sex, sexual orientation, gender identity or expression, age, disability, citizenship, or national origin. I also promise to promote the cause of trade union principles and defend freedom of thought, whether expressed by tongue or pen, with all the power at my command.

I understand there is nothing in this obligation that will in any way interfere with my political and religious rights or that will be in any way inconsistent with my duties arising from any of the relations of life.

item.title: The President's Report: Metro True North Values — Terminations
item.dc:creator: Greg Woodfill
item.content:encoded:
By Greg Woodfill

In the printed headline, the words "True North" are struck through.

Terminations at King County Metro are currently at an unprecedented level. In the first 11 months of 2025, we had 25 terminations. In the last 11 weeks, we've had 22 terminations. Houston, we have a problem. Make this make sense, Metro management.

For many of these terminations, it makes no sense to the Union why management would go straight to proposing termination, then just dig in their heels. We've had twenty-plus-year county public servants with good work records fired for things the Union cannot understand why termination would even be proposed, let alone carried out.

This is not the Metro that many of us signed up for decades ago. We were not expected to be robots incapable of error. The Chiefs, Superintendents, and upper management had actually worked in our front-line shoes. They had the authority to apply progressive discipline along with the experience, wisdom, and courage to do so. They recognized the value of second chances for County employees who had given years of service, and that the County had so much invested in.

I'm not lumping in or attempting to stereotype all Chiefs, Superintendents, or Labor Relations personnel. Or insinuate that all terminations have no merit or don't meet just cause. The Union does observe and appreciate those who are doing their job correctly, as they should, and are being paid well to do so.

Upper management won't take our concerns seriously and seems to want to circle the wagons around their management personnel, refusing to investigate their out-of-line disciplinary actions and discharges, or to believe they could do no wrong.

From more than one person in upper management, I've heard, "We don't want to come across as not supporting our managers." What about supporting your long-term front-line employees? The ones who actually do the work, and who, without them, there would be no need for management jobs.

With the benefit of hindsight and frame-by-frame video review, it's easy to sit in warm rooms and pass judgment. These are people's lives; they deserve the legal and contractual protections of the just cause standard for discipline or discharge. They deserve to be disciplined with dignity and respect, taking their work record and difficult working conditions into account. Every person and every situation is different, and those differences need to be seriously considered before deciding on termination.

What is a "just cause" standard? In 1964, labor arbitrator Carroll Daugherty introduced "The seven tests of just cause" in the form of seven questions.

  1. Fair Notice - An employer may not discipline an employee for violating a rule or standard whose nature and penalties have not been made known.
  2. Prior Enforcement - An employee may not be penalized for violating a rule or standard that the employer has failed to enforce for a prolonged period.
  3. Due Process - An employer must conduct an interview or a hearing before issuing discipline, and must take action promptly. Once assessed, discipline may not be increased.
  4. Substantial Evidence - Charges must be proven by substantial and credible evidence.
  5. Equal Treatment - Unless a valid distinction justifies a higher penalty, an employer may not assess a considerably stronger punishment against one employee than it assessed against another known to have committed the same or a substantially similar offense.
  6. Progressive Discipline - When responding to misconduct that is short of egregious (very serious), an employer must issue at least one level of discipline that allows the employee an opportunity to improve.
  7. Mitigating and Extenuating Circumstances - Discipline must be proportional to the gravity of the offense, taking into account any mitigating, extenuating, or aggravating circumstances.

In the last year, we've observed Metro violating all seven items on the list above. Some of Metro's proposals on discipline in our current contract negotiations would weaken our just cause protections.

This Union will spare no expense or resources to defend our members, who we believe were subjected to discipline or termination without just cause.

The termination numbers listed in the first paragraph above don't include the greatly stepped-up termination of probationary employees at Metro, both at bus and rail. Management chose to unilaterally apply the part-time operator probationary points standard to full-time probationary employees.

When upper management was pressed to justify this inequity, they admitted they intentionally wanted to tighten the standards, saying that too many were "getting through probation." And that they viewed this as "a liability."

While probationary employees' employment is ultimately at their employer's will until they pass probation. Metro has long-established policies to guide its decisions on terminating probationary employees. Applying policy guidelines for terminating probationary employees rather than picking and choosing whom managers want to fire demonstrates the True North values that Metro claims to be guided by.

Recently, when upper management was presented with facts that they hadn't followed their probationary termination standards, they said the quiet part out loud, "We just don't want them back," and asserted their ability to fire at will regardless of policy.

Sadly, I must report that terminations that don't meet the just cause standard aren't limited to King County Metro. Kitsap Transit management is also jumping right to proposing terminations for things that, per their policies, call for applying progressive discipline, not termination.

Both Metro and Kitsap Senior management should stop blowing off our concerns and direct their managers to follow their contracts and policies, which include meeting the Just Cause standards before issuing discipline or terminations. Our union will react accordingly if need be.

ATU 587 – We Are One

item.title: In Loving Memory…
item.content:encoded:
"It is not length of life but depth of life" ~ Ralph Waldo Emerson

We were saddened to learn of the passing of:

It is with deep sadness that we announce the passing of retired Central Base operator, Mary Hopson. Mary started her transit career in 1980 and in that time, earned a 37-year safe driver award, and in 2019, earned Operator of the Year. Mary enjoyed driving routes out of Downtown and was a well-known figure on the route 106 that ran out of Central Base. Mary retired from Metro in June 2019 and enjoyed traveling and spending time with her family. Mary was born and raised in Seattle and will be greatly missed by her loving family, extended family, friends, and the community that she served on her route 106 that has grown to love and appreciate her for her loving spirit and compassion. Mary is survived by her husband of 42 years, two children, and five grandchildren.

Please place these members and their families in your thoughts and hearts

Please notify the union office of any member's passing so that this information may be shared with the rest of our union family.

item.title: The 1st Vice President's Report: Good Stuff
item.dc:creator: Cory Rigtrup
item.content:encoded:
By Cory Rigtrup

It is an honor being appointed as your Vice-President. The shoes I must fill are mighty big. I'll do my best to wear them honorably.

I have been helping out during Ken's absences. Before that, I was helping out with bargaining and representation for more than a decade. I've been around fighting pretty much every fight I could, now it's time to pass on what I've learned to all.

When I first took office in 2018, on average our Local was representing two terminations a month. The last few months, we've seen that number increase to two a week. That is a lot of people losing their jobs. In that same time, we were able to see five members return, three from Kitsap Transit, two from King County. As invigorating as it is to see folks return, the ratio isn't healthy.

It is an exciting time where I am meeting some pretty smart and helpful people. The workload is overwhelming, but there are good people that are willing to help. I've run into some of these folks at the bases, and I appreciate the engagement into conversation. There are also good people that are willing to you, we call them stewards. We put their name on a list and post that list on your worksite's union board. Our Local provides these stewards with training and you give them the opportunity to learn and grow. Feel free to look them up and reach out.

Shop Stewards:

In February we held two shop steward classes, one for Rail, one for Bus. We kind of broke Rail by holding the class on a Saturday. Half of the members we sent union details were denied. I guess we live and learn. The next Rail class with be held in the middle of the week later this month for all those who were denied.

3rd Vice-President:

This month we are voting on the creation of another assistant business agent. The proposal caveats out representation for all the smaller properties and almost half of Rail. It also has a delayed implementation to coincide with our regular cycle of elections. I support the proposal.

The Vice President duty is to represent all members. The addition of the 3rd Vice President doesn't change that. What changes is the workload. The current workload is suffocating if our Local is to stay committed to providing stellar representation to members. With the addition of the 3rd Vice President, I speculate the workload of the Vice President reduces by 30-40%, at the same time increasing resources to the smaller properties.

Out Local has been utilizing Board Officers to help out and create exposure to membership issues. It does help. However, the weight and responsibility that members demand are best served by a full-time officer who has the day-to-day information and resources that will enable us to build our Local into something even stronger.

Come to anyone of the six union meetings in March. Be loud, be quiet, but vote.

Update, Ben-Damnati Arb:

Arbitrator awarded Ben-Damnati his job back in June, with a make whole remedy. Metro did not calculator overtime time earnings into lost wages. Currently, our Local is suing King County in Superior court for wage theft for refusing to pay the full award.

Update, Grant Arb:

Arbitrator awarded Grant his job back in July, with a make whole remedy. Metro did not calculator overtime time earnings into lost wages. Our Local has retained jurisdiction of the arbitrator and demanded a full award to include lost overtime earnings.

Thomas Arb:

March second and third is the arbitration for operator Melissa Thomas. Like most folks with sick kids, she ran into attendance issues. This will be a hard-fought arbitration, where we believe we can show that one, if not more, or the attendance marks should not have occurred. Settlement talks failed, so we gear up to through down. Stay tuned, arbitrations are like a crapshoot, you just never know.

If you see me around say hi. I like to help.

item.title: The Maintenance Vice President's Report: Discipline, Outsourcing, and Grievance Update
item.dc:creator: Jeff Stambaugh
item.content:encoded:
By Jeff Stambaugh

This might sound like a repeat of last month's article, while it's not the same article, the same issues seem to continue.

Discipline

The seemingly never-ending cycle of discipline continues. There have been several more investigatory meetings as well as Loudermill hearings around work performance and "time theft". Metro claims employees are not working during work hours and claiming pay for such hours or employees are not on the property during work hours. Please do not put yourself in this position.

Outsourcing

Several more grievances have been filed over outsourcing of Local 587 work, somehow management still hasn't figured out the language.

Grievances

Currently I have 59 open grievances, while a few of these have been resolved at a low level, I truly don't understand why others have progressed so far into the process rather than finding a resolution somewhere along the way. Sometimes I think Metro is just attempting to frustrate The Union and trying to keep us busy.

Bus Facilities Maintenance

Does it ever end?

Apparently not.

As most of you recall in 2024 TFD management proposed pick positions outside the Collective bargaining agreement, The Union filed an unfair labor practice and MOA's were written and agreed on how to move forward. Those agreements expired Dec 31,2025. Prior to the expiration of those agreements, The Union put TFD management on notice those agreements were going to expire. TFD failed to address the expired MOA's. Now TFD has once again proposed pick positions outside of the language of the Collective Bargaining Agreement based on expired MOA's.

At the pre-pick meeting, The Union requested that the pick positions be updated to reflect the language in the collective bargaining agreement, TFD management so far has refused.

TFD management has tried to insinuate that The Union has held up the pick, that is not true, The Union has instructed management to post and conduct the pick in accordance with the Collective Bargaining Agreement.

item.title: The Recording Secretary's Report: Rail and Streetcar Operator Pick
item.dc:creator: Latrelle Gibson
item.content:encoded:
By Latrelle Gibson

Pick time is right around the corner, well, for the Rail folks, you just had a repick in January, but for Streetcar, it's been a good minute since the Fall 2025 pick. The absentees should be at the bases, Rail and Streetcar driver timecards, the run cuts, and the Seniority list should be out by the time this article is published. The driver timecards for both Rail and Streetcar should be on the website as well, those are usually up prior to the seniority list.

Pick Dates

Rail Operator Pick will be conducted March 9 – 11 and Streetcar pick will be conducted March 13.

Vacation Pick

This is the vacation must pick for Rail. If you're filling out an absentee, please be sure to indicate the vacation periods you want to pick on your absentee. For reference, please log onto the Union Website to view the 2026 vacation periods. Just another note, this is not vacation pick for Streetcar, that will happen during the Fall pick.

Pick Process

For Rail, there will be a pick preview outside of the pick room. The work is generally updated in live time, so you'll know what is left to pick prior to entering the pick room. For absentee picks, please be sure to give us a good working phone number that you will be able to be reached at. For Streetcar, you can view the work 20 min prior to your pick time. If you receive a call from an unknown number, please answer as this may be us trying to contact you for your pick. Remember, if you miss your pick, the Union will have to pick for you, and Union picks cannot be grieved.

Happy pick and see you there!

item.title: It's Nothing Personal…
item.dc:creator: Jim Dimpsey
item.content:encoded:
By Jim Dimpsey

Most of you have by now noticed the unexplained plastic discs stuck on parts of our coaches. They're about three inch rounds and come in black or yellow, depending on where they're stuck. Look closely, and you'll see a word indented into the inner circle.

When I first saw them, I knew what they were immediately. But I was in a unique position. Twenty-two years ago I worked with someone who helped start the company behind those discs.

I worked a few other jobs as well as Metro back then, including one driving some pretty weird vehicles around Seattle. One of the mechanics at that other job, John, told us about a local freight hauling company that had a truck involved in an accident. No biggie, but when the State Patrol asked the driver for his inspection records, the driver (who was new) had no idea what they were.

Oops. The company was slapped with a fine.

You see, after every twelve hours of operation, someone must physically inspect commercial vehicles on the road and make sure they are safe and sound. This inspection must be documented, and that documentation kept onboard the vehicle and presented on demand. (I assume that since our vehicles are run close to home, the primary inspections are performed by Vehicle Maintenance, and inspection records kept locally, Metro has been given an exemption to the onboard record-keeping requirement.)

Someone at Oak Harbor Freight mulled over that fine. That someone was technically minded, and got an idea. He was also a friend of my coworker John. He and his partners (who hired John) developed an electronic inspection recording system for commercial vehicles. They called the new company Zonar.

That's the word indented on those little discs. Though it hasn't been officially introduced to drivers, I've heard enough corroborated rumors to know that Metro has signed a contract with Zonar, and that soon operators will be asked to use Zonar equipment to conduct their daily coach inspections.

Which raises a very, very serious problem.

You see, Zonar has technologically moved on from their humble beginnings two decades ago. The original electronic inspection reader was a custom-made yellow device. Today, Zonar uses a simple tablet computer.

A tablet. A large touch screen with a camera and some speakers. EXACTLY the kind of device Metro SPECIFICALLY PROHIBITS its drivers to use in the yard. Don't believe me? From The Manual, read section 10.06 on Personal Electronic Devices (PEDs). After listing what electronic devices can do, go to the second sentence, where you'll read: "These include, but are not limited to… tablets…."

Ah, but keep reading! The final sentences in the section reads: "Yard Policy: PEDs are also considered a hazard in base yards. Employees may not walk while using any PED."

So, I hope you are asking: how am I supposed to do a "walk"-around inspection of my coach "while using" the Zonar tablet, which definitely falls into the category of "any PED"?

I sadly expect management to hand-wave away the clear and present danger policy 10.06 was written to prevent. They might try to specifically train us to never "walk" while walking around with the device, but to comically stop at each inspection point and only then bring the device toward the inspection disc.

Or they might get even more convoluted. Since the rule was introduced, forbidden electronic devices were prefaced with the word "Personal." Maybe Metro will label Zonar tablets something other than "personal." Which is complete nonsense!

First of all, the section does not specify that prohibited PEDs are "personally owned" by the operator; rather, the section quite pointedly avoids the ownership issue, focusing only on what PEDs are. After all, what if you were caught using a PED and defended yourself by noting it was a device you borrowed from a friend? Shout all you want about the borrowed device not being "personal," I strongly suspect that you'll see that five days off without pay (or worse, if it's not your first PED rodeo).

Rather, even if they didn't mean to, it seems Metro quite wisely used the term "personal" to define the device as "on the operator's person" as well as one being used. So I see no exemptions in The Manual for Zonar tablets… well, nothing that passes the smell test.

Meaning when the Zonar rollout arrives, we drivers must insistently refuse to use these tablets in the yard simply because doing so is specifically noted in The Manual as forbidden. And the rule is there for a very good reason: as multiple psychological studies have confirmed, doing so creates a distraction and is therefore simply dangerous!

Yes! That prohibition is a very good idea! I personally agree with both the spirit and letter of rule 10.06 against the use of all electronic devices in the yard, personal or otherwise, simply because I regard my own safety has sacrosanct. I hope you agree.

Furthermore, I do hope our Union Officers and Executive Board members will back me and my safety-minded colleagues when it comes to insisting that Metro avoid imposing on its drivers any unsafe inspection regimens, especially when they violate Metro's own procedures.

Please, let's not let Metro tell us something incredibly stupid, like using a Zonar tablet in the yard "is nothing personal." Any compromise to our safety absolutely is.

From the News Review, March 2026, page 8. Open in the PDF · Original file on atu587.org

item.title: Resolution No. 2026-01: Affirming Solidarity, Equality, and Mutual Respect and Condemning Racism, Islamophobia, Xenophobia, and Attacks on the LGBTQIA+ Community
item.content:encoded:
A RESOLUTION AFFIRMING SOLIDARITY, EQUALITY, AND MUTUAL RESPECT AND CONDEMNING RACISM, ISLAMOPHOBIA, XENOPHOBIA, AND ATTACKS ON THE LGBTQIA+ COMMUNITY AGAINST MEMBERS AND COMMUNITIES REPRESENTED BY ATU LOCAL 587

WHEREAS, the Amalgamated Transit Union was established on the principles of unity, solidarity, and mutual aid among working people, and the ATU International Constitution affirms the equal dignity, rights, and protections of all members without distinction as to race, color, creed, religion, national origin, gender, gender expression, LGBTQIA+ community, or background; and

WHEREAS, ATU Local 587 represents a diverse membership that includes immigrants, refugees, asylum seekers, naturalized citizens, LGBTQIA+ people, and U.S.-born workers who collectively operate and maintain public transportation systems relied upon by the communities we serve; and

WHEREAS, a substantial portion of ATU Local 587 members work in public-facing and safety-sensitive positions, including bus and rail operations, supervision, and frontline service, where they are highly visible and frequently exposed to public interaction; and

WHEREAS, racism, Islamophobia, and xenophobia, including attacks on immigrant and refugee communities based on national origin, culture, language, religion, or perceived immigration status, LGBTQIA+ status undermine social cohesion and directly threaten the safety, dignity, and well-being of transit workers; and

WHEREAS, xenophobia and homophobia often manifests through collective blame and dehumanization of entire communities and does not distinguish between citizenship, immigration status, or legal standing, thereby placing all members associated with targeted communities at risk; and

WHEREAS, rhetoric originating from public officials or positions of authority carries significant influence and can normalize discriminatory behavior, embolden harassment, and create hostile conditions for transit workers who cannot disengage from the public while performing their duties; and

WHEREAS, Muslim members, particularly women who wear hijab or other religious attire, as well as immigrant members from historically targeted or war-torn regions, and the LGBTQIA+ communities experience heightened vulnerability during periods of increased fear-mongering and xenophobic and homophobic and transphobic rhetoric; and

WHEREAS, many members of ATU Local 587 have personal or family histories shaped by war, displacement, or political instability, and membership in the LGBTQIA+ communities, and are acutely aware of the real-world consequences of dehumanizing language and divisive rhetoric; and

WHEREAS, ATU Local 587 acknowledges that racism, Islamophobia, and xenophobia, homophobia and transphobia can also appear within workplaces and union environments through casual remarks, stereotypes, jokes, or dismissive language that demean coworkers based on culture, accent, religion, gender, gender identity and expression, or national origin; and

WHEREAS, such conduct, whether intentional or casual, erodes trust, damages morale, and weakens the solidarity upon which the labor movement and this Union depend; and

WHEREAS, the ATU International Constitution places responsibility on all members to uphold the honor and integrity of the Union and to refrain from actions or language that bring harm, division, or discredit upon fellow members or the Union as a whole; and

WHEREAS, true solidarity requires not only collective defense against external threats to members, but also accountability and respect within our own membership;

THEREFORE, BE IT RESOLVED, that ATU Local 587 unequivocally condemns racism, Islamophobia, xenophobia, homophobia, and transphobia, including attacks on immigrant, refugee, and minority communities, whether expressed by public officials, institutions, or individuals; and

BE IT FURTHER RESOLVED, that ATU Local 587 reaffirms its commitment to ensuring that every member, regardless of race, religion, national origin, immigration status, language, LGBTQIA+ status, or cultural background, is treated with dignity, respect, and fairness in the workplace and within the Union; and

BE IT FURTHER RESOLVED, that ATU Local 587 calls upon all officers, representatives, stewards, and members to actively uphold these principles in their conduct, language, and actions and to challenge behavior that undermines unity or creates a hostile or unsafe environment; and

BE IT FURTHER RESOLVED, that ATU Local 587 affirms solidarity with Muslim members, immigrant members, refugee members, and all members whose communities have been targeted by xenophobia, homophobia, transphobia and supports their right to work and participate in union life free from harassment, intimidation, or discrimination; and

BE IT FURTHER RESOLVED, that ATU Local 587 encourages education, awareness, and dialogue consistent with union values to strengthen understanding, reduce harm, and reinforce solidarity among members; and

BE IT FINALLY RESOLVED, that ATU Local 587 declares that racism, Islamophobia, xenophobia, homophobia, transphobia, and all forms of dehumanization have no place in this Union, and that unity, respect, and solidarity remain foundational to the mission and strength of the Amalgamated Transit Union.

ADOPTED this __27__ day of ___January_______, 2026

By the Membership of Amalgamated Transit Union Local 587

item.title: February in Action: Solidarity, Reflection, Representation, and Building for the Future
item.dc:creator: Hassannoor Aden, Minority Affairs Officer, ATU 587/King County Labor Delegate
item.content:encoded:
By Hassannoor Aden, Minority Affairs Officer, ATU 587/King County Labor Delegate

February has been one of the most active and meaningful months we have had in a long time. As your Minority Affairs Officer, I have seen how workplace issues, community concerns, and broader social realities are all connected. This month was not only about responding to challenges. It was about building structure, strengthening relationships, and preparing for the work ahead.

One of the most important moments this month was the Immigration Listening Session held at Atlantic-Central Base. The turnout was strong. Members came ready to speak honestly about what they and their families are experiencing. There were concerns about immigration enforcement, fear of family separation, and the possibility of racial profiling based on skin color, accent, name, or religion.

Some members shared that they feel pressure every time immigration is discussed in the media. One of the most difficult parts of the listening session was hearing members talk about their children. Several members shared with me, that their worry does not stop when they clock in. Some are concerned about daycare centers and schools becoming targets, especially in communities that have already experienced hate incidents. When you are driving a bus or working in operations, you are responsible for public safety. At the same time, your mind is on your child and whether they are safe.

A few members spoke with me, about making painful decisions out of fear. Some mentioned sending their children out of the country temporarily to stay with relatives because they did not feel secure keeping them here during uncertain times. No parent should have to make that kind of decision. It shows how deeply these issues are affecting families.

These are not abstract political debates. These are parents trying to protect their children. These are workers trying to focus on their duties while carrying emotional stress that most people do not see.

As Minority Affairs, it is important that leadership understands the full picture. When members are worried about their children's safety, it impacts concentration, morale, and overall well being. A safe workplace must also recognize the broader realities employees are facing outside of work.

Others who spoke with me about relatives who are undocumented or in temporary status, and the anxiety that creates at home. A few described how quickly rumors can spread in immigrant communities, increasing fear even when the facts are unclear. These are not small issues. They affect focus, mental health, and overall well being.

King County has one of the largest immigrant populations in the state. Many Metro employees are first generation immigrants. They are hardworking individuals who show up every day to serve the public. They are raising children here while supporting family members abroad. Some send remittances every month. Some are helping siblings or parents navigate paperwork and legal systems that can be confusing and expensive. They carry responsibility on both sides of the ocean.

It mattered that Metro management acknowledged these realities and clearly communicated county policies that protect employees. The reminder that certain immigration related information cannot be shared without proper legal authority gave reassurance. It also mattered that ATU 587 leadership stood firm in defense of our members. When labor and management can sit at the same table and commit to dignity and fairness, it strengthens trust across the system.

February also carries deep meaning as Black History Month. For our Black members, whether African American or Black immigrants from Africa and the Caribbean, this month is both a celebration and a reminder. It is a celebration of resilience, leadership, and contributions that have shaped this country. It is also a reminder that discrimination and profiling have long histories.

Several members reflected on how concerns raised in the listening session connect to that history. The idea of being judged first by appearance, accent, or background is not new. That is why these conversations require honesty and awareness. Black History Month challenges all of us to look at how far we have come and how far we still need to go.

Day to day, these issues show up in simple ways. Members question whether they are being treated differently. Some hesitate to speak up because of their accent. Others feel they must work twice as hard to prove they belong. These quiet pressures build over time. As Minority Affairs, our responsibility is to bring those concerns forward in a constructive way and advocate for fairness and equal treatment.

This month was also significant beyond Metro. I had the opportunity to attend Lobby Day in Olympia and meet with elected representatives from our districts. Speaking directly with lawmakers about the realities facing transit workers and immigrant communities was eye opening. Policies around transportation funding, worker protections, and civil rights are shaped in those rooms.

Many first generation immigrants are not always familiar with how state government works or who represents them. Lobby Day reminded me that engagement is power. When we show up and tell our stories, we influence the conversation. Representation is not automatic. It requires participation and awareness. As Minority Affairs, we will continue encouraging members to learn about their districts, register to vote if eligible, and stay informed.

Another major accomplishment this month was the successful launch of the ATU 587 Minority Affairs Committee. This is a milestone for our local. Up until now, much of the work fell on one office. By creating a committee, we are building long term structure and shared responsibility.

The committee will help delegate key tasks such as outreach to different cultural communities within our membership, organizing educational workshops, coordinating with other committees, and supporting members who raise discrimination or equity concerns. It will also create opportunities for leadership development among members who want to be more involved in union work.

We are setting clear goals for the committee, including strengthening communication between minority members and union leadership, promoting civic education, supporting mentorship, and building partnerships with community organizations when appropriate. This ensures that Minority Affairs is not reactive only when there is a crisis, but proactive in strengthening unity across our membership.

February has shown us that solidarity requires effort. It requires meetings, hard conversations, education, and organization. From the Immigration Listening Session, to Black History Month reflections, to Lobby Day in Olympia, to launching the Minority Affairs Committee, this month has laid important groundwork.

As your Minority Affairs Officer, I remain committed to protecting the dignity, rights, and representation of every member of ATU 587. Our diversity is not a weakness. It is a strength. When we recognize it, organize it, and stand together across race, language, culture, and background, we build a union that is stronger, more informed, and better prepared for whatever comes next.

Thank you to every member who showed up, spoke up, and stepped forward to lead. The work continues, and together we are moving in the right direction.

From the News Review, March 2026, pages 10–11. Open in the PDF · Original file on atu587.org

item.title: Open Bargaining — Strength Through Engagement
item.dc:creator: Chuck Lare, Atlantic Base Shop Steward
item.content:encoded:
By Chuck Lare, Atlantic Base Shop Steward

For the first time in ATU 587 history, your union is negotiating our Metro contract with the doors wide open. This isn't happening in some back room where deals get cut behind closed doors. Open bargaining means you—every single member—can walk in, pull up a chair, and watch your contract being forged in real time.

This is your invitation. Your bargaining team needs you there.

Why This Matters

When management sits across the table from our negotiators, they need to see more than a handful of union reps. They need to see the workforce they're actually negotiating with—operators, mechanics, maintenance workers, the people who keep Metro running every single day. Your presence sends an unmistakable message: we're watching, we're engaged, and we're not accepting a raw deal.

Open bargaining strips away the mystery of contract negotiations. You'll witness firsthand what our team is fighting for and what obstacles they face in winning fair terms. You'll see management's tactics, their priorities, their pushback. You'll understand why certain battles take time and why solidarity matters.

Knowledge is power. When members understand how their contract gets made, they become stronger advocates for themselves and their coworkers. They see what's possible and what's at stake. They stop relying on rumors and start trusting what they've witnessed with their own eyes.

How We Got Here

I've been advocating for open bargaining since 2014, writing about its virtues in these pages. Credit where it's due: our ATU 587 President fought for and won Metro's agreement to open these negotiations to membership observation. That's a victory before we've even signed a contract.

This transparency isn't common. Many locals still negotiate behind closed doors, leaving members guessing about what happened until after the ink dries. We're doing something different because we believe our members deserve better.

The Contract Action Team

To maximize member engagement, ATU 587 has formed the Contract Action Team (CAT). This team exists for one purpose: getting members to these bargaining sessions. CAT members are reaching out, organizing attendance, and building momentum. They understand that open bargaining only works when members actually show up.

From CAT's efforts, we're seeing increased attendance at sessions. More importantly, we're building trust. When members see the process unfold transparently, they trust the outcome—whether it's a hard-won victory or a tough compromise. They know their negotiators gave everything because they watched it happen.

What You Need to Know

Before attending, review the Code of Conduct for Bargaining Observers at: https://atu587live.s3.us-west-2.amazonaws.com/wp-content/uploads/2025/12/04153952/Code-of-Conduct.pdf

These guidelines ensure sessions remain productive while protecting everyone's ability to observe freely. They're straightforward: be respectful, stay quiet during negotiations, and understand you're there to witness, not participate directly.

To learn more about the power and mechanics of open bargaining, watch "Open Up Bargaining! News Guild Workshop" at: https://youtu.be/BcDht-BRPgQ?si=gzQ_fWFPkD0rDdD8

Your Move

Open bargaining only delivers its full strength when members engage. An empty observers' section tells management we don't care enough to show up. A full room tells them we're unified, informed, and serious.

Your bargaining team is fighting for your wages, your benefits, your working conditions, and your future. They're doing it in full view because they believe in transparency and member power. Now it's your turn.

Show up. Watch your contract being built. Put your eyes on management. Stand with your union.

This is our contract. These are our negotiations. This is our moment.

From the News Review, March 2026, page 12. Open in the PDF · Original file on atu587.org

item.title: Structure Before Expansion: A Different Way to Think About VP #3
item.dc:creator: Andy Price, Shop Steward, Local 587
item.content:encoded:
By Andy Price, Shop Steward, Local 587

There has been significant discussion about the proposal to add a 3rd Vice President. The workload concerns being raised are real. Contract enforcement is harder. Management behavior has deteriorated. Bargaining is more complex. No one disputes that.

At the same time, we should acknowledge something broader: our Local still operates largely on a governance model built in the 1800s — where structural decisions are made only by those physically present at a meeting. For routine matters that may be workable. For major, long-term financial commitments, it deserves reconsideration.

The question before us is not whether the work exists.

The question is how we structure ourselves to do that work effectively, proportionally, and sustainably.

What Our Structure Was Designed to Do

Under our bylaws and the ATU Constitution and General Laws, full-time officers are generally elected by the membership at large. That principle exists for a reason. It ensures that those who hold the highest authority in the Local are accountable to the entire membership — not just one craft or property.

This does not mean craft-specific positions can never exist. It does mean they should be created carefully and only when truly necessary.

That is also why we have an Executive Board of roughly twenty elected representatives and an established Shop Steward system. Those positions were designed to distribute work, engage membership talent, and prevent concentration of authority in too few hands.

The President of this Local is not only a presiding officer. The title reflects it clearly: President/Business Agent. The Vice Presidents serve as Assistant Business Agents. Their responsibility includes organizing, delegating, training, bargaining, and mobilizing the membership — not personally carrying every grievance.

If workload is overwhelming, the first structural question should be: Are we fully utilizing the officers and stewards we already have?

Capacity Already in Place

It is important to acknowledge the professional office staff we already have. Our office manager and staff handle substantial behind-the-scenes work — tracking grievances, managing documentation, coordinating scheduling, and maintaining operational continuity. Much of that work is not visible, but it is essential.

These are not political positions. They provide institutional knowledge and stability regardless of election cycles.

If enforcement capacity truly needs expansion, another option would be strengthening professional staff support — for example, adding a dedicated enforcement or grievance support position to assist with investigations, document preparation, research, and brief development across all classifications.

Unlike an elected Vice President, a professional staff position could have its duties adjusted as needs evolve and could support the entire membership without being tied to a specific electorate.

A Capacity Question — Not a Feelings Question

Other ATU locals of comparable or larger size, including those with rail divisions, operate with one Vice President. They rely heavily on trained stewards and Executive Board members to handle day-to-day enforcement and preparation.

That model is not about copying other locals. It is about using capacity intelligently.

We already have the ability to detail Executive Board members when workload spikes. That flexibility is built into our structure.

Instead of permanently expanding the officer structure, we could:

  • Detail Executive Board members during high-demand periods.
  • Invest more consistently in steward training and coordination.
  • Strengthen professional support staff.
  • Modernize participation tools to engage more members in real time.

These approaches increase capacity without locking the Local into long-term structural expansion.

The Financial Reality

A full-time officer is not just a salary. It includes benefits, pension contributions, and a vehicle allowance. At present, five full-time officers receive both salary and car allowance. Adding a sixth represents a substantial and ongoing financial commitment.

This is not a temporary adjustment. It is a structural expansion.

At a time when arbitration costs and budget considerations are often weighed carefully, we should be cautious about adding permanent fixed expenses that reduce flexibility elsewhere.

Financial stewardship is part of representation.

Proportionality, Accountability, and Participation

Our current structure allows the membership at large to choose its leadership. Full-time officers accountable to the entire Local must weigh priorities proportionally across all crafts and properties.

While our current structure already includes one craft-specific Vice President, expanding that model further represents a significant structural shift that deserves careful consideration..

Major structural and financial decisions should also involve the broadest possible participation. Our bylaws already require publication and notice. Allowing members to cast votes electronically on major bylaw proposals would modernize participation without eliminating in-person meetings. When long-term commitments affecting thousands are decided by a relatively small number present at a meeting, it is reasonable to ask whether we can do better.

Before expanding the number of elected offices, we should fully utilize the capacity already built into our system.

A strong union is not defined by how many titles it has. It is defined by how effectively it organizes the talent, experience, and commitment of its members.

For these structural, financial, and democratic reasons, I cannot support this proposal as written. I believe there are more effective and sustainable ways to strengthen enforcement and representation. For that reason, I will be voting no.

From the News Review, March 2026, pages 14–15. Open in the PDF · Original file on atu587.org

item.title: Letter to the Editor: Vote NO on a 3rd Vice President
item.dc:creator: Tzur Wilfand, Bellevue Base
item.content:encoded:
By Tzur Wilfand, Bellevue Base

Dear Editor,

Opinion: Vote NO on a 3rd Vice President. Let's spend our money on members, not more full-time union officers

Our union is asking members to vote on a big change: adding a third Vice President (VP).

I have been a shop steward for over 26 years. I care deeply about our union and our members.

In my opinion, adding a third VP is the wrong choice. I am asking you to Vote NO.

Why I say NO

1. It costs too much

A new Vice President will cost about $180,000 every year.

This money comes from your union dues.

This new VP would mainly represent only about 20% of the members.

It is not right to use everyone's money for a position that helps only a small group.

2. Use the leaders we already have

We have already elected Executive Board members to represent us at our bases and properties.

They were elected to help members with problems and grievances.

Before we spend money on another top position, we should fully use the leaders we have already elected.

They should represent all members at their assigned bases.

That is what we elected them to do.

3. A better idea: a Union Lawyer

If we want to spend money to help members, there is a better way.

We should hire a full-time Union Lawyer—a lawyer who works only for our union.

A Union Lawyer would:

  • Know our contracts very well
  • Fight King County and other employers faster
  • Work only for our members, not outside clients
  • Help us get better results in bargaining and disputes

Other unions do this, and it works.

This is a smarter and stronger use of our dues.

The bottom line

A third Vice President costs a lot of money and does not fix our real problems.

It does not help the whole membership.

Please Vote NO on the 3rd Vice President.

Let's spend our money in a way that helps all members.

Let's build a stronger union by using our dues wisely.

Tzur Wilfand, Bellevue Base 26+ Years as Shop-Steward

ATU 587 reserves the right to edit or refuse all letters to the editor. All letters to the editor are the views of the authors and do not necessarily reflect the views of ATU 587. Letters are expected to be the sincere personal views of the authors as opposed to canned reproduced statements.
