Shop Steward 2026 (Jefferson Transit)

Bulletin dated February 12, 2026. To: Local 587 Members at JTA. From: Latrelle Gibson, Recording Secretary.

Pursuant to the Bylaw Article IV, Section 2, Jefferson Transit Authority (JTA) bargaining unit shall have one Shop Steward for every 10 members, or part thereof to be elected for a one-year term in office.

The Shop Stewards for 2026 are:

  • Stephanie Sherwood — email: stephaniesherwood1982@gmail.com, Phone- 971-244-3056
  • Leah Waugh — email: leahwaugh@gmail.com, Phone- 425-314-5769
  • Dan Stenberg — email: bigdan220@gmail.com, Phone- 360-821-1062

Thank You for your willingness to serve the membership!

Shop Steward Elections for Spring/Summer 2026 Shakeup (King County Metro)

Bulletin dated February 17, 2026. To: All Local 587 Members at KCM. From: Latrelle Gibson, Recording Secretary.

Pursuant to the Bylaws and Rules of Order of Local 587, Article IV, Section 6, Paragraphs (a), (b), (c), and (d), this notice serves to open nominations for Shop Stewards. Nominations must be submitted in writing to the Union office no later than Friday, April 10, 2026. Any members in good standing interested in being a Shop Steward must nominate themselves. Nomination forms will be available at the worksites, on the ATU 587 website or E-mail nominations are accepted by sending an email to the Recording Secretary, Latrelle Gibson recsec@atu587.org.

Any worksite requiring an election will be scheduled as needed.

Anyone interested in serving as Chief Shop Steward should submit their request in writing at the same time, although nominations will be accepted for the Chief Shop Steward position for a period of five (5) days past the election of the Shop Stewards.

WPSL Changes & Explanation (Kitsap Transit)

Bulletin dated February 11, 2026. To: All ATU 587 Members at Kitsap Transit. From: Latrelle Gibson, Recording Secretary.

We are hearing that there is still some confusion over the upcoming changes to WPSL. All Full-Time and Extra-Board Operators will receive 20 hours of GL. If you are Part-time, you will NOT receive these hours.

Please note that your GL Bank will determine the number of hours designated as WPSL.

If your GL bank has 80 hours after the additional 20 hours are added, 40 of those hours will be designated as WPSL-qualified. If you took 2 weeks (10 days at 8 hours) without working additional hours, you would eliminate all your GL and WPSL designated hours.

If your GL bank has 40 hours after the additional 20 hours have been added, all 40 hours will be designated as WPSL. Please note that if your GL bank is empty, you will receive the 20 hours of GL and have 20 hours of WPSL designated.

A bar chart (in hours) illustrates the three cases: 80 Total, 40 Total, and 20 WPSL.

Executive Board Vehicle Maintenance Position #3 Vacancy

Bulletin dated February 17, 2026. To: All ATU Local 587 Vehicle Maintenance Members. From: Latrelle Gibson, Recording Secretary.

At this time, due to Cory Rigtrup being appointed to Vice President #1, the Executive Board position #3 that represents Vehicle Maintenance is now vacant.

Pursuant to Article III, Section 2 (i), this vacancy will be filled by a majority vote of the remaining Executive Board members. All Vehicle Maintenance members wishing to apply for this position must submit a letter of interest to the Executive Board for consideration. A letter of interest may be emailed to the recording secretary recsec@atu587.org or sent to the Union office. These letters of interest must arrive no later than Monday, March 23, 2026, by 12:00 p.m. Any applicant wishing to appear before the Executive Board must state so in their letter and be available to address the Executive Board between the hours of 9:00 a.m. and 12:00 p.m. on Tuesday, March 24, 2026.

This vacancy will be filled at the Executive Board meeting of March 24, 2026. Installation of the new officer will take place at the following Charter Membership meeting on April 6, 2026.

To: All Members of Local 587
From: Recording Secretary Latrelle Gibson

Proposal To Change Bylaws: Table of Contents; Article VI Duties of Officers, Section 4-8; Article III Officers, Section 1. (d-i) The Regular Officers of the Local; Article III Officers, Section 2. (j) Executive Board; Article IV Committees, Section 7. Wages and Conditions Committee; Article V Salaries and Compensations, Section 1. (a-f) 3rd Vice President/Assistant Business Representative through Section 7. Executive Board Shall Create a Budget in February; Article XIII General Election – Election of Delegates, Section 1. Delegate Eligibility

Submitted by Jeff Stambaugh and Abdiwahab Adan on January 20, 2026

In accordance with the Article XV, pertaining to bylaw proposals, the following proposal will be published in the February and March 2026 edition of the News Review and will be voted upon at the March 2026 cycle of meetings.

In the New Proposed Language, the printed proposal strikes through deleted text and underlines added text. Here, deleted text is marked as deleted and added text is in bold.

Current Language

Contents

Article III Officers

(a) President/Business Representative

(b) Vice President/Assistant Business Representative

(c) 2nd Vice President/Assistant Business Representative - Maintenance

(d) Financial Secretary/Treasurer

(e) Recording Secretary/Correspondent to In Transit

(f) Candidates for President/Business Representative, Vice President/Assistant Business Representative, Financial Secretary/Treasurer and Recording Secretary/Correspondent to In Transit shall be elected by the membership at large.

(g) Candidates for 2nd Vice President/Assistant Business Representative - Maintenance shall be nominated from and elected by all members within Vehicle Maintenance; Facilities Maintenance; Rail Vehicle Maintenance; Way, Power and Signals, and Streetcar Maintainers as listed in the current labor agreement with King County/Metro.

Section 2. Executive Board

(j) If a vacancy occurs for any reason in any of the following elected positions: President/Business Representative, Vice President/Assistant Business Representative, 2nd Vice President/Assistant Business Representative- Maintenance, Financial Secretary/Treasurer or Recording Secretary, a special election will be held to fill the unexpired term. The special election will be held in compliance with Article XII of these Bylaws and Section 14 of the Constitution and General Laws of the Amalgamated Transit Union.

If a vacancy occurs within 18 months of the normal expiration of the term of office in the position of President/Business Representative, the Vice President/ Assistant Business Representative shall preside and perform all duties pertaining to the office of the President until the regular general election is held.

If a vacancy occurs within 18 months of the normal expiration of the term of office in the position of Vice President/Assistant Business Representative, Financial Secretary/Treasurer or Recording Secretary, the Executive Board shall meet prior to the next regular union meeting and select a member of the Executive Board to fill the unexpired term. The appointment must be approved by a majority vote of the members in attendance at the next regular meeting of the Local. If a vacancy occurs within 18 months of the normal expiration of the term of office in the position of 2nd Vice President/Assistant Business Representative-Maintenance, the Executive Board shall meet prior to the next regular union meeting and select a member from the Vehicle Maintenance/Facilities Maintenance Executive Board Officers to fill the unexpired term. The appointment must be approved by a majority of the members in attendance at the next regular meeting of the Local.

Article IV Committees

Section 7. Wages and Conditions Committee

The members of the Wages and Conditions Committee shall consist of the President/Business Representative, Vice President/Assistant Business Representative, 2nd Vice President/Assistant Business Representative-Maintenance, Financial Secretary/Treasurer, Recording Secretary and all Executive Board members. A selection shall be made by these members for the Local's negotiating committee. All full-time officers shall be members of the Local's negotiating committee by virtue of their office.

Article V Salaries and Compensations

Section 1. Setting Full-Time Officer Wages

The Executive Board shall review and adjust the wages for the office of President/Business Representative, Vice President/Assistant Business Representative, 2nd Vice President/Assistant Business Representative-Maintenance, Financial Secretary/Treasurer and Recording Secretary at the regular December Executive Board meeting. item.title: January Operators' LMRC Meeting (February 5, 2026)
item.dc:creator: Lisa Nault #3647 and Rachael Buchanan #21341; ATU 587 Bus Reps
item.content:encoded:
By Lisa Nault #3647 and Rachael Buchanan #21341; ATU 587 Bus Reps

Labor Management Relations Committee — to discuss, approve and/or propose resolutions to issues or problems of Metro policies which affects the Union and which either party requests to be placed on the agenda, and issues or problems of contract administration other than formal grievances.

Attendees: Greg Woodfill, Rachael Buchanan, Lisa Nault, Jabari Hampton, Cory Rigtrup, William McCoy, Collin Dunphy

Follow Up

ADA Placards: Trying to push it forward and the logjam we keep running into is who is going to pay for it. People are pointing fingers at Bus Ops, but we just aren't getting any traction on who is going to pay for it. The last number we got was $200,000.00. There is disbelief that 1500 stickers can cost that much. Not really a reliable number.

Customer Relations Classes: SSQA had 174 respondents to surveys. How satisfied are the attendees? 4.58 out of 5, How confident do you feel with using the tools presented? 4.56 out of 5. There has been agreement on the third class to start rolling out in March, which will also tie into FIFA. Let's start looking at continuing education next month. Might have to be pushed a bit until July.

Tukwila Base: The Union has noticed the routes that are to be electrified do not have the new Gillig buses running. They aren't going out on every route, but they are going out. On the first day there were some problems on some of the coaches, and this gives us a chance to work out problems. Will there be a map of the base at pick? The Superintendent had conversations with training on route movement in the yard and we're hoping to have signs installed to direct Operators to the proper location after parking in the garage. The signs are at the base; they just need Facilities to install them. We have a couple of Union Boards to get set up. Executive Board officer has volunteered. How many Board Operators and Reports. Only 47 operators, so it will be small. We will follow up one more month. There will be 6 Report Operators, 3 am and 3 pm.

Building a Successful Probationary Program for FTO: We had a bit of a conversation, and since we last talked about doing business a little different? What if we just extend the Operator Probation Period. When we have those people who need a little more guidance, we have a clear path and we're going to give you another 3 months, and here's the things you need to do to be successful. With mutual agreement, we have the ability to extend probationary periods. If this person doesn't have a mentor, let's get them assigned. How is it applied. If we have someone that's struggling, let's get them help and show them clear expectations, and then Metro reserves the right to terminate if those aren't met. We do it everywhere except Bus and Rail Ops. You believe in the Employee, and we believe in the Employee, let's work together. Is this informal? No, this is in the CBA, it just takes a mutual agreement. The Union Vice President will provide examples of about 20 that have taken place in VM. Let's get away from the rigid policy. Metro agrees that that is the goal. Follow up

Shawn Yim Memorial: In regard to Shawn Yim, we all gathered 3 weeks ago for some moving events and the County really came through and we honored him. Part of that was the installation of the bench. Part of the problem was the logo was incorrect. The bench was covered up, and it looks like it's been forgotten about and it's an emotional concern and would like Management to address that to get it fixed and properly installed. Metro will get with the Superintendent at the base to get their thought processes on that. Sounds like it might need a work request to be put in. Additionally, Mark McLaughlin's plaque was supposed to be moved, and we understand that hasn't happened at Atlantic/Central base yet. If there's someone in the chain of command that can help with that, we would appreciate that.

Preventability Process Before Imposing Discipline: A large portion of the issue is with probationary employees who have had accidents, were fired, and then the accident is overturned. In the end, we hear that, "Its managements rights, and we just want to get rid of them." We had some issues between Management and the Union on the reread process and we're working on solving those issues and bringing someone back after they've been fired has proved difficult. Over at Rail this happened and the Union told them they were going to end up with a shortage of labor and that's proving to be the case right now. The Union understands that Metro only wants the best of the best, but the bus side is going to end up in the same position if we don't change the process. Management tries to gloss over the issue and tries to move on. The Union asks for a response because management doesn't seem to be responding to our concerns. Metro claims there isn't a question or an action item. The Union wants to know if this is just dropping off the table. The Union has concerns that nothing is being accomplished and it is very frustrating for Operators to be ignored at these meetings. Metro changes course and asks if the discipline topic is just a general concern because if something has already been decided above this level, the Manager won't chase it down. The Union stresses that the concern is about letting people go before their accident has gone through the process.

Back Door Entry outside of CBD: The concern was going to the card readers at the back door, and a bulletin was put out that stated it was the Operator's call to open the back door for entry or not. It's a safety concern for Operators and is a critical tool for operators to not have to use the back door. Are we going to all door boarding and is that discretion being taken away from the Operators? What is Metro doing to educate the public? Metro can't answer that. The bulletin says, "While we are.." Does that mean the policy is going to change? Is Metro trying to implement all door boarding? If we are, we want to know that now. Operators need to feel safe. There's a reason this was put out and the first sentence pretty much spells it out. If it's not an issue, then why was that bulletin put out? The recollection is that Metro started putting readers at the back door with the intent of going to all door boarding and it was apparent that it was an issue and that's why the second bulletin was put out. Customer education is needed at this point. It was a great theory, but Metro has now backtracked. If you put out a bulletin to tell the Operator, that does nothing to educate the public. This will be a long-term process, but we're going to see operators who don't care about the rules and are causing issues for operators who are. Operators need support. We can use loaders, Fare enforcement officers, etc… Metro complains that we won't solve this here and thinks we shouldn't discuss it. The Union points out that this is an Operator LMRC and this is an issue that Operators face. The Union would like the Metro Committee members to bring it up and take it further. We are going to bring up Operator Issues in the Operator LMRC. The Manager backtracks and promises to take it up the chain further. The attitude coming across from Management is that it's not their specific concern, so they don't want to respond. Metro admits there are some things they can directly affect, but some of the overall policy things that are somewhat beyond their control, will take it further and bring it back. Clarification on policy and support of the Operators. Policy in the end is imperfect because the real world doesn't work that way. Policy should be a guideline, but it should support Operators where safety is needed. The LMRC is a conduit for ideas and concerns to flow upwards to upper management. It's a valuable tool so they know what concerns are. Follow up next month.

Vacation Verification: Are Operators at all bases verifying their vacation a few weeks prior to the start, so they remember when it is? South Base does, but East Base and some Downtown Bases discontinued the process during COVID. Metro wasn't able to check on that but will send an email out today. We'll follow up again next month.

New Business

No new business.

Meeting adjourned at 10:03.

Have a topic you want brought up in the LMRC Meetings? Contact Lisa or Rachael to submit your topics.

item.title: Report Safety and Security Incidents on Mobile Devices with the New SSaM Access Anywhere QR Code
item.content:encoded:
Read from a scanned image on page 24 of the PDF, so it may contain errors. View page 24 in the PDF.

Dear colleagues,

The Safety, Security, and Quality Assurance (SSQA) team is excited to share an alternative way for employees to report security incidents through the Safety and Security Management (SSaM) system without having to use a computer.

The SSaM Access Anywhere QR code allows employees to access SSaM directly on their mobile device (e.g., cellphone) to report an incident, submit a near miss/close call, or share safety suggestions. This functionality was created based on feedback my team received to help improve accessibility and use of SSaM.

SSaM – Security Incident Mobile Update w/ QR Code

Use the QR Code to Report a Security Incident/Drug Use/Other Safety Reports:

Instructions:

  • Using your cell phone, open your Camera app
  • Point your phone's camera at the QR code
  • Follow your phone's prompt to open the link in a browser
  • Click that link and it should open your browser and take you to the SSaM login page

The QR code itself is on page 24 of the PDF.

I will work to promote the best interests of this Union and encourage my fellow workers to become members of the same. I will not take the place of any member of this organization, or any other union worker who may be on strike or locked out. I also promise to promote the cause of trade union principles and defend freedom of thought, whether expressed by tongue or pen, with all the power at my command.

I understand there is nothing in this obligation that will in any way interfere with my political and religious rights or that will be in any way inconsistent with my duties arising from any of the relations of life.

This obligation I take upon my honor, and solemnly promise to keep the same, as long as I remain a member of this Union.

item.title: The President’s Report: My Response to Minneapolis
item.content:encoded:
Both personally and in my capacity as President of ATU Local 587 I stand in solidarity with ATU Local 1005 and their membership in Minneapolis as they deal with the effects of the large deployment of ICE and its current tactics in their community.

Just like our Local they have a large segment of members who are legally living and working in this Country but must now live in fear of possibly being stopped, detained, deported solely based on their appearance or accent.

Union members do and should expect their Union to support them when their employment is put in doubt, and their safety on the job is placed at risk. Union officers work for the members and should always represent their interests and wishes to the best of our ability and judgement. Many of our members are asking where the support, preparation, and direction from both their employer and their Union is in case Seattle becomes the next Minneapolis?

The Union has set up a meeting with senior Metro management and the members calling for support to hear their concerns and experiences. And to develop plans and guidance going forward.

Up until now, the Union, Metro, and the County have

By Greg Woodfill shared the same concerns about not taking actions that could draw attention from ICE to our diverse workforce and the potential negative effects on our members. We’re now well past the point of remaining silent without direction or plans.

This is solely about Unionism and collectively standing up for, protecting, and fighting for fellow Union members and NOT about politics, or which side of our nation’s bitter political divide that you stand on or identify with. A harm to one is harm to all!

Our Local, through our members’ voluntary donations to COPE, has a long history of supporting politicians and initiatives that support public transit, our local, and Unions in general. We do NOT use members’ dues for this or support or represent a political party or a party’s agenda.

Our COPE committee sends its recommendations on elections to the E-board and, subsequently, to the membership, based on interviews with politicians. The membership has the final say on these recommendations, and it’s just a recommendation for members to know who the COPE committee believes will be more supportive of Transit and Unions. It’s NOT the Union telling you who to vote for, or which party to support. It’s NOT the Union attempting to represent your political point of view for you.

Please consider donating to or increasing your contribution to COPE. This Union has significant political clout on local transit funding and laws that directly affect our jobs and working conditions, thanks to our long history of endorsements. A portion of your donation goes to the International COPE committee, which lobbies our interests with national and state politicians on transit funding, laws, bills, and initiatives.

You could not like, agree with, or participate in our system of politics/lobbying and still recognize the need for your Union to advocate for and protect your interests within the system we are forced to deal with.

We need to be players in this game to have our voices heard, our power felt, and our interests properly represented. It has historically worked out very well for this Union to do so.

New and future generations of ATU 587 members must learn about and choose to participate in COPE if we want to maintain the political clout that we’ve spent decades building through voluntary member donations to COPE. It’s everyone’s responsibility who understands this to talk with their peers about COPE and its importance. It’s your Union; it requires the membership's active participation to remain viable and strong.

The 3rd VP

You’ll see in this News Review a bylaw proposal to add a third Vice President. The Full Time Officers have spent the last year and a half trying to find the perfect formula for adding an additional VP for this local and there just isn’t a perfect solution for everyone. We are pushing forward with what we believe is the best solution that is a win-win for all members. With now 4,800 active members two Vice Presidents are not sufficient to properly deal with the amount of work thrown at them on a daily basis.

If we had a VP for all of rail including VM it would take too much work away from VP two, go back to a VP representing both operations and VM, and not lighten the load of VP 1 enough.

With a new VP representing Rail Operations and our other four properties it is a perfect balance of total members for VP 3, and lightens the load of VP 1 which allows VP 1 to Just focus on Metro Bus Operations which is a net positive for those members.

The new VP can now focus on Rail Operations and our four other properties that ATU 587 represents. This VP will be voted on and come from these groups. For those who are concerned about a VP needing to have knowledge of Rail, the Peninsula properties and Solid Ground my counter is that is exactly what VP 1 has had to do all of these years, along with handling the thousands of members in King County Metro operations. Should the membership approve this bylaw proposal All non Vehicle Maintenance members of this Union will be represented by a VP with a much lower workload that can devote more timely attention to each members issues.

Farewell and good luck to Ken

I wanted to take this last opportunity to again thank Brother Ken Price for his decades of service to the public, the union, and our members. I always knew that Ken was passionate about defending our membership, but watching it firsthand for the last year and a half showed me how deeply personally he took each heavy-handed discipline or termination that our members faced. Congratulations, and enjoy your well-earned and deserved retirement, brother Price!

item.title: The Maintenance Vice President’s Report: Discipline, Outsourcing, and Grievance Update
item.content:encoded:
Discipline

This month we continued to be busy with more final determination letters with attached discipline, we have now moved into the grievance process for several of the members who were issued discipline.

Outsourcing

It seems The Union might need to put on a class to all of Bus and Rail Maintenance what outsourcing means and when to call The Union. As of this writing I have several more reports of Bus Facilities management taking it upon themselves to call vendors to do Local 587 Union work even after several previous griev-

By Jeff Stambaugh ances were filed and resolved in the Unions favor, yet somehow it continues to be a thing. Rail Maintenance management has apparently decided they want to test the limits of outsourcing without Union involvement by outsourcing seat replacement that has previously been done by our 587 members and not to be left out, Bus Maintenance decided to call a vendor to “recover” a coach in a ditch after our members had safety concerns over the recovery, don’t get me wrong I’m all in for doing things safely and correctly, I’m not about sending 587 Union work out the door without an understanding from The Union! In all of these situations Metro Failed to notify or inform The Union until after the fact, if at all.

Grievance Update

Currently there are 58 open grievances in all of Maintenance, these generally fall under one of two main categories, discipline or contract violations. Discipline is usually pretty easy to define, it includes things like, written reminders, suspensions, and terminations. While contract violations are an element in discipline, contract violations are generally defined around issues such as, OT was not assigned per the CBA, pick wasn’t posted properly, promotions didn’t follow the CBA, or ATU work was outsourced. There has been some positive movement from management to resolve some issues in a timely manner that is in the best interest for all involved, there is lots of room for more improvement and better ways to find resolution that works for everyone.

As your elected VP I would rather spend my time finding better ways to improve your working conditions (think contract negotiations), than spending enormous amounts of time and resources fighting over things like outsourcing and heavy-handed discipline. I promised to fight for you and I will, however, Management, You can do better!

By Paul Neil

item.title: The Recording Secretary’s Report: Spring/Summer Pick
item.dc:creator: Latrelle Gibson
item.content:encoded:
By Latrelle Gibson

Thank goodness the time too pick has arrived! I know most are not loving these long shake-ups. Please know that we are trying to bargain for the 3rd pick to return. Below, I have provided some information to try and make pick fast and easy as pick can be stressful for a lot of folks.

Shop Steward Nominations

The Fall/Winter Shop Steward List is out, and you will be able to find the list in the January edition of the News Review. The list is also available on the Union Bulletin boards at the bases, and on the Union Website. If you missed the deadline to put in for Shop Steward, no worries, you will get a chance to nominate for Shop Steward in February. Please remember, every member will have to submit a nomination every shakeup, so for the Spring/Summer 2026 Nomination, all will need to nominate themselves during the open nomination period that will start during the February pick preview. The reason for this is due to the shakeup being where some will change bases, decide they want a break from being a Shop Steward, want to nominate for Chief Shop Steward, or nominate for Shop Steward for the first time. This is not a live list, so please be sure to read the bulletins and or the News Review for the Nomination dates. Once the Nomination closes, and the list comes out, please let me know

ASAP if you don’t see your name on the first SS Nomination list that is posted so I can get you added. Once the second revised SS nomination list comes out, there will be no revisions to this list and you will have to remember to nominate yourself when nominations open again. And with that, thank you to all who are willing to step up and sever the membership, you’re all very much appreciated by this local and those who you represent.

Not going to be at Pick?

Please fill out an absentee form. You can locate these forms in the following places: The Union Website, the Window, and in the pick room during pick preview. You can return your completed absentee pick form to; The window at your base, emailed to me @ recsec@atu587. org, and during pick preview, to the pick room. When pick starts, please turn in absentees to your base window or email them to me, please don’t enter the live pick room to turn in your absentee. Please remember to leave a good contact number where you can be reached, and if you’re going to be out of the country we can contact you via WhatsApp, just be sure to indicate on the absentee pick form that you will need a call via WhatsApp. If you choose to have a friend pick for you, please make sure they pick no more than 2hrs before or after you pick. For those volunteering to help your classmate, family, or friend pick, please remember that if they pick right ahead or right after you that you will not have your 20min to preview the work, so again, to ensure that you or the person you’re picking for will have the 20min pick preview, don’t agree to pick for someone that picks within a hour or less of your pick. If I see that you don’t have enough time after knowing you’re picking for someone else, I will tell you to go preview the work and I can look up the work they want and remind you of this article. Remember, this is why the Union is in the pick room, to ensure everyone who is supposed to be picking, can and will pick. Lastly, please remember, Union picks are not subject to the grievance process, so please be sure if you submit an absentee and are not available by phone that you clearly indicate your work choices.

Vacation Pick

If you’re not going to be at pick, please indicate your preferred vacation periods on the absentee form. Please note that the Union does not pick vacations, this is done via the vacation pick room. At the conclusion of picking your work, the vacation pick room will call you to pick your vacation. Please be sure to be available when the vacation room calls.

Not Listed on the Pick List?

If you’re not on the pick list, this is likely due to being out on medical or other continuous leaves during the shake up(s) and you have not returned to work prior to January 2026. You will want to contact Transit Disability Services and/or your Chief to let them know you’re cleared to return to work. For medical, you will want to send your updated medical that clears you to return to work, full duty, no restrictions, to Transit Disability Services prior to your pick date.

Pick Room Phone # (206) 477-0208 FOR EMERGENCIES ONLY

Once pick has started, please note that we’re in a live pick on the pick room floor and will not always be able to answer the phone, therefore, please only call the pick room for emergencies only, e.g., running late for your pick, not going to make it to pick in time. All other calls will be returned after pick.

Thank you all for taking the time to read all of this information. I’m here to help and make your pick easier, so please feel to reach out to me if you need any assistance. Happy pick and see you all at pick!

item.title: Alternate Rail Schedules and Their Impact on Frontline Staff
item.dc:creator: Barbara Pastores and Muhammad Ehsan (ATU 587 Schedulers)
item.content:encoded:
By Barbara Pastores and Muhammad Ehsan (ATU 587 Schedulers)

For Operators, a schedule is not an abstract idea. It is the foundation of the workday. It determines when they work, when they rest, how they are paid, and how they plan life beyond the cab. To understand why recent disruptions have been so difficult, it is important to understand how Link Light Rail schedules are created, changed, and put into practice; and what can be done to improve the process with fairness, clarity, and compassion.

At its core, train run times are developed through engineering standards, field testing, safety requirements, and historical performance data. Run times define how long it should take a train to travel from one point to another under normal conditions. Sound Transit develops running times and shares them with King County Metro Scheduling staff as part of each service change package.

Using the service change package as a guide, Schedulers build vehicle schedules taking into consideration headways, terminal recovery time, and systemwide operating limits. Together, these elements form the underlying schedule, which becomes the backbone for Operator duties. Duties are then created to align with the current Collective Bargaining Agreement (CBA), which sets rules for maximum spread, break frequences and durations, and pay protections. For planned service changes (Shakeups), this system provides predictability and fairness. However, things become far more com-

plicated when the system is constantly changing during a service change.

Planned maintenance, infrastructure upgrades, and system expansion are necessary investments in a reliable future. However, each of these projects can require changes to service patterns. When any segment of rail network is affected, the underlying schedule shifts, and Operator duties shift with it.

These changes can escalate quickly. Single track operations extend run times. Track closures introduce bus bridges. A station closure may force a new fallback location with limited facilities. What may appear on paper as a two-hour closure late in the day can completely reshape an Operator’s entire shift.

For Operators, these disruptions are not just operational. They are personal. Sudden duty changes can interfere with childcare plans, second jobs, and rest cycles. Repeated, short-notice adjustments create uncertainty and fatigue, especially when they occur back-to-back. Operators are not resisting change. They are absorbing it, often quietly and often at personal cost.

The real question is not whether disruptions will happen. They will. The question is how they are managed. There are clear steps that can lead to a better path forward.

First, project planning timelines that require schedule changes need clearer structure and expectations. The current Intergovernmental Agreement (IGA) and CBA do not include sufficient language addressing schedule changes during a service change. If scheduling receives change requests well in advance, modifications can be completed earlier, and impacts can be communicated sooner. Clear and timely communication allows Operators to plan, adjust, and make informed decisions.

Clear and timely communication also helps First Line staff prepare for the day of disruption. This can create opportunities for voluntary sign-ups, swaps, or other flexible solutions that reduce stress and confusion.

Second, there must be clearer definitions of what truly qualifies as an emergency. Not every disruption qualifies as an emergency. Clearly defining emergency work builds transparency and trust.

Third, emergency work must be fairly compensated. When genuine emergencies require short notice changes, Operators should be paid accordingly. Recognition in pay matters just as much as recognition in words.

Finally, the strength of the workforce lies in its union. When expectations, protections, and processes are clearly written into agreements, they are implemented. When they are not, work still gets done, often at the expense of frontline Operators and First-Line Supervisors. Putting solutions in writing is not about rigidity. It is about respect. It ensures consistency, accountability, and fairness, even during disruptions.

None of this should overshadow one essential truth. Operators and First Line Supervisors have performed extraordinarily well under extraordinarily difficult conditions. They have adapted to constant change, navigated unfamiliar service patterns, and delivered reliable service despite ongoing disruptions. Their professionalism has kept the system moving. They deserve not only gratitude, but systems and agreements that truly honor their effort.

item.title: A Man Named Ken
item.content:encoded:
Like fire, this guy with slicked back hair walked into my life. Now he is gone like wind over the sheets. Love you Ken Price, keep living till the air leaves your lungs.

I first met Ken over a decade ago. He presented as a cleaned up, blue collar heavy hitting union steward. Quick with the lip, and sly enough to get you to agree with him. At that time, Ken had a reputation for being likable, hardworking, emotionally charged and popular. Destiny collapsed our circles, where I learned the strategic and manic side of Ken, which of course is nature’s building blocks for genius.

Ken possesses several priorities that I value, family, love, fighting and money. He also displays a few behaviors that masquerade as unpredictable, erratic or surprise. That is the beauty of Ken Price, loyal as hell, but don’t know what he’s going to do.

Ken ran his political campaigns the same way I did, by reputation. He would later tell me that he ran for president be-

item.title: Letter to the Editor:
item.content:encoded:
Dear Editor,

On December 3rd, 2025, our nation’s president referred to Somalians as “garbage.”

I understand that our Union tries to stay politically neutral, but I believe we have the obligation to protect our members in every unjust situation. As a country, as a Union, as citizens, as metro employees, we cannot accept disrespect, discrimination, anti-ethical statements from anyone, and

Submitted by Cory Rigtrup VM Board Rep cause he wanted to help people, and why not he had the hair. In 2018 when we started sharing ridiculous hours, I would grow to learn he still supported people who disagree with him and refused to talk bad about them, even in private.

I remember the summer of 2019, killing time with him in Port Townsend. Discussing lessons learned from childhood and how “mom’s” teachings should filter into a contract. Acceptance, repentance and redemption. Then strategize about the next few plays on how to make it happen. Years later, those childhood lessons of how people should be treated when mistakes are made, have filtered into many contacts and many jobs have been saved.

I also remember a time when our Local built coffins and marched in Seattle, only to be marched by a Me-2-protest. It was cool, we had a marching band, Ken spoke like a bad-ass, it was so much fun!

Shortly after came a couple hundred layoff, followed by a couple hundred vaccination this president, or any other, must understand that such statements are not acceptable.

I’ve met and worked with two metro drivers from Somalia, and both are hardworking colleagues, and as important metro employees as anyone else. Furthermore, at this moment in our nation, any other immigrant might be mistreated by authorities that should be an example instead of bullying honest people.

termination. Ken stated this Local is going to fight, every member gets representation. He knew the vaccinations would bear a heavy polarizing cost, Ken kept silent on his personal views and fought through the ugliness as a president should. That part of Ken I truly admired, when the chips are down, just keep swinging.

I sat in countless meetings with Ken, in every property. He would often reserve speaking and let others pound the position. His method of operation was to listen, reserve judgment, and make decisions later, often after his walks. However, in those meetings, when things got tough, he would revert back to how this affects the operator in the seat. Ken would become emotional, language aggressive, voice sharpen, and he would start overtalking everyone until he had enough, then blast out of there like a dynamo. This mania was Ken’s true power, it was awesome! Because inevitably the phone would ring, the answer was always the same, “I don’t know

I’d love to see our Union stand up and condemn this type of behavior. I’d also think we should stand up for the way ICE enforcement’s is behaving since the Supreme Court authorized them to ‘racially profile’ people everywhere, all immigrants who currently work for Metro are now at risk of being stopped and humiliated in the middle of the streets. At least a word of support is necessary and important.

where Ken is at, but he’s pissed, so you better change your position.”

What I will miss most about Ken is our early morning talks. Both of us would come in before the office opened to focus on certain things before the drudgery of work pulled us away. Always positive, we would talk about our families and run through life goals. When the conversations switched to work, we would talk strategy. He would float ideas of what he wanted to do, and I would layout out the pieces that needed to be on the table. It was jovial, like two kids planning to rob a candy store. These scheming conversations went on for years, and when it switched to money or benefits, the electricity was incredible. Ken wanted our Local to be number one, both in wages and benefits. Ken fought above our Local’s weight and delivered!

Ken’s exit strategy is true to his nature, unpredictable. But then again, is it? 65 years old, house in Neveda, hide your cards and play your game. Love you Ken Price, thank you for all the memories!

I hope you understand what I’m trying to say.

Thanks, Marcelo Albernaz.

item.title: Safety Reporting Is a Right — Not “Unauthorized Overtime”
item.content:encoded:
Safety in our workplace does not happen by accident. It happens because workers speak up, document hazards, and take the time to report conditions that could injure someone or worse. That process is not only encouraged — it is protected.

Under Washington State workplace safety law and our collective bargaining agreements, employees have the right to identify and report unsafe conditions without fear of retaliation. Joint health and safety committees exist for this very reason: to ensure hazards are found, documented, and corrected before they result in injuries. That protection matters, because safety reporting is real work.

Safety reports take time — and that matters

Anyone who has completed a safety report knows it is not a casual exercise. It requires logging into a system, documenting conditions accurately, explaining why an issue matters, and sometimes identifying patterns across equipment or vehicles. This takes focus and time, and policy recognizes that reality.

For that reason, members are permitted to be compensated for the time it takes to complete legitimate safety documentation. This is not an abuse of the system — it is the system. A reporting structure that demands accuracy but refuses to acknowledge the time required to achieve it is fun-

By Andy Price, Shop Steward, Local 587

damentally broken. Reframing good-faith safety reporting as “unauthorized overtime” is not only incorrect — it is counterproductive.

Why labels don’t change the facts

Calling safety-reporting time “unauthorized overtime” does not change what actually occurred: a worker identified safety deficiencies and documented them through an approved process. The law does not look favorably on attempts to discourage safety reporting through wordplay or after-thefact recharacterizations.

The real question is not how the time is labeled, but what the effect is.

If workers begin to believe that taking safety reporting seriously might expose them to discipline, fewer reports will be written. Hazards will go undocumented. Problems will spread quietly instead of being fixed early. That is not speculation — it is exactly why safety laws exist.

The chilling effect is real

A workplace where people hesitate before reporting safety issues is a workplace heading in the wrong direction. Fear is the enemy of safety.

When even one worker is challenged, scrutinized, or disciplined for submitting a safety report in good faith, the message travels quickly. Others notice. Conversations happen. People begin to ask themselves whether it’s “worth it” to speak up.

That chilling effect doesn’t just harm individual workers — it undermines the entire safety culture.

Your rights extend beyond the report

Members should know that their rights do not end once a report is submitted.

You have the right to: • Report unsafe conditions without retaliation

• Be compensated for authorized safety-reporting time

• Ask questions about safety policies

• Seek union representation if management challenges your actions

• File a grievance if safetyrelated rights are violated

Shop stewards play a critical role in this process. If management raises concerns about a safety report, that is precisely when members should involve their steward — not after the fact, and not alone.

Safety reporting benefits everyone

Safety reporting is not about pointing fingers. It is about prevention. Every documented hazard is an opportunity to correct a problem before it causes harm. Every report strengthens the record and improves accountability.

Management often emphasizes the importance of collecting safety data. That data does not appear magically. It comes from workers who take the time to document what they see. Undermining those efforts — intentionally or not — defeats the very purpose of the system.

Getting safety culture right

A healthy safety culture requires consistency. Workers must be confident that reporting hazards will be met with corrective action, not suspicion. Management must recognize that encouraging safety reporting means accepting the time and effort it requires.

Safety reporting is not insubordination.

It is not misconduct. And it is not “unauthorized overtime.”

It is a protected activity — and a responsibility we all share.

item.title: Black History Month, the Ongoing Struggle, and the Moment We Are Living In
item.dc:creator: Hassannoor Aden, Minority Affairs Officer, ATU 587/King County Labor Delegate
item.content:encoded:
By Hassannoor Aden, Minority Affairs Officer, ATU 587/King County Labor Delegate

February is Black History Month, a time set aside to reflect on the history, struggles, and contributions of Black Americans. Each year, communities prepare events to honor this history, but Black History Month is not meant to be symbolic or ceremonial. It exists because the full story of this country has too often been ignored, distorted, or minimized. This month is a reminder that Black history is not a side chapter. It is foundational to the United States.

From slavery to segregation, from civil rights to labor movements, Black Americans have consistently pushed this nation toward its stated ideals, often at great personal cost. Progress has never come easily, and it has never come without resistance. Understanding this truth is essential, especially at a time when division, fear, and xenophobia are again shaping public discourse.

Dr. Martin Luther King Jr.: Justice Beyond Words

Dr. Martin Luther King Jr. is often remembered through selective quotes, but his work was far more challenging than many are comfortable acknowledging. Dr. King believed that justice required structural change, not just goodwill. He understood that racism, poverty, and exploitation were connected, and that civil rights without economic justice would always be incomplete.

Dr. King stood with workers because he knew dignity at work was central to dignity in life. His support of the Memphis sanitation workers was not accidental. Those workers were demanding basic respect, safety, and fair pay. Dr. King saw their struggle as a continuation of the civil rights movement. He believed organized labor had a moral responsibility to fight injustice and that unity among working people was a powerful force for change.

Nonviolence, for Dr. King, was not weakness. It was discipline. It required courage to stand unarmed in the face of violence and to remain focused on justice rather than revenge. His message challenged systems, not just attitudes. That message remains relevant today.

Malcolm X: Naming Reality and Reclaiming Dignity

Malcolm X spoke from lived experience shaped by poverty, incarceration, and constant exposure to racism. He rejected the idea that Black Americans should wait patiently while being denied basic rights. Malcolm X emphasized selfrespect, political awareness, and accountability. He insisted that people had the right to defend their humanity and reject narratives that portrayed them as inferior.

His speeches resonated because they named realities that were often dismissed or denied. Malcolm X challenged both white power structures and Black leaders who avoided hard truths. Over time, his worldview expanded through travel and reflection. He came to see racial oppression as part of a global system and emphasized solidarity among oppressed people worldwide.

Malcolm X’s evolution reminds us that growth matters. Learning does not weaken a movement. It strengthens it. His legacy teaches that justice begins with honesty, even when that honesty makes people uncomfortable.

Abraham Lincoln, Emancipation, and the Limits of Law

Black History Month also requires honest reflection on America’s legal and political history. President Abraham Lincoln’s Emancipation Proclamation was a turning point in the Civil War. It declared freedom for enslaved people in Confederate states and redefined the moral purpose of the war. It also encouraged enslaved people to escape bondage and join the fight for their own liberation.

However, emancipation was not a single act of generosity. It was the result of pressure from abolitionists, resistance by enslaved people themselves, and the realities of war. The Thirteenth Amendment formally abolished slavery, but freedom did not translate into equality. Reconstruction was followed by segregation, racial terror, voter suppression, and economic exclusion that lasted for generations.

This history matters because it shows us that laws can open doors, but they do not automatically dismantle injustice. That work requires vigilance and continued struggle.

Black History Month in the Face of Modern Xenophobia

Today, we are witnessing a rise in xenophobic attacks against immigrant communities. Immigrants are being blamed for economic instability, crime, and social change. This rhetoric is familiar. It mirrors the same language once used against Black Americans, Irish immigrants, Chinese laborers, and others deemed “undesirable.”

Xenophobia thrives when fear replaces facts. It turns neighbors into targets and workers into scapegoats. Immigrant families face harassment, profiling, and threats of deportation. Many live with constant anxiety, even when they are lawfully present or long-settled in this country.

These attacks often overlap with anti-Black racism and Islamophobia. People are targeted not just for where they come from, but for how they look, speak, or worship. This climate creates division among working people while shielding those truly responsible for inequality and exploitation.

History teaches us that fear is a political tool. When leaders

Afail to offer solutions, they offer enemies instead.

Why This Moment Demands Solidarity

For working people and unions, Black History Month carries urgent relevance. Black workers and immigrant workers have always been essential to this country’s economy. They built infrastructure, staffed public services, and carried industries forward while often being denied fair wages, protections, and respect.

Division weakens collective power. Solidarity strengthens it. Dr. King warned that injustice anywhere threatens justice everywhere. Malcolm X demanded that people stop accepting mistreatment as normal. Their words speak directly to this moment.

Standing against xenophobia is not separate from honoring Black history. It is part of it. Both require rejecting narratives that dehumanize people and confronting systems that benefit from division.

Carrying the History Forward

Black History Month is not about nostalgia. It is about responsibility. Remembering history means recognizing patterns and refusing to repeat them. It means speaking out when communities are targeted and standing with those facing fear and exclusion.

As we prepare Black History Month events, we should approach them with honesty and purpose. The goal is not comfort. It is clarity. The history we honor demands action, unity, and accountability.

Black history teaches us that progress is possible, but never guaranteed. It must be defended, renewed, and passed forward. February reminds us that the struggle for justice did not end in the past. It is happening now, and each of us has a role to play.

item.title: Metro Operators Unite on Safety Concerns at Seven-Base Caucus
item.dc:creator: Chuck Lare, Shop Steward, and Atlantic Base Safety Committee Chair, #12497
item.content:encoded:
By Chuck Lare, Shop Steward, and Atlantic Base Safety Committee Chair, #12497

Twe nt y- e i g ht K i ng County Metro operators representing all seven operator base safety committees gathered January 5th for another "Safety Bootson-the-Ground" safety caucus, addressing critical workplace concerns ranging from protective shields to inadequate break schedules.

Operator Protective Shields Under Scrutiny

Metro Fleet Engineering's Fariba Fuller and Josh Arreola presented the current Operator Protective Shield (OPS) design, but operators raised significant concerns. The most pressing issue: the shield automatically locks each time operators leave their seats, requiring a cumbersome T-Key to unlock and restricting quick access to the emergency assistance button. Not all operators consistently have their T-Key accessible.

Additional OPS concerns include ensuring adequate space for large wheelchairs per ADA requirements, addressing the open space left when fare boxes are removed, and the inability to comply with policies requiring the shield to block the aisle during ramp deployment. Metro may consider a fully enclosed operator barrier with operator’s exclusive front door use and rear wheelchair lift access for future bus purchases. Operators await responses on how these concerns will be addressed.

Communication System Improvements Needed

Operators reached consensus on requested changes to the DDU's public service announcements and messages. Key concerns include TCC frequently overlooking operators’ DDU Send Messages, negating their purpose. Operators requested that pressing the emergency assistance button display "Call 911" on outside signs, and that they receive notification whenever live camera monitoring is activated.

Base Safety Committee Operations Vary Widely

A survey revealed substantial differences in how base safety committees operate. Monthly hours detailed for committee work range dramatically from just one hour at East Base to 16-18 hours at Atlantic, Central, and South bases. Guest attendees at meetings typically include representatives from SSQA, Speed and Reliability, Vehicle Maintenance, Comfort Stations, Service Quality, Scheduling, and TCC.

Committees identify unsafe locations through word of mouth, tabling, official forms, Transit Safety Advisors, and management reports. However, shared challenges include difficulty tracking issues to resolution, lack of computer access between meetings, miscommunications, delayed responses, and insufficient follow-through.

Break Time Crisis

Operators identified a critical safety issue: inadequate break time between trips prevents proper mental and physical recovery, creating unsafe conditions for both operators and the public. Current schedules combine break time with bathroom access time, forcing operators to choose between necessary breaks and basic biological needs.

Affected operators my want to collectively file workplace rights complaints with Washington State L&I's Employee Standards Program and, for Seattle routes, with the City of Seattle. These collective filings could provide relief for operators facing these untenable scheduling conditions.

Additional Safety Priorities

Operators called for enhanced safety training, particularly programs like the Red Kite Project that build resilience for handling difficult on-the-job situations. The caucus emphasized that documenting and publishing safety issues creates accountability and establishes public evidence of known hazards.

Other concerns raised include clarifying Metro's policy on auditing live camera monitoring usage, improving communication methods for unsanitary passenger situations, displaying rolling messages on interior overhead signs, connecting ramp deployment with automated announcements, and automating “last stop all passengers must exit” announcements.

Moving Forward Together

The caucus concluded with action items including planning the March quarterly "Safety Boots-on-the-Ground" meeting and encouraging collective workplace rights complaints regarding break time issues.

Operators’ consensus emphasized the importance of operator engagement: follow up with your base's safety committee members elected to represent your interest in safety, and your elected union representative to the Joint Union and Management Safety Committee. We are better together and when we demand nothing about us without us; whereas we cannot necessarily fix all we face, we certainly cannot fix what we do not face.

The caucus demonstrated that when operators from all seven bases unite on safety concerns, they create a powerful voice for workplace improvements that protect both transit workers and the riding public.

The uniform committee facilitator is present and is in the process of working with Don’s to procure a proper winter coat with a safety vest implemented. The coat they are looking at is red and orange. They are working on that process. Is the jacket Union

By Lisa Nault #3647 and Rachael Buchanan #21341; ATU 587 Bus Reps made? The jacket comes from the same place as all the other uniform items. Trying to work out price and just replace the blue raincoat. The Union noted that the contract with Don’s Uniform Apparel was extended another 18 months. The Union brought this up a few months back that the term was coming to an end. Metro stated that the Uniform Committee can’t control what procurement does, and it’s a staffing issue up there. They are currently short-staffed and haven’t been able to work on it. We have to comply with their processes. Our last meeting was agenda-less and needs to be put in place to avoid those issues in the future. The Uniform Committee should share updates with their bases. What can we do about being proactive about getting the bid process going? Nothing. We don’t have that influence over another division and tell them how to prioritize their work. Every department has to work through their own procurement team and Operations doesn’t have authority over that process.

Tukwila Base:

The Union noticed the front chargers installed on the front gantry had been removed and asked about this. The front chargers needed a new switch, and they were taken down to replace that, but everything should be complete and turned over to

JANUARY 8, 2026

Metro in early February. Once enough operators are trained, they will start putting Gillig BEB’s in service at South Base. Need enough operators qualified to do that, but qualification is ongoing. Metro doesn’t know how many operators need to be qualified before that happens but are trying to qualify the board first.

School Zones:

Spoke to training whether to deviate would be a change. 20mph is something they’ve always taught but, the 24/7 is new verbiage that seems new to the Union. The language is so generic that it can be enforced. The Union asked whether it is reasonable to expect Operator’s to follow that rule at 2:00am and the response was, “They might be in night school.” Violations will be given out on a case-bycase basis and if you want to fight it, then go for it.

Encampments:

SIR’s are reviewed by the Base Security Committees and if it’s not being solved, then let’s continue to let the Union President work on these issues. And encampment is an immediate danger that should be a call to the Coordinator and they will send Supervisor right away. Still needs to be documented when getting back to the base so it can be addressed long term. Information is also being displayed on monitors at the bases. If a member deems a zone is unsafe, what is the protocol in the meantime for operators. Fill out an SIR, and for observed near misses, but noting it matters, and security is in tune with that and knows to look for those as well.

Building a Successful Probationary Program for FTO:

Article 3 in regard to probation extension and trying to utilize that in regard to probationary employees and that’s not being done. Counseling is being done and is not considered discipline, but they are used as probationary points. We’re missing out on some really great employees because we aren’t giving them opportunities. Probation Extension, and non-point counseling. Metro thinks there’s always an opportunity to extend probation. There are times when an extension is appropriate and it has recently happened. As for counseling letters, Metro doesn’t separate based on points, but whether or not the operator is a good fit, but if you have to do that over and over again with the same operator, that’s a problem and you’re supposed to be on your best as a new hire. When it’s not appropriate, Metro says they should not. Would a valid complaint be counted as points? That’s not points, but if things aren’t changing and there are a lot of complaints on one opera-

tor, that’s not a good sign for that operator. The Union thought the probationary policy was points, it’s always been a guideline. You can fail probation with less or more. Metro insists probationary employees are “At Will” employees and at any time in the first 6 months can be let go without cause. Section 4.9

New Business:

Preventability Process Before Imposing Discipline:

Why are we imposing discipline before the reread process is complete? Metro states there is more than just the reread and it would be unreasonable to keep someone on PAL for such a long period. Is there a mechanism to have an unpaid leave status versus firing? Doesn’t know what the payroll implications are and could be a legal issue that Metro needs to find out about. Accident Review Committee doesn’t happen very often. The Union has seen members put on PAL for a very long time or forgotten about, and the union wonders why Metro doesn’t finish the investigation, but for this, where you’re going to separate and the last points are accident and that puts you over, Metro doesn’t want to wait for that reread process to be completed. From the Union standpoint, we know we’ve had some problems with rereads, but we’d like to solve those and speed up the process. Metro will look into it. And 4.5 can apply

Back Door Entry outside of CBD:

There was counseling happening in regard to outside the CBD because of complaints received of the back door not being opened for entry. There are specific locations and times for all door boarding. Then in

March, there was a policy put out and there is confusion and operators are receiving valid complaints for not opening the doors when it’s a security issue.11.06. This is a tool operators have used for years to avoid safety issues and if the bulletin put out was if the operator feels safe. When people board through the back door, operators don’t have the feedback and the information needed to understand who is on their coach. The bulletin stated while orca card readers are installed, but there was no policy that was put out to say all door boarding on all coaches. Metro has been a pay on entry system for a long time, but there was confusing language, and the bulletin was put out in March 2025, so it’s saying that it’s not required to open all doors for boarding? Correct. So, if there is counseling happening, we’d like everyone to be on the same page and that our members won’t be disciplined. Several situations have occurred at Ryerson operations and maybe Central. The public is also confused by the whole policy. Metro might miss out on a lot of revenue with FIFA coming up. A lot of this came from operators not opening the front doors coming out of COVID. This was a reminder that Metro has a front door boarding policy. Follow up next month.

Vacation Verification:

Vacation list, you verify you have vacation, South base still does it, but it slipped away during COVID, and we would like consistency. Metro will bring it up in their next meeting and we’ll follow up.

Meeting adjourned at 9:57.

Have a topic you want brought up in the LMRC Meetings? Contact Lisa or Rachael to submit your topics.

In Loving Memory...

You will be missed...Rest Easy

We are saddened to announce the passing of retired transit operator Vicente “Vince” Caceres #544, on Monday January 5, 2026. Vince was born in 1941 in the Philippine Islands and immigrated with his family to Seattle in 1953 at the age of 12. He graduated from Ballard High School in 1959, served for 6 years in the National Guard, and worked at Boeing for 5 years before starting his transit career with Seattle Transit in 1971. He operated the monorail and drove bus routes out of Mercer Base, Jefferson Base, Ryerson Base, and then finished his career working out of North Base until his retirement in 2003. Vince is survived by his wife of almost 59 years, Leslie. His two children, daughter and North Base operator Kim Stark, son Mike Caceres, Operator/First Line Supervisor/Senior Scheduler. He enjoyed 22 years of retirement, spending his time gardening, golfing, long walks, trips to the casino as well as Disney trips with his family. Vince will be greatly missed by his Family and friends. A Memorial service will be held on February 4th, at 1:00 pm at Floral Hills Funeral home.

It is with great sadness that we announce the passing of transit operator Larry McGhee. Larry started his transit career in July 2001 and spent most of his time working part time out of South base. He will be greatly missed by his loving family, coworkers, and the passengers on his regular work who were happy to have him as their driver. There are no services planned at this time.

We are deeply saddened to announce the sudden passing of transit operator Abdullahi Mohamoud. Abdullahi started his transit career as a part-time operator in November 2022, then promoted to full-time in August 2023. He enjoyed working out of the downtown bases and serving his community. Abdullahi will be greatly missed by his loving father, First Line Supervisor, Osman Said, his loving family and supportive community, and all who had the pleasure of interacting with him. Services for Abdullahi have taken place at the All-Muslim Cemetery on Friday, January 9.

Please place these members and their families in your thoughts and hearts

Please notify the union office of any member’s passing so that this information may be shared with the rest of our union family.

ATU 587 Oath of Obligation

I,.................................., in the presence of God and the members of this Union, do solemnly promise and pledge (without any reservation or evasion) to support the Constitution and General Laws of this Amalgamated Transit Union. I will keep myself in good standing by paying all dues, fines and assessments required. I will work to promote the best interests of this Union and encourage my fellow workers to become members of the same. I will not take the place of any member of this organization, or any other union worker who may be on strike or locked out. I will not reveal any of the private business to anyone not entitled to know the same.

I will not engage in activity evidencing gross disloyalty nor in conduct otherwise unbecoming a member, and will not knowingly wrong a member or see one wronged if in my power to prevent it. I will not appeal to any legal authority in matters pertaining to this Union until I have exhausted all means of redress provided by its laws. I will be considerate of others in word and action and will never discriminate against a fellow worker on account of race, religion, color, creed, sex, sexual orientation, gender identity or expression, age, disability, citizenship, or national origin. I also promise to promote the cause of trade union principles and defend freedom of thought, whether expressed by tongue or pen, with all the power at my command.

I understand there is nothing in this obligation that will in any way interfere with my political and religious rights or that will be in any way inconsistent with my duties arising from any of the relations of life.

This obligation I take upon my honor, and solemnly promise to keep the same, as long as I remain a member of this Union.

item.title: The President’s Report: A Year of Reflection and Determination
item.content:encoded:
This year started with us gathering at the Lumen Field Event Center to honor and mourn the painful loss of our Union Brother Shawn Yim. It ended at AB/CB, with the unveiling of a remembrance bench built by our members to forever remind us of Shawn and the dangers front-line transit workers face daily.

Much of the year in between revolved around our desire and determination not to let Shawn's loss of life by the hands of brutal murderer go in vain. We hastily called a press conference at our Union Hall on the day of Shawn's murder to deliver a list of demands, which included our call for the establishment of a regional task force on Transit Safety. Metro Management met with us at our Union Hall the next day to fill us in on how they would meet all of our demands.

We gathered where Shawn was murdered for an emotional and powerful candlelight vigil.

Our members were at Shawn's murderer's arraignment, where we publicly vowed to attend every one of his trial hearings, and met with the King County Prosecutor, who promised to keep our Union updated on every aspect of the upcoming trial. We met with the outgoing King County Executive,

By Greg Woodfill the King County Sheriff, and her staff to receive an update on the County’s plans, efforts, and commitment to establish a much larger Metro Transit Police force.

We testified at City and County Council meetings until legislation was put forward by the County Council establishing the regional task force that we had been calling for, starting 6 months before Shawn's murder. We held two regional task force meetings at the Seattle IAM Union Hall, where 130 regional leaders and police forces met to help workshop and commit to the task force.

We had 587 members at every task force subcommittee meeting, and they contributed most of the 130 recommendations that emerged.

We rushed Union officers to every major transit safety incident in the last year to give interviews demanding faster action and calling for the public to pressure their political representatives to take their share of responsibility for their citizens' safe access to public transportation.

We’ve participated in and signed off on every step of procuring the new safety barriers to retrofit the entire fleet. We are all frustrated at the time it’s taken for this procurement, but unfortunately, it’s just the reality of how long public agency procurements take. Prototypes of the winning bid will be installed any day now for operators to test and the Union to sign off on. Then around 12

weeks later, the barriers will arrive and be installed by our members at a rate of 120. The timeline that was initially envisioned for barrier installation to start before the end of 2025 has been moved up to March 2026.

Our Union demanded the closure of 12th and Jackson, and we are awaiting King County's promised action to quickly restore safety at those zones before we are forced to publicly demand their closure again.

We are transit workers, not politicians, police, or transit agency managers. It’s not our job or responsibility to restore safety, order, and accountability for one's actions on and around public transit. Our job is to push and hold accountable all those whose responsibility it is. Promises of future action are just words. Our membership will not be satisfied until they see and feel meaningful and measurable change. We will not rest until we get there. Our members' and passengers' lives literally depend on it.

A harm against one is harm against all!

Our Union's power lies in its diversity and collective will to fight together and fight for ALL. We stand firmly in support of any and all segments of our membership under attack by anyone's agendas of division or hate. And are prepared to stand with and fight for them.

This philosophy extends to our fight against a growing number of managers at several properties we represent who lean toward punitive vs corrective discipline, with ever-increasing levels of discipline and or terminations that violate our contractual protections of progressive discipline, due process, and just cause. This Union will devote whatever resources or time necessary to fight back against these malicious misguided or incompetent managers who come after our members.

I hope you all enjoyed the holidays. ATU 587 – We Are One!

item.title: The Maintenance Vice President’s Report: Negotiations, Toys for Tots, Discipline, Bus Facilities, Rail, Bus VM
item.content:encoded:
Negotiations

We have finally passed our protected positions across the table and will get into the true heart of negotiations starting early January, see the scheduled dates elsewhere in the news review

Toys for Tots

This year was another great success with nearly 2000 toys collected, with North Base Vehicle Maintenance having another amazing year collecting nearly 750 toys.

Discipline

This month was another busy month, I attended several Loudermill hearings as well as several final determination

By Jeff Stambaugh meetings. Fortunately, this month’s discipline was not as heavy handed as it was the last few months. Hopefully we continue to move forward in a positive corrective manner with discipline as opposed to punitive.

Bus Facilities

More on the outsourcing that reported on last month. Come to find out, not only did management decide to do what they wanted rather than follow the CBA, TFD decided to call a vendor and outsource both Local 587 work as well as IBEW 77 work. When one of our members attempted to file a grievance, the chief refused to accept the grievance instead wanted to work out the issue without a grievance. When I intervened and attempted to turn in several grievances the chief still did not want to accept them and instead wanted to discuss the timelines, after I explained that he was committing an unfair labor practice by refusing to sign and accept the grievances he changed his mind. I am happy to report that Labor Relations has reached out and as of this writing we have tentative settlement agreement. Hopefully this starts a more positive approach to the way TFD management does business.

Rail

Last month I reported on the ongoing expansion of rail, and due to this movement and the addition of new employees and new positions, we have had move-ups and will continue to have more as we work through expansion.

I have heard reports that a few select employees have been directed by a chief to check in with their chief or lead before they leave the property at the end of their shift. Im working on gathering the facts but if someone from management could reach out and explain why and where this is coming from because I’m confused at where the CBA or Policy allows this.

Bus VM

By Paul Neil
