item.title: The Recording Secretary’s Report: Rail Repick and Various Rec Sec Info
item.dc:creator: Latrelle Gibson
item.content:encoded:
By Latrelle Gibson

For those at rail, you’ve probably heard that a repick is coming. Had it been MY choice, I would’ve told Sound Transit to wait until the Spring/Summer pick, that way runcards could’ve been provided and the simulated I-90 service could’ve been picked then. Wait, I did suggest this and also asked why couldn’t rail just assign the work via the board and whatever was left, sell it at O.T, even perhaps run the simulated service at half until the pick in March. The answer was this would cost too much for Sound Transit. I was under the impression ST had some serious deep pocket coins, seeing that they receive taxes from 3 counties and all, but maybe I’m mistaken. That being said due to this, an MOA was signed to allow for this repick which is scheduled for Jan 7 – 9. This pick will take effect February 14, 2026 and will still run until March 28. The regular pick will still be the week of March 9 – 11.

The driver timecards, run cuts, and seniority pick list are available on the website to view. We will NOT be picking vacation at this repick, that will be during the regular pick in March. When operating the simulated service, please make note of the run times and be sure to report them if there is not enough time in the run for turn backs or restroom usage. Due to the rushed nature of this simulated service, there may not have been time for proper review of these run times.

RSIT Seniority List

The RSIT Seniority list is available on the Union Website to View. Please keep in mind the reason for the delay was due to the MOA that was just signed, which would’ve required a revision. This MOA’s language is consistent with O&MSIT’s language, which places those currently at Rail first in seniority order, followed by others in King County, followed by External Candidates. This Seniority list will reflect this MOA change. Thank you, Abdiwahab, Greg, and (I’m going to pat my own self on the back for suggesting using the same language as streetcar during the contract survey meetings and helping get the language drafted to propose in bargaining) for working hard on this language, now Rail is consistent with other classifications. We will still need to bargain this MOA into the new language as it is set to expire once the new TA is signed and ratified, and this language has been presented in our contract proposals.

Seniority Adjustments

I know I’ve written a lot about seniority and how it works. However, this topic is important to discuss as this is all we have when it comes to choosing our work shifts, work locations, vacation time, ETC. The Union CANNOT just change one’s seniority. Remember, the seniority list is the employer’s list, and the Union cannot alter their list, only the employer can do this. Seniority adjustments and seniority restoration are different animals. Adjustment speaks to making someone whole and restoration speaks to restoring a member to their previously held seniority date and rank.

For seniority adjustments, this would normally be the result of a settlement agreement or a forfeiture. If a member obtains an attorney, and they reach a settlement agreement with Metro, and part of this agreement is to adjust one’s seniority to what it should’ve been, this is what the Union IS REQUIRED TO COMPLY WITH. A settlement is a legally binding agreement, and many settlements have been in the works for 4+ years before getting to this point. So, although some may be upset when an adjustment happens, know that there is nothing the Union can do about this. We have to comply with the settlement agreement.

For seniority restoration, this action is usually the result of a medical separation, transfer, or promotion. If a member is medially separated, and returns to their classification held at time of separation within 3 years, they will have their seniority restored. Medical Separation is a process, one cannot simply quit and state they were medically separated. The other instance would be one transferred or promoted to a job outside of 587 but within King County and decided to return to their previous classification within a year, they would have their seniority restored. If a member for instance promotes to SIT, and decides to return to operator, they would return to their bus operator classification with no loss in seniority, HOW- EVER, if they decided to go back to SIT, they would lose all rights to the seniority they held in that classification.

Bargaining

Open bargaining will return in the New Year. This is when the “stuff” gets real! I don’t know if we’ll be able to always say what articles we’ll be addressing, however, I will try to keep the membership updated to help members know when show up for their classification although there is nothing wrong with just simply showing up to observe. The bargaining dates will be indicated in this News Review and were listed in the December edition of the News Review. I am going to be working with our staff to get the proposals we pushed across the table uploaded to the website. This will not be something that will happen quickly, as this is new for us and we will need to figure out how to upload such large files to the website, this is the entire contract being uploaded to the website and this takes a lot of work to do. We appreciate your patience as we work to get this uploaded and see you at the next bargaining session!

In Solidarity, RecSec Gibson

item.title: Notification of Respect
item.content:encoded:
King County Metro does NOT respect it’s employees. King County Metro is required by the CBA to adopt specific behaviors that are commonly associated with respect, but make no mistake, it does NOT respect you. Your Union Represented Supervisors are getting tired of the disparities behind the scenes. I will be bringing one of these to light in this article.

The CBA contains dozens of references to “notifications” and “notices” required between Metro and Union Members. Metro is required to inform Members of matters pertaining to them, and Members are required to keep Metro informed of matters in kind. On the surface, this sounds like a fair exchange.

Article 4.2 in the CBA states clearly “When an immediate supervisor wants to discuss an existing or potential disciplinary matter with an Employee, they shall notify the Employee in writing of the purpose and time limitation for having the meeting.” Operators see these notices as “See me” slips from their chief, with the express written obligation to meet with their Chief within five days. Supervisors have not been getting this luxury. Over the last contract duration, numerous Supervisors have been intercepted while signing in or out for their shift, being dragged into an office with a Chief and a Shop Steward, and been subject to disciplinary hearings with no prior notification.

Additionally, the “Written Notifications” are being slid across the table at these very same meetings, and Supervisors are being forced to sign them in acknowledgment. Per the CBA “The Employee shall sign the pro-

By Ian Nielson, FLS Shop Steward posal to suspend or discharge to acknowledge receipt of the same.” At one of the meetings I attended as a Supervisor Shop Steward, this “Written Notification” stated that the meeting would be held at 10:00 AM, and the Supervisor was asked to sign it at the beginning of the meeting at 12:30 PM, while still having no idea what the meeting was about! Metro's stance on the subject is that the language of the CBA does not require a specific time frame for notification, and that this disrespectful practice is therefore “in compliance.”

I assert that this is clearly NOT the intention of the CBA, nor is it fair or equitable to any degree. Compare the notifications in other parts of the CBA, for example:

Leave Donations require a full pay period of notification to central payroll. 10 days notice for SDAs being offered. Grievance language carries multiple notification time frames of 15 calendar days. Rehire notifications are at 10 and 15 calendar days. Metro wants to know about your Jury Duty as soon as you receive the summons. Sick Leave requires “reasonable notice,” later defined as “10 calendar days,” or “as soon as possible prior to the start of the Employee’s work shift.” Bids for Holiday work must occur seven days in advance. Metro wants to know information from you early, so it can plan ahead.

This is only a portion of the references. Strangely, we find that information flowing the other direction, is very much when Metro feels like it. Consider the following examples:

For VM, “With at least twohour notice to an Employee, METRO may cancel an overtime assignment in its entirety” and “Metro will attempt to provide written notice,” or “The employee may agree to shorter notice.” For Supervisors, “When a shift is canceled, the unit Superintendent or designee will notify the UNION,” or “a Relief Supervisor’s extra assignment may be changed by more than four hours and with less than twelve hours notice.”

Metro wants you to provide a fair and reasonable notice, as soon as is practicable, but thinks a fair notice to you is two and a half hours after the proposed start to a disciplinary meeting. Metro wants you to believe that an organization that consistently responds to changing current events throughout the greater King County area on a minute by minute basis is completely incapable of delivering a more timely notice to the dedicated employees that keep it running. They would also have you believe that it is socially acceptable for Metro Staff to treat you with a lower standard of professionalism than is required of you.

Employees have lives, families, feelings, and all the other things that make us human. We deserve to be treated with human dignity and respect. We’ve tried talking it out, and following the grievance procedure. Metro’s behavior is reprehensible and detestable on this front, and it has unapologetically drawn a line in the sand. There’s been quite enough of it, and it needs to stop.

I will remind all employees that they are allowed to notify Metro that they intend to use sick leave after reporting for their shift. All employees are allowed to notify Metro that they wish to review their disciplinary record, or their attendance record. Employees are allowed to request feedback for a recruitment process. Employees are allowed to file a grievance for a contract violation. You are allowed to notify King County Metro of any one of a number of wonderful things you can think of, and literally inundate the organization with paperwork, all at the same time, last minute, and without prior warning, as long as it is not an explicitly defined time frame in the CBA. Because responding quickly to emergent events is what Metro does best. Metro does NOT respect its employees... Yet.

item.title: Stories From Metro’s Frontline Workers, Shared with Heart, and Purpose “
item.content:encoded:
Life is political, not because the world cares about how you feel, but because the world reacts to what you do.” ICE and Boarder Patrols’ abduction of workers — designed as spectacles of terror — demands a rapid-response program.

Nationwide at least 60,000 immigrants are detained in privately contracted prisons. In this expanding dragnet, communities are staging a bulwark against federal assaults. The numbers reflect the significant effort the Trump administration has put into its escalating immigration crackdown.

Last spring, as attacks on immigrants escalated and schools became potential sites of terror, the United Teachers Los Angeles (UTLA) union led trainings on immigrant rights and protections. Activists were able to get dos and don’ts out quickly because the union has an effective communication network within schools and across regions: area representatives communicate with school-based representatives, who communicate with members.

Chicago Teacher’s Union organized rapid-response teams and distributed red cards with know-your-rights information. When the attacks came in earnest, the training expanded to include information about how to film ICE, how to report ICE, how to warn of a raid.

Our union, ATU587, must be seen prepared for when we face more direct attacks. When the National Guard arrived in D.C. the soldiers’ assumed positions around Metro stations where students gather; students rely on Metro trains to get to school.

By Atlantic Base Shop Steward and Safety Committee Chair Chuck Lare

The soldiers harassed and intimidated students.

The D.C. community—anchored by groups like Empower Ed and Free DC—responded by organizing an adult presence at the Metro stations and posted lookouts on street corners. They formed text-message groups to educate people about what was needed, how to support families, and how to track and respond to federal agents.

There is so much to put in place to have a response, we need both management and ATU 587 collaboration. Anywhere raids are happening people are traumatized and afraid – a federal spectacle of terror.

Currently those with authority appear to be thinking through the lens of liability, not resistance. We need ATU 587 and management material commitment to build out a plan and team to prepare resistance. Here is a proposed two-point plan:

  1. Every Base have an initiative-taking plan that includes NW Immigrant Rights Project (NWIRP.org) material roleplaying workshops addressing “what to do if ICE shows up”, develop response teams and post signs explicitly indicating that ICE is not allowed.

  2. ATU 587 and management on going county-wide collaboration - education through video logs (Vlogs) and quarterly inperson presentations by frontline workers with everyday living experiences.

This would be a follow-up to what I started by proposing to our Atlantic Base Superintendent a monthly “Taste of Cultures” - storytelling by first and second-generation immigrants’ living experiences. This initiative culminated in Metro funding with catered food the December 3rd’s “Mosaic of Us: Many Cultures One Community” hosted by the Refugees and Immigrants Support and Empowerment (RISE) employee resource group, Atlantic Base Operations and Metro’s EEO,

I facilitated the bringing together ATU 587’s frontline workers who spoke of their living experiences from: Sudan, Ethiopia, Kenya, Somalia, and S. Asia. These fellow members courageously shared personal stories of migration, resilience, and service. Their words illuminated journeys of loss and bold new beginnings, and the pride of serving the public they once stood among as newcomers. The room was quiet, tearful, and deeply connected.

The frontline speakers had a difficult challenge, striking a balance where they are experiencing their own trauma. Things that are so big and out of the norm are happening, and then you continue to have to come

You can find advice on defending members at the NW Immigrant Rights Project, NWIRP.org and Resources for Immigrant Workers and Allies at labornotes.org/immigration. Ref. https://labornotes.org/2025/12/iceraids-turn-schools-battlegrounds-defend-students to work each day wondering if more trauma awaits. We need to be held responsible for creating a space that is structured and safe where the frontline worker knows and feels they are protected. We need support from ATU587 to make this not a one-and-done and be inclusive of the other nationalities of our ATU587 membership.

This is a challenge when the union is also in the middle of contract negotiations – but when guided by social purpose we can serve the common good and create long term progress. We as a union can continue to grow through future gatherings, storytelling spaces, and learning opportunities that meet our members where they are, across shifts, languages, cultures, communities, and work sites. We learn best from sharing stories, building solidarity and will better serve and strengthen community - a better workplace for all to succeed.

This is community building in a changing immigration landscape.

Janaury 2026

item.title: Building Trust and Equity in Rail Operations
item.dc:creator: Hassannoor Aden, Minority Affairs Officer, ATU Local 587/King County Labor Delegate
item.content:encoded:
By Hassannoor Aden, Minority Affairs Officer, ATU Local 587/King County Labor Delegate

Safety Culture and Building Trust

In September, I attended the Safety Culture Training in San Diego a four-day workshop designed to improve how organizations like King County Metro approach safety, communication, and inclusion. It was a very informative and engaging experience that reshaped how I think about safety and teamwork.

The training focused on creating a culture of trust, where both management and frontline employees feel respected and heard. It highlighted one of the biggest issues we face today the gap between management and employees when it comes to trust.

Too often, operators or supervisors who report safety concerns end up being treated as if they caused the problem, rather than being recognized for identifying a potential hazard. This reaction discourages open reporting, which in turn weakens safety across the system.

As someone who has worked at Metro for over a decade, I’ve seen how easily concerns can get lost in the layers of management from supervisors to chiefs, to managers, to directors. The more layers we have, the harder it becomes to get issues resolved promptly and fairly.

The training reminded me that a true safety culture depends on relationships built on respect and trust. Managers and supervisors should be seen as allies, not enforcers. When an operator speaks up about a safety issue, it should be viewed as a contribution to system improvement, not as a reason for punishment.

King County Metro’s Safety Policy and Just Culture Principles support this approach, encouraging employees to report safety issues without fear of retaliation. But for this to work, it must be applied consistently across all levels of management.

When we invest in trust, both sides win operators feel valued and management gains valuable insight from the people who experience the work firsthand.

Training Equity and Language Barriers

Another area that needs serious attention is training equity, especially for minority and bilingual employees. Over the past year, many have shared experiences of unequal treatment during evaluations including feeling misunderstood because English is not their first language.

Under Article 2 of the ATU Local 587 Collective Bargaining Agreement (Non- Discrimination) and King County’s Equal Employment Opportunity (EEO) Policy, every employee has the right to fair training, evaluation, and promotional opportunities, regardless of language, origin, or background.

Yet, we continue to hear stories of unfair grading practices and bias. For bilingual employees, it’s not about ability or knowledge, it’s about communication. Some trainees have been told they “Failed” tasks when, in reality, there was a misunderstanding due to language interpretation or unclear instructions.

This issue also connects to religious accommodation. An operator had been asked to provide written authorization from HR before being allowed to pray during training hours. That requirement directly conflicts with King County Metro’s Religious Accommodation Policy and federal law under Title VII of the Civil Rights Act of 1964, which requires reasonable accommodation for religious practices.

At Metro, we have many Muslim employees who perform daily prayers. Their right to pray should not depend on an HR letter. Metro’s policy already allows for religious accommodation unless it creates an undue hardship and taking five minutes for prayer does not meet that threshold.

Training environments should be inclusive, supportive, and fair. When an employee feels respected for who they are and what they believe, they perform better. ATU Local 587 will continue to advocate for equal access to training, transparent grading standards, and fair evaluation practices for all members, especially our multilingual and faith-based communities.

Scheduling and Contract Compliance

As Link light rail continues to expand, the workload and complexity of scheduling have increased dramatically. We now have multiple service layers Federal Way extensions, Angle Lake turnback’s, Pinehurst single tracking duties, and others each with unique reporting times, layovers, and route transitions.

While expansion is a positive step, it has also led to frequent schedule adjustments, sometimes communicated to operators on short notice. This has caused confusion and frustration among many rail operators.

The ATU Local 587 Rail CBA, Article 20 (Picks and Assignments) clearly states that any change to a picked assignment must be communicated at least five (5) days in advanc e. This rule exists to protect operators’ personal time and ensure predictability in their schedules.

However, several operators have reported receiving notice of schedule changes while they were on vacation, out on leave, or during their regular days off sometimes with less than five days’ notice. This not only violates the CBA but also disrupts work-life balance, which is a key value under King County’s Healthy Workplace Guidelines.

Metro’s success depends on clear communication and respect for the labor agreement. Scheduling adjustments should always follow the five-day rule unless there is a documented operational emergency. When management honors the contract, it strengthens morale and builds the mutual respect that keeps our service running smoothly.

Moving Forward Together

As rail operations continue to grow, so must our commitment to fairness, inclusion, and safety. Every policy, every rule, and every action should reflect respect for the people who move this system every day, the operators, instructors, supervisors, and support staff.

We all want the same thing: a safe, respectful, and supportive workplace. That goal is only possible when everyone from the Director’s office to the front line operates with trust and integrity.

The Safety Culture Training reminded me that a true culture of safety starts with listening, empathy, and fairness. Whether it’s a safety report, a training challenge, or a scheduling issue, the first step is to treat every employee with dignity.

We are stronger when we stand together when we speak up for one another, support fair practices, and make sure every voice is heard. As ATU 587 members, that’s not just our right, it’s our responsibility.

The mocking and targeting of Muslim women, including comments about elected officials who wear hijab, is especially concerning. A woman wearing hijab on public transit should not have to worry about becoming a target because of statements made by national leaders or reinforced by everyday comments in the workplace. Yet that is the environment this rhetoric creates. In that spirit, I also encourage solidarity with our Muslim female coworkers. Those who choose to wear a hijab or scarf in support are showing a simple but meaningful sign of unity and respect, especially at a time when Muslim women are being unfairly targeted and made to

This is a call for awareness, accountability, and solidarity. We must look out for one another, challenge harmful language when we hear it, and support members who feel targeted or unsafe. Our strength as a union comes from standing together, even when the conversation is uncomfortable.

Every member deserves dignity, safety, and respect, whether on the job, in the breakroom, or out in the community. That is not just a value we talk about. It is a responsibility we must live up to.

Janaury 2026

To discuss, approve and/or propose resolutions to: • Issues or problems of Metro policies which affects the Union and which either party requests to be placed on the agenda. • Issues or problems of contract administration other than formal grievances.

item.title: Dangerous Rhetoric Has Real Consequences for Our Members
item.dc:creator: Hassannoor Aden, Minority Affairs Officer, ATU Local 587/King County Labor Delegate
item.content:encoded:
By Hassannoor Aden, Minority Affairs Officer, ATU Local 587/King County Labor Delegate

Recent remarks by President Trump attacking the Somali community and immigrants from Africa are not only offensive, but they are also dangerous. Referring to entire communities as “garbage” and labeling African nations with degrading language places minorities in a vulnerable position, especially those who work in public-facing jobs like transit.

Words from the President of the United States carry weight. They shape public behavior and set the tone for what some people believe is acceptable. When racist language comes from someone in such a powerful position, it can legitimize hatred and embolden individuals who already hold harmful views. For transit workers, this can translate into increased harassment, threats, and physical danger while on duty.

Many of our members spend their entire workday interacting with the public. Bus operators, rail operators, supervisors, and station staff do not have the option to walk away when tensions rise. When certain communities are singled out and dehumanized, our members from those communities often feel the impact first. They are visible, accessible, and exposed.

It is also important to be honest and acknowledge that these attitudes do not only exist outside our workplace. We have some members within our own union who share or excuse the same kinds of views expressed in the President’s remarks. That reality makes this issue even more serious, because harm does not always come from strangers.

This reminds me of an incident at South Base back in 2017, where one of our own members casually referred to coworkers during a conversation as a “fish market,” implying they were loud and smelly. Comments like that may be dismissed as jokes or casual remarks, but they carry racial and cultural meaning. They reduce people to stereotypes and create a hostile environment. That kind of language, even when spoken casually, reflects the same mindset behind national-level rhetoric we claim to oppose.

As someone from the Somali community, I know how painful and alarming this language can be. Many Somalis fled a brutal civil war and have lived through the consequences of dehumanization and feardriven politics. When leaders or coworkers use similar language, it reopens old wounds and reinforces a sense of being unwelcome or unsafe.

feel unsafe.

Our workforce at King County Metro and throughout the county reflects the diversity of the communities we serve. We work alongside immigrants, refugees, asylum seekers, permanent residents, and U.S. citizens. These members are not outsiders. They are essential workers who keep the system moving every day.

Racist rhetoric does not differentiate between immigration status or citizenship. It does not stop to ask who was born here and who was not. Once a community is labeled as inferior or “other,” everyone associated with it becomes vulnerable.

As a union, we have a responsibility to confront this honestly, both externally and internally. That means speaking out when public figures use language that puts our members at risk, and it also means addressing harmful behavior when it comes from within our own ranks. Respect on the job is not optional. It is a basic expectation.

From the News Review, January 2026, page 17. Open in the PDF · Original file on atu587.org

item.title: November Operators’ LMRC Meeting
item.content:encoded:
Attendees:

Rachael Buchanan, Lisa Nault, Jabari Hampton, Cory Rigtrup, William Mc- Coy, Amanda Thames

FOLLOW UP:

ADA Placards:

That one is still stuck in Service Information. They take our design and finalize it and then give it to CSC who produces it. Dragging on month after month and Metro is sorry about that. It’s the same thing we already have on the new Gillig’s, which is a metal plate, so the language has already been approved. The Union would like to know how a decal is different when nothing about the design should be changed. Metro doesn’t know.

Customer Relations Classes:

Update from Training as of November 25th, is that the AVADE training is at 53% completion rate. 1st class available is at 85% completion, and they’re trying to incorporate that class into the AVADE class to make it a full 8 hours of training. Metro believes Operators are being detailed off their work to attend. It is easier for Metro to detail Operators for the entire 8-hour class than it is to relieve them for a 4-hour block. The Union would like to know if feedback is being given after the classes are taken, and what that looks like. A survey is offered at the end of

By Lisa Nault #3647 and Rachael Buchanan #21341; ATU 587 Bus Reps every class. Metro is not sure of the results.

Uniform Committee:

One LMRC Member was at one Uniform Committee meeting where the Metro Lead didn’t attend and wasn’t at the one the Metro Lead did. It’s cold out and Operators have no jackets. Metro contends that it’s not a uniform committee item and can’t change what’s currently in the contract. The committee can only make recommendations according to the CBA. Who has that authority? The Director does. Can the director get jackets? “The Director can’t do that.” Metro asks, “Don’s doesn’t have a parka?” The parka is not a winter jacket. Don’s contract expires at the end of the month, and the bidding process is out. Metro will start with confirming what’s currently available. The contract does call out a parka, and we need to figure out what is allowable for a winter coat, because it’s only going to get colder. If members are being called out for out of uniform for winter coats, please bring it back to us.

Tukwila Base:

Painting offices today and the coaches are being tested with the chargers. The 3 routes will run out of South Base on the weekdays. Those three routes will only run weekday service out of Tukwila Base and that will be the only RDO option at the first pick when the base opens.

DECEMBER 4, 2025

They will run those routes out of South Base on the weekdays. 21 buses have been delivered and are in varying states of readiness for service. Training has started qualifying on the coaches because Metro wants to get some service on them before the base opens in March.

School Zones:

Metro was able to have a conversation with upper management, and it sounds like it’s been elevated further, because Metro recognizes the Union’s point that the policy as written is excessive. Metro believes there is a revision to that bulletin but was unable to find it during the meeting.

Encampments:

Continue writing SIRs! At East Base, Route 522 lays over Ravenna Blvd between on and off ramps for I-5, there are encampments on both sides of the street, and there are concerns to the public and to our operators who park there. These are just examples of locations all over the county that we have to deal with. Metro just got feedback from the security groups thanking us for filling out those reports. There were a couple that alerted them to problem areas, and they were ablet to go out and address them. If you are writing them and not seeing action, bring it to the base safety committee.

Meeting Times:

This day of the week is pretty much locked in and if we need to change the time, we can look at that. The recurring time on the calendar appears to work. The Union VP has Supervisor LMRC an hour before that. We could move this to 9am on January 8th as a trial. And then going forward, the 1st Thursday of the month at 9am. If that doesn’t work, we’ll revisit at that time.

New Business:

Building a Successful Probationary Program for FTO:

Executive Board Officer VM Position 3 is filling in for the Vice President and in a month, a lot of things have happened. What he is seeing is that since we’ve hired off the street, the standards have not changed from PT. Employees are trying to filter into the Metro system and learning how to drive. The point system hasn’t changed, and some new Operators have racked up a few probationary points, and they get fired only to be brought back a few days later. It’s stressful and unnecessary. If Metro can identify that this employee is borderline, you get pulled in, evaluated, and given an action plan. Our contract calls it decision-making leave, but we think that’s a far better process than what we’re doing now, which is completely unnecessary. Where we see Super-

intendents actually believe in the employee, it’s much better. The Union’s position is let’s give them a chance because putting them on notice and giving them the opportunity to change is a good thing. Metro agrees that the process needs to change. We’re throwing operators on the street on their first day on a Saturday with no resources and there’s a lot to be desired in their care and success. Some care is happening, but overall, it’s not. There’s a lot of labor for the Chief to keep track of people and the Union is aware of the CBA regarding probationary employees. The process is about as good as it gets for right now until we can change the points or increase coverage on the weekends. Metro hears and agrees with the Union on the care and success of new employees. Hiring and firing is very expensive, and Metro doesn’t want to waste the public’s money on hiring and firing. Metro will have some results early in the year in terms of overall numbers. There is a desire to have more Chief’s available on weekends. What’s being done right now and what can we do wholistically. The Union wants to avoid the step of having an Operator lose their job and have all that stress about caring for their family. Let’s have the conversation now. Metro kind of lets the bases run those processes. If the Superintendent isn’t there that day, the person is getting fired, and there’s not a lot Metro can do about that. Metro would like to know if this is anecdotal or happening on a larger basis. There are a lot more instances because Operations is so large. If the Union sees an actual epidemic of this, Metro definitely wants to know so they can investigate and address the process of hiring and firing of people. Shop Stewards have been active, especially at East Base where there are 3 subcontracts that have to be filled and going on the Extra Board right out of class is a lot more stressful. Can we send a message to Training that the initial pairing for long periods didn’t work and then going down to zero hours also didn’t work. We would like some consistency with pairing that isn’t painful for everyone. We are training our operators on school trippers when there are 5 reroutes and it’s unreasonable to expect brand new people to understand that training. Shop Stewards told Metro to send them out as many times as you can to get them familiar with the process, and Metro said it sounded good, but we don’t think it actually went into practice. We need to spend more time on route qualifications rather than learning it just one direction and be qualified on the whole route. Metro agrees they can be flexible and sometimes people need help. Is there a safety aspect to this we can propose to the safety committee? Is this a safety concern or a service concern? It is a safety concern because we’ve had two very senior report operators make mistakes and if it’s complicated for someone with 30+ years’ experience, it’s very complicated for someone who is brand new. Metro might need to involve a few extra work groups in this process.

Preventability Process Before Imposing Discipline:

Scheduled meeting time reached before topic could be discussed.

Federal Way Trains:

The Union recognizes there are 3 new

Link Light Rail Stations opening on December 6th. Operators have not seen anything regarding the route into, out of, or around the Kent/Des Moines Station or the 272nd Street Station. The routing was already changed to accommodate the Downtown Federal Way Station. Metro doesn’t have anything about that with the procession of events happening. Metro was caught off guard about the new stations opening. Metro has to see what the plan is for today. They recognize that they are very limited but there will be significant changes in the Fall of 2026. Metro did not print any mid-shakeup schedule changes. If your run card changes, please let us know. Metro stated they had to build the bus zones inside the new Rail Stations. That doesn’t mean we’re going to use them right away.

Meeting adjourned at 11:53.

Have a topic you want brought up in the LMRC Meetings? Contact Lisa or Rachael to submit your topics.

I,.................................., in the presence of God and the members of this Union, do solemnly promise and pledge (without any reservation or evasion) to support the Constitution and General Laws of this Amalgamated Transit Union. I will keep myself in good standing by paying all dues, fines and assessments required. I will work to promote the best interests of this Union and encourage my fellow workers to become members of the same. I will not take the place of any member of this organization, or any other union worker who may be on strike or locked out. I will not reveal any of the private business to anyone not entitled to know the same.

I will not engage in activity evidencing gross disloyalty nor in conduct otherwise unbecoming a member, and will not knowingly wrong a member or see one wronged if in my power to prevent it. I will not appeal to any legal authority in matters pertaining to this Union until I have exhausted all means of redress provided by its laws. I will be considerate of others in word and action and will never discriminate against a fellow worker on account of race, religion, color, creed, sex, sexual orientation, gender identity or expression, age, disability, citizenship, or national origin. I also promise to promote the cause of trade union principles and defend freedom of thought, whether expressed by tongue or pen, with all the power at my command.

I understand there is nothing in this obligation that will in any way interfere with my political and religious rights or that will be in any way inconsistent with my duties arising from any of the relations of life.

This obligation I take upon my honor, and solemnly promise to keep the same, as long as I remain a member of this Union.

item.title: The President’s Report: Our Voice, Our Power!
item.dc:creator: Greg Woodfill
item.content:encoded:
By Greg Woodfill

can and should rally around are the protection of our Jobs, wages, benefits, working conditions, transit funding, transit infrastructure, and transit laws.

You may not like many or any of our local or state politicians. You may not agree with endorsing or donating to Politician’s whose beliefs/agendas don’t align with yours. The cold hard reality though, is that the only way our union can have any influence, or protection is to play the political game. We didn’t create the game or have any control over it; we don’t get to choose who runs. We interview everyone who asks for our endorsement and ask the same type of questions to best gauge where they stand on Public Transit and Unions in general.

Just to be clear, COPE will absolutely endorse a conservative politician if they say the right things about Transit and Unions. We’ve had recent feelers from Conservatives in Olympia who want to explore working more closely with our Union on Public Transit. Conservative Republican

County Council Member Dunn introduced the County Legislation to create the Transit Safety Task Force and continues to support us on vital transit issues.

If you are a 587 Member, your wages and benefits were earned on the backs of the thousands of dues-paying members who came before us. Whatever job you currently have at the County, you wouldn’t be making nearly as much in wages and benefits if we weren’t in a Union, nor would we have the level of public support demonstrated by votes to raise taxes for Public Transit funding.

This was an incredibly challenging election cycle for our Union. Both the County Executive and the Seattle Mayors’ race pitted people we have always supported against each other. Ultimately, our COPE committee recommended endorsing Claudia & Bruce mainly for the length of time they’ve supported and worked with our Union and promoted public transit. But it was a difficult choice, including considering and deciding against dual endorsements.

All along, our Union felt that no matter who won the County Executive and Seattle Mayor races, we would have two leaders our Union has supported and worked well with, who would be champions for Labor and Transit. Obviously, our choices for these two offices lost, and many of our members would have preferred that we endorsed the eventual winners.

I have personally met with and congratulated Girmay twice and Katie once since the Election. They both assured me that they understood our union’s endorsements, that there were no hard feelings, and that they are both ready and looking forward to working with our Union.

I called them both the moment the Union approved endorsing their challengers and checked in with them throughout the Campaign. I was invited to and attended Girmay’s ceremonial swearing-in ceremony.

Our Union is YOU. If you’re not happy with who we endorse or how we decide, throw your name in for consideration to join the COPE committee. Follow the News Review and attend meetings during the election cycle, as the COPE committee's endorsement recommendations are merely recommendations accepted or rejected by the membership at the monthly Union meetings.

If you currently contribute to COPE, thank you for adding to our Union’s power! If you’ve never contributed to COPE, please consider contributing even the minimum $5 per paycheck for the protection of your job, its compensation, and your working conditions. We have many plaques on the walls of our Union Hall recognizing our Local for contributing the most to COPE for a union of our size. We took pride in that recognition; it mattered.

We could literally get back to winning these awards if every member who doesn’t contribute signed up to contribute at least $5 per paycheck. And every member who currently contributes signed up to contribute at least $1 more.

The Union does not speak for members’ political beliefs nor tell them who they should or must vote for. Your Union Dues are never used for political purposes; voluntary donations to COPE by our Members are the only dollars used for politics.

Our endorsements and contributions aren’t deciding factors in who is or isn’t elected. They just give us better access to be heard on the transit issues that matter to us. Historically, we have cultivated politicians who tend to vote pro-transit when we most need pro-transit votes.

Even if you despise politics, or despise the West Coast, King County, or Seattle politics, it absolutely is in your best interest to contribute to COPE. Politicians pick up the phone and listen when we call them directly for help. They draft and vote for pro-transit funding and initiatives.

ATU International’s current slogan is “Our Voice, Our Power!” Our COPE committee, its endorsements, and its contributions are literally ATU 587’s political Voice and Power. Please consider contributing or contributing a little more to the power of our voice, it matters, it makes a demonstrative difference.

ATU 587 – We Are One!

item.title: The Maintenance Vice President’s Report: December Maintenance VP Report
item.content:encoded:
Bus Facilities Maintenance

Does it ever end? Will it ever get better?

Last month I reported on the Constructors pick and TFD managements bullying and intimidation tactics. The saga continues, while TFD management finally relented on their ability to add that an employee must have a certain certification to pick a certain spot (4/10 shifts), I was having a discussion with a TFD chief about the tactics used to get employees to get certifications tell me “We are trying to incentivize employees to get certified.” Mind you, all these certifications are optional and not required as part of their employment. We have agreed to a repick without certifications being required to pick spots, however management has retaliated by removing desired 4/10 positions. If that isn’t the definition of bullying and intimidation, I don’t know what it is. Along with

By Jeff Stambaugh all that TFD management still does not seem to have a clear grasp of what the Term outsourcing means. Back in July, TFD management decided to outsource Local 587 Union work to a vendor, grievances were filed, discussions were held, grievance hearings were held and TFD Management saw the wisdom in doing the right thing and paid the grievant’s the monies due for outsourcing at first step. There was hope things were going to get better.

During the discussions, the Union was very clear that if TFD management felt they needed to outsource work, TFD needed a written agreement with the Union to do so. Unfortunately, TFD management has outsourced work again, not only is there no written agreement with the Union, there was no discussion with the Union either. As of this writing, grievances have been filed, and hearings have been scheduled. I’m optimistic we will receive a positive first step response.

Bus Vehicle Maintenance

The ongoing dispute over Metro issuing Unexcused Absences to employees agreeing to work OT or Holiday assignments and later change their mind continues. Metro has refused to engage in a resolution to this issue and instead has decided to attempt to drag it through the grievance process in hopes of strengthening their position, however through the process the Union is now in possession of emails that shows Metro’s attempt to unilaterally change working conditions without following the proper process.

The Union has now filed an Unfair Labor Practice.

Prior to the filing, the Union engaged Metro at several levels trying to resolve this issue. As of this writing, Metro has been unwilling to work to a resolution. More to come as we work through the process with the Public Employees

Relations Commission, commonly known as PERC.

Discipline

It has been a rough month for discipline.

Between TFD and Bus Vehicle Maintenance there have been nine (9) terminations or proposed terminations, and several other members were issued heavy handed discipline.

Most all this discipline is related to work performance issues and attendance.

Rail

Rail continues to expand and hire, resulting in adding several new maintenance positions throughout the system that has created opportunities for promotions and movement as well as confusion as how the movement is accomplished. Do we do re-pick or move-ups? That depends on several circumstances all spelled out in various sections in the contract.

item.content:encoded:
So, many of you probably ask the question “why does it take so long to get the Shop Steward Nomination list out”? Well, there’s many factors at play when getting this list together. Just before pick preview, I will get a bulletin out alerting the membership of nominations being open. Nominations typically remain open through the first month of the new shakeup to allow the Supervisors to nominate during their pick. Once that has happened, I will put out Shop Steward list #1. Once members see this list, some may realize they missed the nomination window and email me requesting to be placed on the Shop Steward List. This is where list #2 comes to play, this is the revised list.

Now comes the fun part, Chief Shop Steward Nominations. Now, per our locals’ bylaws, if a member wishes to be Chief Shop Steward at their base and they’re the only ones running for this position, no election will be needed as they’re unopposed. However, if there are multiple members running on a particular base, I will need to conduct a vote. The vote is conducted via operator mail at their respective base. The instructions are to vote for one, sign the ballot, return the ballot to the provided white secrecy envelope, and give it to the window so they can place them in the manilla envelope for me to pick up. If all goes as

By Latrelle Gibson planned, the results are next day. But, if things don’t go as planned, well, this will cause a delay in getting the Shop Steward List out to the bases.

I’m going to be working on a revision to make it clearer on how to vote, and I’ll be sure to send out bulletins to our windows letting them know that I will be conducting a Chief Shop Steward vote and have instructions on what to do with the ballots and who will be picking up the ballots for the window. I will also place reminders in the News Review so everyone will get that reminder, because I truly appreciate all of you who’re willing to step up for the membership and help in any way. This greatly helps us in the Union office when we have that support at the bases.

By the date of this article being published, the list will be out and if timing allows, will also be placed in this very publication for everyone’s convenience.

item.title: Fair Representation, Weingarten Rights, and Why Process Matters in Every Union
item.dc:creator: Andy Price, Shop Steward local 587
item.content:encoded:
By Andy Price, Shop Steward local 587

Most union members have heard the phrase “Duty of Fair Representation,” often shortened to “DFR.” It’s something we assume our union has “covered,” but very few members ever get a clear picture of what the duty really requires — or why it exists in the first place. DFR is not some abstract legal technicality. It is the backbone of trust inside every unionized workplace.

What the Duty of Fair Representation Actually Means

The Duty of Fair Representation developed from a long line of court decisions, starting with the U.S. Supreme Court. The core idea is simple:

When a union represents a member in grievances, discipline, contract enforcement, or negotiations, it must act fairly, honestly, and without discrimination or arbitrary decisionmaking. DFR is not about guaranteeing a victory in every case. It is about guaranteeing a fair process for every member.

Members have the right to expect:

• a reasonable investigation • contract-based explanations • timely responses • consistent procedures • absence of retaliation or favoritism • honest evaluation of the facts • communication about decisions.

enormous pressure, often juggling many cases at once. Members may not see the amount of work that goes on behind the scenes. At the same time, members deserve clarity, consistent procedures, and fair treatment. DFR and Weingarten rights give both sides a shared framework.

Strong unions thrive when all parties:

• communicate clearly • follow contract language • apply procedures consistently • ensure representatives are allowed to fulfill their role • document decisions • treat every member equally

These principles strengthen solidarity, protect the rights of the individual, and contribute to the long-term health and credibility of the union.

Conclusion:

The Duty of Fair Representation and Weingarten rights are not abstract rules; they are the pillars supporting fair process, equal treatment, and member confidence. When understood and honored, they help create a union environment where every member knows they will be heard, represented, and respected — no matter the issue. A strong process makes a strong union.

Yours in solidarity

Andy Price Shop Steward local 587

Because the union is the exclusive representative, the law requires it to use that authority responsibly.

A Real Example (From Outside ATU or King County)

One well-known case often used in labor education is Vaca v. Sipes (U.S. Supreme Court, 1967). In that case, the union failed to properly investigate a member’s grievance before dropping it. The Court held that a union violates DFR when its handling of a grievance is:

• arbitrary (no investigation or explanation) • discriminatory (treating members differently for irrelevant reasons) • in bad faith (dishonest, retaliatory, or personal motive).

Many unions use Vaca v. Sipes in steward training programs as an example of what not to do — not because unions are malicious, but because the legal standard is strict, and consistency in procedure is essential. Using publicly decided cases like this is safe, educational, and widely practiced.

Why Consistency Matters More Than Outcomes

Across the country, unions win some grievances, lose others, and settle many.

DFR does not guarantee results — but it does guarantee fairness. A union can deny or drop a grievance if it has a rational, fact-based reason.

What it cannot do is: • ignore evidence • fail to investigate • base decisions on personal relationships • communicate nothing • violate its own published process • silence a member’s representative • refuse to explain its rationale

Members are not required to win — but they are entitled to a fair chance.

• help clarify facts relevant to the issue

These rights exist because workers should never navigate a potentially disciplinary meeting alone or unsupported. When understood together, DFR and Weingarten rights create a balanced system where unions and members each have defined roles, responsibilities, and protections.

Why These Rights Matter to Everyone

Some members may believe these issues only matter when something goes wrong.

But that’s not true. Healthy unions maintain strong representation practices all the time, because:

• They protect the legitimacy of grievance outcomes. • They strengthen the union’s credibility with management. • They build member trust and stability. • They prevent preventable conflicts, misunderstandings, and legal exposure. • They reinforce that the union belongs to all members equally.

Even if a member never files a grievance, these rights create a foundation of fairness that protects the entire bargaining unit.

A Shared Commitment

Union officers work under

item.title: Building Trust Through Accountability: A Conversation Worth Having
item.content:encoded:
Recently, I had a candid conversation with a King County Metro operations chief that got me thinking deeply about accountability, trust, and how we show up for each other in this work. What struck me most was their genuine care—for us as operators, for the riding public, and for creating a workplace where everyone can do their best.

They shared frustrations about moments when drivers seem defensive about policy violations or push back on feedback. But underneath that frustration, I heard something else: a leader who truly wants to support us, who understands the complexity of what we do, and who feels caught in the middle trying to balance accountability with advocacy. It made me ask myself some hard questions. And I think they're worth asking together.

Where Accountability Meets Trust

Here's the thing: accountability isn't about catching people doing something wrong. It's about all of us taking ownership of our impact—even when that impact is unintended. When we roll through a stop, miss a call-out, or respond curtly to a passenger on a rough day, we might have reasons. Valid ones. But those actions still ripple outward—affecting riders who depend on us, coworkers who cover for us, and supervisors who field complaints while wanting to have our backs. The question isn't whether we make mistakes. We all do. The question is: can we stay open to hearing about them?

By Balaramdas Stern, Bellevue Base Operator #23327

The Defensiveness Trap

Defensiveness is human. When someone approaches us about our performance, especially if we're already stressed, tired, or feeling undervalued, our first instinct might be to protect ourselves. We might hear criticism even when someone's offering feedback. We might assume they're building a case against us rather than trying to help us grow.

But here's what I'm learning: when we lead with defensiveness, we make it harder for people to support us. We shut down conversations before they can become collaborative. We miss opportunities to share our perspective, explain context, or find solutions together. What if, instead, we got really curious? 'Help me understand what you saw' or 'What would you have done in that situation?'

One Goal

Feedback comes from everywhere—peers, passengers, supervisors, shop stewards, even our families. Each source offers a different lens on how we're showing up. Our coworkers see our professionalism. Riders experience our customer service. Supervisors track our compliance. Our loved ones notice when work stress follows us home.

None of these voices alone tells the whole story. But together, they help us see our blind spots and build on our strengths.

The operators I most respect aren't perfect—they're the ones who can hear hard things without crumbling, who admit mistakes without shame, and who ask for support when they need it.

Bridging the Trust Gap

I get it. When a supervisor wants to "hear your side," it can feel like a setup. Sometimes past experiences make us skeptical. Sometimes the power dynamic makes us guarded. But most of the time, they genuinely want context. They want to understand what happened so they can advocate effectively—for us and for the system we all serve.

We can help bridge this gap by:

• Sharing facts clearly without minimizing or over-explaining

• Acknowledging impact even when our intent was good

• Remembering that asking for support isn't weakness—it's how we all get better

• Recognizing that middle managers care too—often more than we realize

Looking Ahead

Here's what this conversation sparked for me: what if we had access to someone truly neutral when things get difficult? Not management, not union, not HR,—just a trained professional whose only job is to help people work through conflict. They could facilitate conversations between operators, between us and management, even between supervisors and chiefs - and much more. Help us navigate misunderstandings before they escalate, stress us out, and become grievances. Give us a place to turn when we need support that doesn't fit the boxes we currently have. It's worth exploring. Because ultimately, we're all on the same team. We all want safe service, fair treatment, and a workplace where people can thrive.

Look, accountability isn't about never messing up. It's about owning our impact, staying open when feedback is hard to hear, and remembering that the culture we experience is the culture we create—together, one interaction at a time.

What do you think? How do we build more trust and accountability in our workplace? Let's keep this conversation going.

I'd like to hear from you— anonymously and honestly. Scan the QR code below to share your thoughts, experiences, or questions. Your feedback will help shape our next conversation and ensure we're addressing what matters most to each and every one of you.

This article reflects one operator's reflections and is intended to spark dialogue within our workforce. All perspectives are welcome.

item.title: Are You Feeling Safe?
item.content:encoded:
Gun violence on buses and other incidents— whether directed at operators or not—weigh heavily on those of us working routes with the greatest history of violence. What are we to do?

We need action, not rhetoric. Being told “you are an essential worker” rings hollow when operators don’t feel mentally or physically safe. We also carry the additional burden of uncertainty: if trauma occurs, will we recover enough to keep driving? Will we keep our jobs?

Our Union’s Priority:

Protecting Operators’ Jobs

Without our jobs, everything else is secondary. The best practice is preventing trauma from occurring in the first place. While there are practical limits to investing in more security personnel, our union President deserves recognition for his leadership in bringing the county-wide Regional Transit Safety Taskforce to fruition. But like any high-risk environment, there are limits to preventive protection.

Because of these limitations, advocate for robust training and adequate recovery time— giving operators the tools to protect both their health and their jobs.

Evidence-Based Training: The Red Kite Program

Effective, evidence-based training programs like the Red Kite Project have demonstrated real-world success in helping operators manage conflict and reduce burnout. Unlike other organizational change models, it utilizes a sciencebased approach tested in civil conflict and war zones. The Red Kite Project began its work

By Atlantic Base Shop Steward and Safety Committee Chair Chuck Lare in conflict transformation in post-war Bosnia, learning that obstacles and conflict can be transformed into something healthy, even under the most adverse conditions.

With a diverse team including mental health professionals, the Red Kite Project can address operators’ needs, no matter how dire the situation. Their work around the country has shown results: fewer incidents, safer stations, and more confident riders.

The Critical Need for Recovery Time

Adequate recovery time is essential. Without it, operators don't have time to process the allostatic (cumulative) stress load from their previous trip. This makes operators more susceptible to PTSD and prevents proper recovery when incidents occur, potentially costing operators’ jobs. The hypothesis could be substantiated with a University of Washington study of operators’ susceptibility to PTSD from job-related allostatic loading—similar to their existing free therapy study.

Free Therapy Available Now Through 2026

To digress, many operators may qualify for the FREE therapy offered by the UW PTSD Study PATH (Positive Processes and Transition to Health). PATH is a research project investigating innovative treatment for adults (18–65 years old) with PTSD and depression, funded by the National Institute for Mental Health through 2026.

You may be eligible if: • You are 18–65 years old • You experienced a major life event within the last five years (including physical or sexual assault, loss of a loved one, end of a significant relationship, loss of job/career, w a r - r e l a t e d e x p e r ie nc e s, or COVID-19 pandemic-related losses)

• You’re exp e r i e n c i n g trauma-related and/or depressive symptoms

• At least 12 weeks have passed since the event.

Stress symptoms include: Recurrent thoughts of the stressor, intense fear or anxiety related to the event, nightmares, avoiding situations or people associated with the event, feeling detached from others, or being easily startled.

Contact: 206-685-3617 or visit https://pathway2help.com/

Building Alliances for Change

We need allies to champion operators’ health, jobs, and public service. Metro management has been unresponsive to requesting a meeting with UW PATH’s Dr. Lori Zoellner to conduct a study assessing operators’ susceptibility to PTSD from allostatic job loading.

The new Executive Girmay Zahilay, from his campaigning, may offer some hope in, who will lead King County? (Seattle Times, 10/26/25) the Executive stated, “I always try to ask myself who’s not in the room, who needs to be here, how can we break down silos?” Frontline workers have valuable insights that could improve county operations. We need leadership willing to bridge that gap.

I’m guardedly optimistic after receiving this response from the Executive-elect:

“Thank you so much for reaching out and for your service to this region. I grew up catching the Metro bus to get to school and after school activities (specifically the 106, 107, and the 7). I personally benefited from your work and all of the amazing operators at King County.

I take the role of leading this government with great humility and responsibility. I am in the process of getting my feet under me at the moment, and will absolutely be seeking partnership from frontline workers on both delivering quality service and solving persistent problems like homelessness.

Thank you again for reaching out and I will be in touch soon.”

Take Action

Let’s not leave anything to chance. Ally with those taking action for operators’ health, jobs, and public service. Our safety and well-being depend on it.

item.title: The Ryerson Gang
item.content:encoded:
It’s December and I have returned from union leadership exile. Last month I was sworn in to fill the vacant VM Board position. A position that went vacant when Jerry McKenna stepped down for personal reasons. Jerry is a union powerhouse, so I wish him the best and hope for his swift return to helping out fellow VM members. Enough fluff, here’s my article, it’s about surveillance and discipline.

There have been some Management changes in VM, some retired, some got fired, some forced to retire. Well, the vacated dominoes of invertibility happened to fall is such a way, that a “game of thrones” scenario formed. No, there are no dragons, but there is the conquest of desirous hopefuls pitting themselves against each other for just a few positions. While I believe in nature’s way of competition breeding greatness, this story is not about that.

Submitted by Cory Rigtrup, VM Board Rep up the wage table. However, a very disproportionate large number, and I would say over half of all of VM’ terminations in the last 5 years, were fired.

As the years went on, Metro absolutely failed these members, by not providing them with regular leadership. This issue was the number one issue discussed at VM labor management meetings over the years. So, in 2024, when VM posted a Leaderships recruitment for these crews of USWs, I saw light of redemption.

Fast forward till a few months ago. Some bases have used these additional Leads to train, organize, report and run these USW crews. Other bases didn’t get the memo and did something different. Ryerson just failed.

Back to the “Game of thrones” scenario. Ryerson got some new management, and it was not going to be run with leadership for USW crews, but with video surveillance and discipline.

video of the one or two people they had issue with, but every single person from every single coach that gang worked on that night. The video was watched for the entire graveyard shift and matched up with all the stories given. As of the date of writing this article, there have been at least 5 loudermill hearings, 3 terminations and a couple suspensions waiting for a decision.

I could go on and on and on, about the value of good leadership in a crew environment, but let’s talk about cameras and our contract. While the contract allows management to basically manage to failure, the surveillance protection language is ancient and should never be touched. What it simply says in cases like these, if it’s reported that there is an issue at work, management may use surveillance to verify the issue. Anything else seen, an employee cannot be disciplined for, with one major caveat. If surveillance shows a major infraction, something like stealing, then they can discipline, potentially justify termination.

There are a lot of good, hardworking people in that Ryerson graveyard gang. Their shifts end at 6:45am, even though their workstations are taken away hours earlier for sign out. Regardless of the standing order to hang loose, the “game of thrones” needed their blood. Stay tuned, more to come.

Even though I am dyslexic as hell, it’s kind of fun to write these articles. I am proud to be back. Thank you.

From the maintenance perspective, Ryerson base hasn’t really changed over the years. Same old narrow shop doors, remote parking lot, and the base is weirdly configured to be in the middle of the yard. What has changed is the crew.

Since covid, Ryerson along with all the other bases, radically grew in Utility Service Workers. Utility Service Workers, aka USW, inside wash, even called bus cleaners, have the lowest starting wage of all 88 job classifications in the Metro bargaining agreement, except for Supported Employees.

The USW classification for the last 5 years has been a revolving door of new hires. While many have seen promotions to other positions, most have stayed put and advanced

One night, management came in early and did a random check of USW work. They determined some of the work was not up to standard, and not all the employees were where they thought they should be. For whatever reason, Ryerson base never issued their USW crews radios or even provided them with a Lead to report too. When not all the employees were found in the weirdly configured base, investigations began.

They brought the whole crew in, one at a time and asked them what they did that night. Then Ryerson did the one thing everyone should be very, very considered about, they started pulling massive amounts of video. Not just

If something occurs, Operators are encouraged to call TCC. If something happens that you feel needs to be escalated, please tell your Chief. Going to close this for now.

TUKWILA BASE:

Still on target to open March 2026. Initially, there will be 3 routes: 105, 128, and 184. They will operate Monday through Friday Service. Eventually full capacity will see 11 – 12 routes. What if people pick the base, will they travel to another base to get a bus? Metro is unsure of the specifics of staffing Operators at base start up.

New Business:

Zonar:

Zonar will be new technology to complete the pre-trip inspection. Metro is not looking to implement it until FIFA World Cup is over. There may be some training beforehand, but that is up in the air as this is being pushed to the back burner due to more pressing items. The Union notices that this is a technological change as stated in the Collective Bargaining Agreement 3.2A. Metro stated that Operators will use a tablet that lives on the coach for inspection. This raised im-

NOVEMBER 7, 2025

mediate red flags to the Union Representative since PED’s are not permitted in the yard. Metro stated that it won’t be a “personal” device. The Union wants to be transparent about what we’re using it for. Zonar can be used in other ways not specifically stated thus far. The Union will refer this to Union Leadership for discussion in the Joint Management discussions. Metro currently doesn’t know the extent of the discussion between ATU and Management.

School Zones:

There was an update posted (Ops Policy 9/24/2025) that school zones are 20mph 24/7 365 days per week. Why the change? Working conditions change? Have run card run times been changed to accommodate the extra time? Are Operators receiving tickets for exceeding 20mph during OWL service? Are there infractions on Weekends and Holidays? Metro looked up the Manual and noted that it seems to have been policy since 2022. Metro’s advice is to stick to the letter of the manual. The Union notes that the policy seems excessive. Can we bring this up to senior management for consideration? Metro agreed.

Encampments:

Ongoing issues in and around bus zones. Most security is not going around the shelters. Customers, Facilities, Operators, etc. Metro requests that Operators please notify TCC and write them up in Origami on a Security Incident Report so we can get more traction on it. The paper documentation allows us to call the local officials to deal with the situations.

Meeting Times:

Metro has a conflict with a participant not being able to make the current meeting time. Is there an objection to moving the time? Any other day really doesn’t work due to RDOs and Collective Bargaining. Can we move to 9am? The Union Representative doesn’t see an issue with moving the time while keeping the meeting day as it currently is. Metro will notify well before the change happens.

Steward Training:

There will be some meetings tomorrow with members being represented who don’t speak English as their first language and we want to bring in people who can shadow the Steward, so they can help translate and learn how to be a shop steward. Metro suggested the use of caucuses during the meetings to help the Operator being represented fully understand the situation being addressed by the Chief.

Meeting adjourned at 11:37am.

Have a topic you want brought up in the LMRC Meetings? Contact Lisa or Rachael to submit your topics.

13028 Interurban Ave S, Suite 116 Tukwila, WA 98168

In Loving Memory...

You will be missed...Rest Easy

We are saddened to announce the passing of 50-year member, Marlyn Hagemann. Marlyn started their transit career with Seattle Transit in 1968. Marlyn was a transit operator until faced with some medical issues. Due to this condition, they were transferred from Transit Operator to Vault Changer where they spent most of their career working out of North Base until retirement in 1993. Marlyn will be missed by all who knew them. No services have been announced at this time.

Please place these members and their families in your thoughts and hearts

Weingarten Rights and the Principle of

Representation

Another important cornerstone of workplace fairness is Weingarten rights, established by the U.S. Supreme Court in 1975. These rights apply in all unionized workplaces and guarantee:

If an employee reasonably believes a meeting may lead to discipline, they have the right to union representation — and the right to a representative who is allowed to participate meaningfully. Weingarten rights are not merely symbolic.

Courts have repeatedly held that a union representative must be permitted to:

• ask clarifying questions • consult privately with the employee • provide support and guidance • prevent intimidation or confusion
